description: Spin Your Words – Custom Text Grip Fidget Ring This is not just another fidget ring with text on it. This is a fully parametric print-in-place spinner ring where the custom text becomes the actual tactile grip of the rotating outer ring. Instead of using standard grooves, ribs or generic knurling, the external grip is generated directly from your own text, name, brand, nickname, date or message. Your text is not decoration. Your text is the grip. A Personal Message You Can Wear, Touch and Spin Because the grip is generated from custom text, this ring can become much more than a simple fidget toy. It can be a name, a romantic message, a special date, a couple nickname, an inside joke, a maker signature or a short phrase wrapped around a rotating ring. This makes it perfect as a unique personalized gift for someone special. A small object, but with a message built directly into its function. You can turn a name, a date or a love message into a tactile spinning ring. Examples: I LOVE YOU FOREVER YOU & ME MY LOVE ALWAYS LUCA ❤️ SARA SINCE 2024 SPIN MY HEART The message is not hidden inside the model. It is the part you touch, feel and spin. The Key Idea Most fidget rings use a standard external pattern for grip. This model does something different. The outer rotating ring uses raised custom text wrapped around the side surface as the tactile texture. The letters create: the grip the feel the visual identity the personalization So every ring can be different. Minimal, romantic, funny, branded, personal or completely weird: it depends only on the text you choose. Custom Text Becomes Functional Grip The text is placed on the outside of the rotating ring and follows the circular shape of the model. It is not simply stamped on a flat face. It is not just decorative branding. It becomes the surface your fingers touch while spinning the ring. Short texts are automatically repeated around the ring. Longer phrases are repeated only when they fit completely. No broken words. No interrupted messages. Only complete readable text patterns. Main Features Custom text used as tactile grip Print-in-place spinner ring Two-piece rotating structure No assembly required No external knurling Raised side text replaces the grip texture Automatic full-word text repetition No interrupted words or broken phrases Parametric inner diameter Adjustable ring width Adjustable text spacing Adjustable character width Adjustable text relief Adjustable print-in-place clearances Comfort-fit internal profile Chamfered inner edges for easier wearing Supportless design Designed for MakerWorld Customizer Multicolor-ready design Assembly and separate-part export modes What Makes It Different This model combines three things in one object: custom text + functional tactile grip + print-in-place rotating fidget ring The result is a small, simple object with a very clear identity: a personalized spinner ring where the message itself becomes the texture. It is not a ring with a label. It is a ring where the label becomes the grip. Text Ideas You can use names, brands, nicknames, short messages, romantic phrases or maker signatures. Examples: Made by CiCAdesign SPIN YOUR WORDS YOUR TEXT HERE FOCUS RELAX MAKER CREATE CUSTOM I LOVE YOU FOREVER ALWAYS YOU & ME Short words will repeat several times around the ring. Longer phrases will appear only as complete repetitions. Print-in-Place Mechanism The model is made of two separate functional parts printed together: an inner ring that stays fixed an outer ring that rotates around it Both parts rest on the build plate, making the model easier to print without supports. After printing, gently free the outer ring and rotate it gradually until the mechanism becomes smooth. Clearance parameters are available to adapt the model to different printers, materials and calibration levels. Export Modes The Customizer includes different export modes. Use: complete_assembly to generate the full print-in-place ring as one STL. Use the separate modes: inner_ring_only outer_rotating_ring_only text_grip_only to generate the three individual parts separately. The separate-part exports are useful for advanced multicolor workflows where the parts are imported together into the slicer as a single multipart object. Multicolor Printing This model can be printed in two different ways. Single Color Print For a standard single-color print, use the full assembly export and print the STL as it is. No extra steps are required. Select complete_assembly Export STL Import into slicer Print normally This is the simplest option and works like a normal print-in-place fidget ring. Multicolor Print – Single STL Workflow For the quickest multicolor workflow, export the full assembly STL and split it into parts inside Bambu Studio. Recommended workflow: 1. Select complete_assembly 2. Export STL 3. Import the STL into Bambu Studio 4. Right click on the model 5. Select Split 6. Choose Split to Parts 7. Assign a different filament/color to each part 8. Disable Arachne wall generator 9. Use Classic wall generator 10. Slice and print The model is designed to be divided into separate printable parts: inner ring outer rotating ring text grip This allows you to create 2-color or 3-color versions. Examples: outer ring: blue inner ring: light gray text grip: white or: outer ring: black inner ring: gold text grip: ivory or: outer ring: white inner ring: teal text grip: coral Multicolor Print – Separate Part Workflow For the cleanest multicolor setup, you can also export the three parts separately from the same SCAD file. Use: inner_ring_only outer_rotating_ring_only text_grip_only Then import the three generated STL files together into Bambu Studio as a single object with multiple parts. This workflow is useful if you want better control over the three colors and want the slicer to treat each component as a separate part from the beginning. In this workflow, the text grip export is positioned to bond correctly with the outer rotating ring when the parts are imported together. Important Multicolor Note When the complete assembly is split into parts, you may see very thin construction lines connecting the raised letters. These lines are intentional. They are used only to keep the custom text connected as a single selectable text-grip part inside the slicer, instead of having every letter detected as a separate object. These construction lines are necessary for multicolor part detection. They are not intended as visible design details. Do not use Arachne wall generator for multicolor printing. Use Classic wall generator instead. With Arachne enabled, the slicer may try to print these thin construction lines. With Classic wall generator, they should remain non-printable construction geometry and disappear from the final toolpath. So, when using multicolor mode: inner ring = one part outer rotating ring = one part text grip = one connected part This makes it much easier to assign colors in Bambu Studio without selecting every single letter manually. Final practical note: For single-color printing, print the complete assembly normally. For quick multicolor printing, split the complete assembly into parts and assign colors. For advanced multicolor printing, export the three parts separately and import them together as one multipart object. For multicolor printing, use Classic wall generator instead of Arachne. Instructions 🛠️👕 Download the model and open it in Bambu Studio 💻 Print the model using the recommended settings and carefully remove it from the build plate. ⚠️ Handle with care — the model is extremely thin (approximately 0.3 mm) and may tear or deform if bent too aggressively. Set your iron to a very high temperature (almost maximum heat, without steam) 🔥 Allow the iron to fully preheat before starting. Position the printed model on the desired area of the T-shirt and cover it with baking/parchment paper 📄 Apply firm pressure with the preheated iron for 15–20 seconds. description: Give your lost item a way back home FoundIt Halo is a customizable lost-and-found tag designed for backpacks, suitcases and bags. Its simple, universal shape makes it suitable for everyday use, while the QR code connects the finder with the owner through the free FoundIt service. Unlike a traditional tag with a phone number or home address printed on it, FoundIt does not expose the owner’s personal details to everyone nearby. It provides a private way to recover lost belongings without publicly displaying the owner’s or finder’s contact information. How FoundIt works Each tag uses its own individual QR code generated on foundit.cc . When someone finds your item, they can scan the QR code and open a contact form connected to your tag. The finder can: send a message to the owner, attach a photo of the found item, share the exact location where the item is located, optionally provide an email address to enable two-way communication. If the finder confirms their email address, both sides can continue the conversation through FoundIt without revealing their email addresses to each other. The finder does not need to create an account or install an app. Create your own tag FoundIt is completely free and allows each account to create up to 20 tags for personal 3D printing. Before printing: Create a free account at foundit.cc/register . Generate a free tag code. Enter the code in the MakerLab Customizer. Check that the generated QR code opens the correct tag page. Generate and print the model. The visible tag number and the QR code must always use the same FoundIt code. Customization options The model can be adjusted directly in the customizer. You can change: the overall tag size, the position of the text, the attachment-hole style, the edge-rounding style, the printing configuration for the detailed face. The simple shape was designed to remain practical and versatile without limiting the tag to one specific type of item. Example file The included example model uses the tag number: PRM-N2E This is an active public demonstration tag connected to FoundIt. You are welcome to scan it and send a test message to see how the service works. For your own printed tag, replace PRM-N2E with a code generated in your FoundIt account. Recommended print settings Material: PETG Nozzle: 0.4 mm Layer height: 0.2 mm Infill: 60% The model was printed and tested on a Bambu Lab P2S. The printed QR code scanned correctly without any problems. Good contrast between the QR code and the base is strongly recommended. Black and white usually provide the most reliable result. It pairs flawlessly with forest literary fits, minimalist office wear, diving enthusiast outfits and vintage nature styling. Understated and mild for daily work, it harmonizes perfectly with natural themes at art exhibitions or coastal trips. Worn alone, it radiates quiet healing; stacked alongside the collection’s octopus and Medusa rings, it creates striking contrast between soft and bold sculptural layers. Seamless 3D printing ensures uninterrupted fluid lines, while hollow seaweed cutouts balance breathability and artistic detail. Every organic texture is finely refined to replicate authentic marine life. It does not seek dramatic attention; instead, it connects with the wearer through understated natural storytelling, a tiny seagrass bed carried on your fingertip, a portable sculpture to anchor your inner calm. Amid noisy worldly chaos, everyone deserves a quiet resting place beneath the waves. Shaped by a docile manatee and framed by flowing seaweed, Sea Slumber reminds you to move through life with unrushed ease. Within this tiny ring, hold your own gentle, peaceful ocean dream.

3D Printable Replacement Glasses Frame (Custom Fit for Existing Lenses) Description Broke your favorite glasses? Don't throw away those expensive lenses! It embodies dual spiritual meaning: outwardly, the bravery to journey toward distant dreams; inwardly, gentle power for self-protection and inner reconciliation. More than merely a symbol of flight, wings represent the innate strength within every soul to grow upward and transcend limits without external support. Unlike ornate decorative jewellery, Wing Descend adopts minimalist sculptural language to interpret freedom. The unisex design suits all wearers and styling systems. It fits a wide range of scenarios: a subtle, narrative accent for minimalist office looks; harmonising with gothic, vintage and literary aesthetics; standing out at avant-garde art gatherings and creative workplaces. Worn alone, it exudes quiet sophistication; stacked alongside crown and myth sculpture rings from the collection, it builds rich layered accessory styling. Seamless monolithic construction eliminates joint lines, and all feather edges are finely polished smooth, balancing striking sculptural expression with everyday wearability. True freedom comes from the wings grown within your heart. Without ostentatious display, Wing Descend rests lightly on your fingertip, reminding you to preserve passion for the unknown and confidence against worldly restlessness. You do not need to wait for wind — with inner wings, you can reach wherever you yearn to go.

Featured in this Tom's Hardware article . 2.5" SSD Dock + Cartridge System This Collection includes model files for: Inner / Outer Case for the SSD Cartridge (with cutouts for printed artworks) BigDock: Sturdy dock with ball bearings to guide the cartridges in from the front SmallDock: Small, low-profile, simple dock. Cartridge insertion from the top. Blank front plates for both dock versions for your own customization. These docks have been designed with 1 specific USB-to-SATA Adapter in mind: Sabrent (EC-SSHD) Disclaimer SATA data and power connectors are typically rated for 50 to 500 insertion cycles (mating cycles) before pin degradation. Always insert carefully without needing much force. Assembly Notes Cartridges: Because of manufacturing tolerances for SSDs, you might have to put some thin tape on the SSDs before inserting them into the Case. Just make it tight enough of a fit so that the SSDs wont slide out of the case when unplugging from the Dock. The Handle has through holes for screwing in the M3x6 screws to secure the outer case to the inner case. I recommend gluing or double-sided tape the “top end” of the outer casing to the inner casing. Big Dock: Put the Dock into the base first, then slide the Adapter in, and only then screw the adapter cover on. If you put the adapter in the dock first, you won't be able to put the dock into the base. The optional slide guard needs to be glued on or stuck on with thin double-sided tape. The FrontPlate can also be glued on or stuck on with thin double-sided tape. The Bearing Pins is just friction fit to allow easier removal of bearings. They slide in from the bottom. The Dock itself should fit nicely into the base. If it's too lose, feel free to glue down or use double-sided tape. There are 2x M3 holes on the bottom of the dock, in case you want to bolt it down into something. Small Dock: The FrontPlate can also be glued on or stuck on with thin double-sided tape. The Sabrent Adapter only goes in one way. Be mindful when inserting the adapter. Customization Provided are 2 blank front plates (.stp) that you can customize. description: SIMPLE . FLYING . FUN Hummel RC is a simple and fun two-channel RC airplane designed for relaxed flights on a small field. Its modular construction is lightweight, durable and quick to print, with low material use and smooth, stable flight behavior. The adjustable wing position makes CG and pitch tuning easy. Hummel RC continues the ideas of WingStar , COMET , Wespe , SkyStar and DragonFly in a compact and practical RC model made to fly often . 1 - Model Data Wingspan: 405 mm Length: 365 mm Wing chord: 60 mm Model mass (with RC receiver, battery and motors): 43 g. 2 - Equipment RC transmitter and receiver: 2 Channel 2.4G FX803 J3 ( Aliexpress link here ) Battery: 3.7v, 220 mAh, Molex 51005 connector ( Aliexpress link here ) Motors and Props: 2x716 Coreless motors with 2 props diam 46 mm ( Aliexpress link here ) 3 - Materials, Settings, Printing Model design created and tested using Bambu PLA Basi c. Use this material for best results. Do NOT use PLA Matte, especially for the wing parts. Printed parts may deform after removal from the Plate due to internal material strains after cooling. Use recommended print settings. Note: The print profile for A1 mini use slightly higher material flow coefficient (1.03 instead of 0.98). For reliable printing: Clean the printing Plate before printing. After printing, remove the Plate and let it cool for 3-4 minutes Do not remove parts while the Plate is hot. 4 - Model Assembly The model consists of 20 parts, as shown in the figure. 1 – Nose, 2 – PCB Mount, 3 – A-Beam (3pcs), 4 – B-Beam, 5 – Strut (2pcs), 6 – Sting, 7 – Tail, 8 – Fin, 9 – Central Bracket, 10 – Dual-pin, 11 – Right Wing, 12 – Left Wing , 13 – Right Big Rib, 14 – Left Big Rib, 15 – Small Rib (2pcs), 16 – Gear mount, 17 – Gear Strut (2pcs), 18 – Wheel (2pcs), 19 – Pin (2pcs), 20 – BHCS Screw M2 x 4 mm (4 pcs). Note : RC Receiver, Engines, props are not shown. The following assembly steps are shown without the electronic components installed. It is recommended to review them before installing the motors and electronics. Use cyanoacrylate glue where specifically indicated. Assemble the tail unit and fuselage as shown. Assemble the wing as shown in the figure. Use Dual-pin to fix wings. After installing and fixing the wing surfaces, install Big Ribs (13, 14) on both sides. Finally, install the Ribs (15) on both sides. Wing assembly completed. To install the wing on the fuselage, pull the fuselage beam through predefined guide points on the wing Central Bracket, as shown in the picture. A slight pushing force may be gently applied if needed. Assemble landing gear unit as shown on Figure. Install landing gear on Fuselage. To fix finally the wing and landing gear position the M2x4 screws to be installed. Do not fix wing and gear assembly finally on this step! 4.1 - Electronic Components Installation Install RC transmitter PCB on bracket (2). Finally, connect the motors to the receiver board as shown in the illustration. Before final assembly, make sure the motors rotate in opposite directions. For easier assembly and adjustment, the wires should be approximately 130 mm long. The wires are preferable to route through the rib. To install the motor in the rib, gently press it into place and slide it slightly forward until there is no gap. To prevent the motor from rotating during operation, secure it with a small piece of adhesive tape, as shown in the illustration. Install the ribs with the motors onto the wing as shown in the illustration. The motors must be positioned on the outer side of each rib. Install the wing onto the lower beam, approximately at the middle of the span. Then route the motor wires behind the lower beam and around the upper beam in a figure-eight pattern, as shown in the illustration. This routing keeps the wires secure while still allowing the wing position to be adjusted. Only after routing the wires, install the landing gear, followed by the receiver bracket (2). Install the nose part (1) and secure it with screw (20). Install the battery and hold it in place with a suitable rubber band, as shown on picture. The model assembly is now complete. 4.2 - Balancing Perform the pre-flight balancing check with the battery installed. Place the model on a Balancing Stand ( model link here ) using the designated balance points on the wing. The model should remain level or tip slightly nose-down. Fix finally the screws (20) of wing assembly and gear bracket. 5 - Model Flight Launch the model outdoors in calm weather or slight breeze conditions. Recommended wind speed: up to 5 km/h (≈1.4 m/s, ≈2.7 knots) . Always launch the model directly into the wind . Model initially pre-balanced during assembly. Launch the model applying full throttle with a gentle horizontal push. If the model dives strongly, then: Move the wing slightly forward, OR bend the elevator slightly upward. If the model pitches up or stalls, first try reducing the flight speed. If flight speed reduction does not help, then: Move the wing slightly backward, OR bend the elevator slightly downward. Happy Flights and Smooth Landings!

description: Hey everyone, long time no see! Today, I’m introducing my first Cyberbrick creation: the Cyberexcavator. Of course, including its matching remote control. I’ve been eyeing a project like this ever since Cyberbrick was first released. From the very beginning, my plan was to go big and create something truly elaborate. What was also extremely important to me was complete documentation of the entire assembly process. This project is complex and definitely surpasses many other Cyberbrick offerings in its complexity. Nevertheless, everything is explained in such detail in over 100 pages of assembly guide with countless photos, comments, tips, and more that even a dedicated beginner can attempt it! I had always set my sights on an excavator project, but it wasn't until the "Electric Push Rod for Cyberbrick" article was published by Maker Supply, that my ideas finally became feasible. I’ve spent many weeks working on this model - constantly making improvements, printing countless prototypes, going through many spools of filament, and so on. This little excavator handles small stones, sand, and the like with ease, is very precise to control, and of course, it can also pull off the occasional acrobatic maneuver. Here you can see it heading back to where it came from xD. For me, it was exactly the kind of project that’s been "almost finished" for a month and a half, simply because I kept coming up with new ideas! I didn't just want to create a model, but an entire playground - objects that can be interacted with, and so on. I'll tell you a lot more about this model later, but first we have to come to a very important part, which is probably most relevant for most people.: the hardware. To build this model, meaning ONE excavator and ONE remote control including props, you will need the "Cyberbrick Ultimate Hardware Kit ZK003", three "Electric Pushrods PG003", some additional Cyberbrick electronic components, as well as parts such as bearings and screws. To find exactly the items you need, it's best to take a close look at this list (also note the quantities, as some items are needed multiple times): Here, you need to click on „More“ to access the full list. Each thunbnail acts like a link that will guide you to the individual components/kits in the bambu lab store. The desktop version of MakerWorld even has a button that allows you to automatically add all items to your shopping cart - so you don't have to search for everything individually! I tried to keep the number of parts manageable, but this project wouldn't have been possible in this form with the standard kit. What's listed here is precisely what you need to completely recreate the project. The props, which I offer here as a separate profile, naturally don't require any hardware parts and are 100% 3D printed. Though, Not every single part from the Ultimate Hardware Kit is used. So, if you already own some Cyberbrick components, the following list will certainly be helpful to you. I have listed every single component individually here: Article Code Qty. 200mm Servo Extension Cable 3Pin (2PCS) XC011 1 BT2 Socket Head Cap Self Tapping Screws (SHCS) AA193 1 Pack BT3 Socket Head Cap Self Tapping Screws (SHCS) AA112 1 Pack BT3 Socket Head Cap Self Tapping Screws (SHCS) AA108 2 Packs BT3 Socket Head Cap Self Tapping Screws (SHCS) AA201 2 Packs Micro Steel Deep Groove Ball Bearings EA004 5 Packs Wire Pair with SH1.0 IC007 1 030 Micro DC Motor with SH1.0 (2PCS) LA024 2 Packs Dual-axis Plastic Reduction Gear Kit LA017 2 100mm Wire with 2Pin XH2.54 Connectors (2PCS) XC005 2 Packs WS2812 RGB LED with IDC0.8 4PIN (2PCS) KB003 2 Packs Three-Position Rocker Switch Module with 3Pin SH1.0 Connector XA010 1 WS2812 LED Hub with 3Pin SH1.0 Connector (1PCS) XA006 2 14500 7.4V 800mAh Li-ion Battery (1PCS) PC003 4 Momentary Button Module with 2Pin SH1.0 Connector (1PCS) XA008 2 Power Switch Module with 2Pin XH2.54 Connector (1PCS) XA007 4 Dual-Axis Joystick Module with 3Pin SH1.0 Connectors (1PCS) XA011 2 Single-Axis Joystick Module with 3Pin SH1.0 Connector (1PCS) XA009 3 Electric Push Rod PG003 3 Remote Control Transmitter Shield (1PCS) XA005 2 Remote Control Receiver Shield (1PCS) XA004 2 Multi-Function Core Board (1PCS) XA003 4 D4x2 mm Round Magnet (20PCS) CA001 2 Packs However, if you don't own any of the parts yet , it is more cost-effective to order according to the official bill of materials that is found in this post. I’ve looked into this closely, so don't go to the trouble of recalculating it yourself :)f Now that we have discussed everything regarding the hardware, we can return to the model and what makes it special. My idea for the "Cyberexcavator" was to have two completely independently controllable sections: a tracked drive unit and a turret with an excavator arm, each equipped with its own receiver. Why? Because this eliminates the need for cables running between the two sections, allowing the turret to rotate continuously without restriction. This was quite a challenge, as I wanted to keep the model as compact as possible so the scale would align reasonably well with the electric push rods. It was difficult because I had to fit a significant amount of electronics into a very tight space. For me, it was out of the question to design a nice-looking exterior shell while the interior was a chaotic mess of cables and components; every single part has a designated spot where it is securely mounted. The exact same applies to the remote control. I originally designed the drive train with TPU tracks. These offer a bit more grip and deliver the best performance for climbing maneuvers. However, the excavator doesn't spin quite as quickly on the spot with them. The increased friction makes it harder for the tracks to slide across the surface, depending on the terrain you're driving on. For this reason—and because I know many people are hesitant to work with TPU, I also designed a PLA track. After quite a few attempts, I created a version that I personally like even better than the TPU one. It allows for very precise and relatively snappy movement. Pivoting on the spot works wonderfully, even on soft surfaces like a sofa, carpet, or similar. The video where I climb onto the A1 Mini with it, features the PLA tracks; it still works very well, though it requires a bit more finesse with the controls :) Here you can take a look at the various prototypes and part versions that were printed to ensure everything is absolutely right! I decided to set up my main print profile with the PLA tracks. You can find the TPU tracks in a separate profile. However, those require different drive sprockets—which you'll also need to print—and these are included in that profile as well. I cover this in more detail in the assembly guide! I personally really like this part—the turntable that sits between the upper and lower sections of the excavator. It is printed "in place." The outer ring has an internal thread that engages with the corresponding pinion gear on a servo later on. Although I have already noted this in the print plate labels, please do not print this part using matte or fiber-reinforced (CF/GF) filaments. This part requires a filament that produces a smooth surface! For all other parts, the choice of material is technically quite flexible. All battery compartments on this model, as well as on the remote control, are magnetic. For the excavator, the entire upper body section is simply removed, which also provides good access to other components if needed. The powertrain battery can be accessed via a small flap in the base plate, which is also designed as a print-in-place part. It’s much the same story with the remote control. Incidentally, I opted against the disposable battery cases included in the "Ultimate Hatdware Kit" and instead installed rechargeable batteries from the "Cyberbrick" range. I feel that disposable batteries have no place in applications like this in 2026, and it pays for itself very quickly in terms of cost, too. I probably spent two days working on the back section of the remote control alone. Batteries are installed on both sides, each powering a transmitter module. It, too, is printed "in place"—essentially in its closed state. This part gives the remote control an even more industrial look, which is exactly what I’m aiming for. If you have large hands, you might curse a bit here and there when plugging in the batteries—like I do—since it’s all pretty tight. But with some light and a little practice, I can manage it in two seconds now. Here are a few examples of the excavator's controls and functions: The general lighting can be adjusted to two levels and, of course, switched off completely to save battery power. To capture that authentic construction site feel, there is naturally a hazard warning light system, as well as a button that sets the front LEDs to run at full power. You only need the left stick to control the tank tracks. With a bit of finesse - which most people will surely pick up quickly, the model handles beautifully and precisely. There is the most to say about controlling the arm and the bucket, and consequently, there are the most controls for them. When pushed up or down, the right main joystick functions to retract or extend the arm as a whole. The three elements at the bottom control the individual parts of the arm independently. The clue is that identical inputs to the transmitter cancel each other out. This means, for example, that one of the arm segments can be "frozen" while operating the main joystick simply by engaging one of the small levers. Here, for instance, you can see how I achieve a fairly authentic-looking "digging motion" by combining the main stick with the small left lever. By combining the main stick and the small middle lever, for example, you can easily create a movement that allows the excavator to lift itself up. That is exactly what I do in the video when climbing onto the A1 Mini. When I play around with the unit, I hardly ever use more than two levers at a time for the arm—that makes the whole thing relatively simple! However, you can also make fine adjustments to the individual arm segments at any time. I hope you now have a good idea of what to expect from this model—but feel free to reach out via the comments if anything is unclear! The full Assembly guide can be found as a PDF in the „Assembly Guide“ section! In conclusion, I would aslo like to say a few things about printing: This project includes some very small parts—such as the printed dowel pins, which are only 2mm wide, used to assemble the excavator arm. It is therefore crucial that your print bed is very clean before printing this model! I used standard PLA for these profiles, but I am confident that most materials would perform well here, depending on your intended use for the model. For home use, PLA is perfectly adequate. If you plan to use the excavator outdoors, you might want to use a material like ASA. However, keep in mind that you may need to scale up the parts to compensate for shrinkage. As I mentioned earlier—and in the assembly instructions— material choice is most critical for the turntable component. It is not necessarily about the base material itself; PLA, PETG, ABS, ASA, pure nylon, and many others would all work well. However, you should absolutely avoid printing this part using a material with a matte or rough surface finish. So, no matte PLA, no CF/GF (carbon or glass fiber), no glow-in-the-dark, and no sparkle filaments. Basically, nothing containing particles or fibers, and nothing with a matte finish. Please make sure to heed this advice! Otherwise, the servo driving the turntable will immediately let you know that it really doesn't appreciate the increased friction! Aside from that, I’d say this is a relatively easy model to print. Yes, it’s a multi-color print involving quite a few color changes, but even on a single-nozzle machine, the print time doesn't increase excessively, because it is already an extensive print anyway. When printing the lower section of the excavator tower or the decor elelents using a single-nozzle printer, you should either choose a color combination where the contrast in brightness isn't too extreme—unlike yellow and black—or increase purge volumes accordingly to prevent color bleed. Here is an example comparison image showing what can happen if insufficient material is purged during a color change, or when two materials with high contrast are used together. Feel free to let me know if you’d like to see a "no-AMS" profile. However, I do think the model loses a lot of its appeal without the multi-color aspect. The two main parts of the remote control—the housing and the faceplate—require a fair amount of support material. That said, almost all the less-than-perfect areas will be completely hidden once the model is assembled. I’m also considering offering a profile that uses a support interface; please let me know if there’s any interest in that. I really enjoy using those materials myself, though I realize it’s still somewhat of a niche practice. Be prepared to invest a fair amount of time if you want to slice this model yourself (starting from the provided STEP file). The model contains various "print-in-place" objects that first need to be isolated using the "Split to Parts" function, and so on. Therefore, if you wish to make any modifications, I recommend using my 3MF files as a starting point.This project includes some very small parts—such as the printed dowel pins, which are only 2mm wide, used to assemble the excavator arm. It is therefore crucial that your print bed is very clean before printing this model! I hope you like the project and have fun building and playing with it. Feel free to let me know if you’d like to see more Cyberbrick projects. However, my main focus—printer accessories—will remain, so don't worry :) Kind regards, Simon, Made In Meidling I

description: This is my take on a motorized shade solution for automating existing roller-style shades. This works with traditional cordless roller shades (the spring loaded type that you pull down). Its based around a relatively cheap aliexpress geared brushless motor with an encoder driven by an esp32 for use with ESPHome and HomeAssistant. The finished product is capable of accurate positional control and uses a reed switch at the full open position to re-home the system each time the shade is fully opened. They are relatively quiet, very reliable and operate on 12v DC power. You will have to attach a small magnet to the shade (with tape or something). Here is the Bill of Materials: Item Qty Links Socket head cap M3x6 7 Socket head cap M2x4 7 Small Neodymium Magnet 1 CHR-GM25-BL2418 DC12V i34 (130rpm variant) 1 Link Alibaba (cheaper for bulk) MKA17101 Reed Switch NO 1 Link 5v Buck Converter 1 Link 3x7cm Protoboards 1 Link ESP32 1 Link 608 2RS Ball Bearing 1 Link The more of these you build the cheaper they are per unit because you end up buying the smaller components in bulk anyways. If you make 5 of them they end up being around $25 each. Use Alibaba for the motors if ordering more than one or two. In theory you probably don't need a protoboard if you really want to cut costs. There are two versions of the printed files, one with holes sized for heat-set inserts and one with holes meant to be directly threaded into. Here is a diagram of the wiring: Push the reed switch as much towards the esp32 (into the page) as possible to get it closest to the magnet that you will attach to the shade. When attaching the magnet to the shade, it works best if it is mounted sideways rather than flat. Here is a picture of how I did it, and so far it has never failed to home properly after a month of use. Wherever you place it will determine the stopping point of the shade. Magnet on back side of shade The bottom endpoint is configurable inside home assistant. The only issue I have run into is drift over many cycles if the shade isn't homed for a while (eg. 50% →0% → 50%) over and over without fully opening. This happens only when the shade travels down at full speed and abruptly stops. If you add a ramp and run it downwards at around 80% speed there will be no drift even after 20+ cycles. The YAML included has many customizable parameters related to this. Without the ramp function at the end and at full speed, after around 20 ish cycles it will drift downwards about an inch. Even still, as long as they are opened fully periodically, this will never be a problem. Assembly should be pretty straightforward if you follow the exploded view diagram. The gear shroud needs to be snapped on and might require some force, Its not meant to come off again without breaking. I've also included a version of the wall plate with different mounting points for shallower window frames and the hanger I used for the other end of the shade. You may also need to make a different size shade insert to fit in your particular tube. If you leave a comment with the inner diameter of your tube i can add more variants. That's it! Happy printing!

Most 3D-printed phone docks with "speakers" sound pretty bad. They usually just punch a straight, hollow cone into a block of plastic, which traps the low frequencies and makes your phone sound like it’s playing out of a tin can. I wanted a dock that actually worked, and I wanted it to look like a piece of high-end vintage audio gear on my desk. The Monolith hides a mathematically calculated, 100mm exponential horn inside a solid, minimalist block. Instead of just bouncing sound forward, the internal sweep acts as a true acoustic transformer—just like an old-school gramophone. It physically amplifies the volume and actually brings back the warmth and bass of your phone's speaker without using any electricity. Because phone cases make finding a good dock impossible, I built this to be fully parametric in MakerLab. There's pre-sets for different phones with and without phone cases and I also allow for custom measurements. Just hit the Customize button . Features Fits Your Exact Phone Setup: No more wobbly phones or slots that are too tight. Pick your phone model from the dropdown, then choose your case type (Bare Phone, Slim Case, or Heavy Duty Armor). The customizer calculates the exact tolerances so your phone slides in perfectly. Audiophile vs. Charging Mode: By default, the acoustic chamber is sealed airtight for maximum volume. But if you’d rather use this as an overnight charging dock, just check the "Enable Charging Channel" box. It routes a massive 16mm internal tunnel that easily swallows thick, braided USB-C cables. Supported Device Presets The Monolith's customizer includes precise base dimensions (Width x Thickness) for the following devices. You can select your exact phone model and then pair it with your case type for a perfect fit. Apple iPhone 17 Series iPhone 17 Pro Max: 77.6 mm x 8.3 mm iPhone 17 Pro: 71.5 mm x 8.3 mm iPhone 17: 71.5 mm x 8.0 mm iPhone Air: 74.7 mm x 5.6 mm Apple iPhone 16 Series iPhone 16 Pro Max: 77.6 mm x 8.25 mm iPhone 16 Pro: 71.5 mm x 8.25 mm iPhone 16: 71.6 mm x 7.8 mm Apple iPhone 15 Series iPhone 15 Pro Max: 76.7 mm x 8.25 mm iPhone 15 Pro: 70.6 mm x 8.25 mm iPhone 15: 71.6 mm x 7.8 mm Google Pixel Series (Note: All Pixel presets automatically generate an additional 2.5mm of pocket depth to allow the camera visor to sit flush without snagging). Pixel 10 Pro XL: 76.6 mm x 8.5 mm Pixel 10: 72.2 mm x 8.5 mm Pixel 9 Pro XL: 76.6 mm x 8.5 mm Pixel 9 Pro: 72.0 mm x 8.5 mm Pixel 9: 72.0 mm x 8.5 mm Samsung Galaxy Series Galaxy S26 Ultra: 79.0 mm x 8.6 mm Custom Devices Don't see your phone? Select the Custom option in the dropdown and manually enter your phone's width and thickness! Case Allowances Once you select your phone model, choose your case style. The generator automatically adds the necessary tolerances to your phone's base dimensions: Bare Phone: Adds +0.5 mm clearance for a snug, scratch-free fit. Slim Case: Adds +5.0 mm clearance for standard silicone and leather cases. Heavy Duty Armor: Adds +12.0 mm clearance for rugged, multi-layer cases. Print Instructions (Read Before Slicing!) Supports: OFF. Seriously, do not use supports. If you do, the slicer will fill the internal acoustic chamber with grid plastic, and you will never get it out. The printer will bridge the internal gaps on its own. Infill: 10% Rectilinear is fine. Walls: 2 walls min but 3 walls is default (better acoustics). Denser plastic means less sound bleeds through the sides, forcing all the audio energy out the front bell. Drop a make if you print one, and let me know how it sounds!

description: FlightScnr Pi A flight tracker for Raspberry Pi built for the Waveshare 4in touch display. The on-device UI is modeled after my other project, FlightScnr : dark radar aesthetic, animated sweep, map tiles, and gesture navigation. A built-in web portal configures everything from your phone or laptop on the same network. What it does FlightScnr Pi shows live aircraft around your pre set location on a circular radar, with rich flight details when you tap a plane. It combines FlightRadar24 (FR24) , live positions from adsb.fi (free cloud feed — no local ADS-B dongle), Tomorrow.io weather , and optional AirLabs schedule data. Rohradapter / Reduzierstück mit 45°-Übergang Der Rohradapter verbindet zwei unterschiedliche Rohrdurchmesser miteinander. Zwischen den beiden geraden Rohrabschnitten befindet sich ein automatisch berechneter, konischer Übergang mit einer Flankensteigung von 45° . Der Adapter kann sowohl als Reduzierstück als auch als Vergrößerungsstück verwendet werden. Sind beide Durchmesser identisch, entsteht automatisch ein gerades Rohrstück. Einstellbare Parameter diameter_1 – Außendurchmesser der ersten Seite diameter_2 – Außendurchmesser der zweiten Seite thickness – Wandstärke des Adapters length – Länge jedes geraden Rohrabschnitts bis zum 45°-Übergang Die Länge des konischen Übergangs wird automatisch anhand der beiden Durchmesser berechnet. Wichtig diameter_1 und diameter_2 beziehen sich auf die Außendurchmesser des gedruckten Adapters . Die jeweiligen Innendurchmesser ergeben sich aus: Innendurchmesser = Außendurchmesser − 2 × Wandstärke Der Begriff „45°“ beschreibt hier den konischen Übergang zwischen den Durchmessern und nicht eine Richtungsänderung des Rohres. Geeignet für Rohrreduzierungen und Rohrerweiterungen Absaug- und Lüftungsleitungen Schlauch- und Geräteanschlüsse Werkstattadapter individuelle Übergangsstücke 2. Parametrischer Rohrwinkel Das zweite Modell erzeugt ein gebogenes, hohles Rohrstück mit frei einstellbarer Richtungsänderung. Dadurch können beispielsweise 30°-, 45°-, 60°- oder 90°-Winkel erstellt werden. Auf beiden Seiten des Bogens befindet sich ein gerader Rohrabschnitt mit identischer Länge. Einstellbare Parameter diameter – Außendurchmesser des Rohrwinkels thickness – Wandstärke des Rohrwinkels length – gerade Rohrlänge je Seite, gemessen ab dem Bogen angle – gewünschte Richtungsänderung in Grad Der Biegeradius wird automatisch passend zum eingestellten Rohrdurchmesser erzeugt. Wichtig diameter bezeichnet den Außendurchmesser des gedruckten Rohrwinkels . Der Innendurchmesser ergibt sich aus: Innendurchmesser = diameter − 2 × thickness Der Parameter length gilt für beide Seiten einzeln. Bei einer Einstellung von 30 mm besitzt der Winkel daher vor und nach dem Bogen jeweils einen geraden Rohrabschnitt von 30 mm. Geeignet für Rohrleitungen mit individuellen Winkeln Absaug- und Belüftungssysteme Kabel- oder Schlauchführungen Modellbau Prototypen und Sonderlösungen 3. Rohrbefestigung für die Wand Das dritte Modell ist eine U- beziehungsweise Omega-förmige Rohrhalterung. Das Rohr wird vom gebogenen Bereich umschlossen, während die beiden nach außen umgeklappten Enden an einer Wand oder einer anderen ebenen Fläche befestigt werden können. In den beiden Befestigungslaschen befinden sich Schraublöcher. Einstellbare Parameter diameter – Außendurchmesser des zu befestigenden Rohres thickness – Materialstärke der Halterung width – Breite der Halterung entlang des Rohres Die Länge der beiden Befestigungslaschen wird automatisch an den Rohrdurchmesser angepasst. Passung und Schraublöcher Das Modell besitzt standardmäßig ein radiales Spiel von ungefähr 0,4 mm . Dadurch ist der Innendurchmesser der Halterung etwa 0,8 mm größer als der eingestellte Rohrdurchmesser. Hinweise zum 3D-Druck Für normale Anwendungen eignen sich PLA oder PETG. Für wärmere Umgebungen, Werkstätten oder Bereiche mit höherer mechanischer Belastung ist PETG, ASA oder ein vergleichbar widerstandsfähiges Material meist besser geeignet. Fully printed system to make plaster moulds. This produces a 4-part mould (3 sides and a small insert for the base) to cast round tumblers/mugs with a smooth design. You need to cast plaster in the larger mould three times for the sides, for every one cast of the small insert. This gives a complete plaster mould. This print has been scaled to 112% to account for clay shrinkage, with most casting slips this should give a final tumbler size of 6.5cm diameter and 7cm height, or a capacity of around 150ml. With any fully 3D printed mould, you’ll benefit from using a release agent on the base plate surface. I use a generic mouldmaker’s soap, but any product designed for plaster release should be fine. It needs around 350ml of plaster for the side pieces and around 75ml for the base insert, and you can calculate the weight of water and plaster needed with this tool: Plaster Calculator You can get a much better cast surface, even if your plaster mix is full of air bubbles, by using a paintbrush to dislodge any trapped air from the surface. I would suggest that you pour plaster until the ornament surface is covered but it isn’t completely full, then get a relatively small paintbrush and move it around in the plaster so that you’re brushing all of the details on the base plate surface. This will dislodge air bubbles, and once dislodged they’ll float upwards. Once you’ve finished this, pour in the rest of the plaster. If you manage to avoid adding more air as you do it (just brush gently), you’ll eventually remove all the bubbles from the surface and get a perfect cast. This uses the updated 3 part mould design, which is compatible with other updated 3 part moulds but not the original ornament moulds. This new design has slots added to the back to allow the mould to bend slightly when releasing the plaster, making the process much easier.

Here's my take on a guitar → hurdy gurdy style conversion kit. This is a v1.0 release, so I would love to hear your feedback on improvements. You will need to source o-rings and dark rosin to use this as intended. I highly suggest checking out assembly instructions to make things clear on how to properly mount it without damaging anything on your guitar. How it works: It' fastened to the bottom and top string of your guitar and plays on the four middle strings using two o-rings coated with rosin. This creates friction which then vibrate the strings when cranking the wheel. Tips: Using rosin on the o-rings is required, it won't work well without it. Check out part list for more details. It's easier to tune the strings after you've installed the o-rings and before you assemble the Gurdy Wheel. DADA tuning works great, as well as GDAE. Extras: If your guitar has a pick guard, you can print out the + 2mm height foot to offset the height difference. If you need more tension on the o-rings you can use two +2 mm feet instead of the default ones. To apply rosin to the o-rings, use sandpaper or a knife to break up the rosin and slide the o-rings gently across the surface to coat them. Print out TPU feet if you are having issues with movement of the whole assembly when cranking. Also protects your guitar body. O-rings can possibly be printed and are provided with the print profile, but would need to be as soft as possible, as industry o-rings tend to be around 60-70A on the shore hardness scale. I've tried with 95A and that did not work. You can print the bearings and screw if you don't have the hardware available, but I highly recommend steel bearings and bolt for less play between the parts. model_name: Rope Paracord Ratchet Tensioner Outdoor Tie-Down
description: A fully 3D-printed rope ratchet tensioner that tightens your line one satisfying click at a time, and releases with a thumb press. No knots, no fiddling, no metal ratchet wheel to source. Pull the cord, let the ratchet do the holding, and dial in tension with one hand. Inspired by the little aluminum rope-tensioner pulleys you see on tent guylines and grow-light hangers, but reimagined so almost everything comes off your printer . The grip comes from the cord wrapping the knurled wheel (capstan effect) combined with a directional ratchet that only lets the wheel turn one way. Honest performance - Read this first I test my functional models to failure and I tell you the real numbers, not marketing ones. Recommended working load: 3–4 kg (or 20+ kg with a backup knot, read below). Slip point observed in my tests: 5–7 kg , depending on the cord. It does not break under load, when overloaded, the cord slips on the wheel rather than the part snapping. The limiting factor is grip between cord and printed wheel , not the mechanism (the ratchet and clicker themselves hold far more). A steel wheel like the commercial versions grips harder, a printed wheel can't fully match that, and that's the honest trade-off of an all-printed design. Tip to squeeze out more grip: printing the wheel in a slightly abrasive or matte/porous filament increases surface friction and can push the slip point higher. Smooth glossy filament grips the least. Tension is cord-dependent, different cord material, diameter and sheath change the grip. Always test with your own cord before trusting a load. Backup stopper knot — a big safety margin Here's the trick that changes the game for the rare high-load moment: tie a simple stopper knot on the tail (the free end running through). If the cord ever starts to slip, the knot jams against the tensioner and can't pass, and from that point the load is carried by the structure of the part , not by friction grip. In my own testing, with a backup knot I pulled it to 20 kg one-handed with zero drama, and that was the limit of what I could safely pull by hand, not the limit of the part. Beyond that it's the shell and anchor taking the load, and there's clearly more headroom. Real-world use: tensioning a line with a backup stopper knot on the tail for extra security. With a backup stopper knot, it held 20+ kg in hand-testing without failure Where it works well (≈3–4 kg working) Tent and tarp guylines - the core use Tarp ridgelines , camp clotheslines, drying lines Hanging grow lights, lanterns, camp lights (1–3 kg) - the classic rope-ratchet job Hanging planters, bird feeders / birdhouses Backpack compression and lashing light gear Kayak / canoe deck rigging for light gear Tensioning banners, bunting, light signs, shade cloth, awnings Where NOT to use it (please respect this) ❌ Climbing or anything a person hangs from, never. This is not safety equipment. ❌ Hammock body (80–150 kg). Tarp suspension over a hammock is fine; the hammock itself is not. ❌ Primary vehicle / roof cargo tie-down. Use as a light positioning aid only, never as the load-bearing restraint. ❌ Leash or tie-out for medium/large dogs, a single lunge exceeds the working load instantly. ❌ Anything overhead where a drop could injure someone or damage something. Print settings Layer height: 0.16 mm, or adaptive (adaptive is set in the included profile), this matters for the printed closure-screw threads to come out clean. Fully printed system to make plaster moulds. This produces a 4-part mould (3 sides and a small insert for the base) to cast round tumblers/mugs with an angular design. You need to cast plaster in the larger mould three times for the sides, for every one cast of the small insert. This gives a complete plaster mould. This print has been scaled to 112% to account for clay shrinkage, with most casting slips this should give a final tumbler size of 6.5cm diameter and 7cm height, or a capacity of around 150ml. With any fully 3D printed mould, you’ll benefit from using a release agent on the base plate surface. I use a generic mouldmaker’s soap, but any product designed for plaster release should be fine. It needs around 350ml of plaster for the side pieces and around 75ml for the base insert, and you can calculate the weight of water and plaster needed with this tool: Plaster Calculator You can get a much better cast surface, even if your plaster mix is full of air bubbles, by using a paintbrush to dislodge any trapped air from the surface. I would suggest that you pour plaster until the ornament surface is covered but it isn’t completely full, then get a relatively small paintbrush and move it around in the plaster so that you’re brushing all of the details on the base plate surface. This will dislodge air bubbles, and once dislodged they’ll float upwards. Once you’ve finished this, pour in the rest of the plaster. If you manage to avoid adding more air as you do it (just brush gently), you’ll eventually remove all the bubbles from the surface and get a perfect cast. This uses the updated 3 part mould design, which is compatible with other updated 3 part moulds but not the original ornament moulds. This new design has slots added to the back to allow the mould to bend slightly when releasing the plaster, making the process much easier.

Oscillating Desktop Fan – 3D Printable Design This project is a compact oscillating desktop fan designed for 3D printing. It uses two 12V fans, adjustable fan speed control, and an automatic left-to-right oscillation mechanism. The vertical angle of the fan can be adjusted manually. The airflow speed can be controlled using the knob located on the side of the body. The oscillation mechanism is powered by a small N20 geared motor, providing a slow and smooth left-to-right movement. Features Automatic left-to-right oscillation Adjustable fan speed Manually adjustable vertical angle Compact desktop design Two 12V fans 3D printable body and mechanical parts Easy access to the controls and electronic components Suitable for desks, workshops, and hobby rooms Electronic Components 2 × 12V fans N20 6V 30 RPM geared motor DC-DC step-down converter PWM fan speed controller 12V power supply On/off switches Wires, screws, and basic electronic components I used an N20 6V 30 RPM geared motor for the oscillation mechanism. The motor is powered at approximately 3V through a DC-DC step-down converter. In my setup, 3V provides a suitable and balanced oscillation speed. The motor can also be operated at 3V, 3.5V, or 4V depending on the desired movement speed. Increasing the voltage will increase the oscillation speed. You can also use an N20 10 RPM or 15 RPM geared motor if one is available. Since lower-RPM motors may behave differently depending on the applied voltage, I recommend testing the motor speed before completing the final assembly. Electrical Wiring I recommend connecting the 12V power input to the switches first, and then distributing power from the outputs of the switches to the relevant components. With this wiring method, no power will be supplied to the fans, speed controller, step-down converter, or other electronic components when the switches are turned off. In my video, I distributed the power before the switches. However, for anyone building the project, placing the switches between the 12V input and the electronic components is the better wiring method. The general connection order should be: 12V power input → Switches → Related circuits and components This prevents unnecessary power consumption and ensures that the connected circuits are not continuously powered when the switches are off. Printing Notes I divided the project into a total of six build plates. The plates are named according to the type of print surface that should be used. In the project files: Plates named Smooth Plate should be printed on a smooth print surface. Plates named Textured Plate should be printed on a textured print surface. It is especially important to print certain sliding, rotating, or contact parts on a Smooth Plate. These parts require smooth contact surfaces for the oscillation mechanism to operate correctly. If the contact surfaces are too rough, the additional friction may cause: Excessive load on the N20 motor Irregular oscillation movement The mechanism to jam The motor to become unable to move the mechanism For this reason, please check the build plate names carefully before printing and use the specified print surface. Most parts can be printed using PLA or PETG. PETG is recommended for parts located close to the motor or electronic components, especially if the fan will be operated for extended periods. I recommend keeping the prepared print orientations and plate layouts where possible. However, always check support requirements and inspect the slicer preview before starting the print. Assembly and Mechanism Notes Depending on your printer calibration and dimensional tolerances, some parts may require light sanding or minor adjustment. All moving, rotating, and contacting areas of the oscillation mechanism should be lightly lubricated using a plastic-compatible lubricant. Pay particular attention to: Rotating connection points Shaft and bearing areas Plastic surfaces that slide against each other Moving joints in the oscillation mechanism Only apply enough lubricant to create a thin layer on the contact surfaces. Excessive lubrication is not necessary. Make sure that the lubricant is safe for plastic parts. After completing the assembly, check the following: The oscillation mechanism should move freely when operated by hand Moving parts should not rub against the housing Fan wires should not restrict the oscillation movement Wires should not enter or become trapped inside moving parts The motor should be mounted securely Screws in moving joints should not be overtightened Electrical connections should be properly insulated The mechanism should not jam at the left or right movement limits Before powering the motor, move the mechanism slowly by hand and check for excessive friction, resistance, or jamming. If the mechanism does not move freely by hand, do not operate it with the motor. First locate the source of the friction or obstruction. Lightly sand the contact surfaces if necessary and apply lubricant again. Important This project requires basic knowledge of electronics, soldering, and mechanical assembly. Before connecting the power supply, always check the voltage, polarity, and all electrical connections. During the first test, operate the oscillation motor at a low voltage and make sure that the mechanism moves freely. Do not leave the device unattended during the initial tests. Feel free to share your prints, improvements, and modifications on MakerWorld. I would be happy to see your version of the fan.

Fully printed system to make plaster moulds. This produces a 4-part mould (3 sides and a small insert for the base) to cast round tumblers/mugs with a smooth design. You need to cast plaster in the larger mould three times for the sides, for every one cast of the small insert. This gives a complete plaster mould. This print has been scaled to 112% to account for clay shrinkage, with most casting slips this should give a final tumbler size of 6.5cm diameter and 7cm height, or a capacity of around 150ml. With any fully 3D printed mould, you’ll benefit from using a release agent on the base plate surface. I use a generic mouldmaker’s soap, but any product designed for plaster release should be fine. It needs around 350ml of plaster for the side pieces and around 75ml for the base insert, and you can calculate the weight of water and plaster needed with this tool: Plaster Calculator You can get a much better cast surface, even if your plaster mix is full of air bubbles, by using a paintbrush to dislodge any trapped air from the surface. I would suggest that you pour plaster until the ornament surface is covered but it isn’t completely full, then get a relatively small paintbrush and move it around in the plaster so that you’re brushing all of the details on the base plate surface. This will dislodge air bubbles, and once dislodged they’ll float upwards. Once you’ve finished this, pour in the rest of the plaster. If you manage to avoid adding more air as you do it (just brush gently), you’ll eventually remove all the bubbles from the surface and get a perfect cast. This uses the updated 3 part mould design, which is compatible with other updated 3 part moulds but not the original ornament moulds. This new design has slots added to the back to allow the mould to bend slightly when releasing the plaster, making the process much easier.

Microgroove turns the $30 M5Stack Cardputer-ADV into a four-track groovebox: three synth tracks (each switchable between a mono 303-style voice with slide & accent, and 3-voice polyphony for chords), eight drum lanes of 808/909 synthesis or sample playback, live mic sampling, and resampling of its own output. This listing is the shell and keycap label system that makes it playable — the free, open-source firmware lives on GitHub: https://github.com/matoslav/MicroGroove It fits the M5Stack Cardputer- ADV specifically. The screen, USB-C port, and headphone jack all stay fully accessible after the swap. Printing Print with a 0.2 mm nozzle (strongly recommended). A 0.4 mm nozzle works, but the fine label text won't come out clean. The parts: Top + label top — the two-piece face. The label top is multi-color (blue / red / white). Keys — the keycaps, also multi-color. Bottom — optional. Table stand and box with instructions — optional extras. The label top and keys need a multi-color setup (AMS / multi-material or manual filament swaps). If you only print in one color, you'll still get a working shell, just without the colored labels. Assembly Glue the top and the label top together, slide in the keys, and swap the assembly for the original top your Cardputer-ADV came with. Two screws hold it in place — gluing the two face pieces matters because without it the edges lift. What the firmware does Three acid synth voices — saw/square/tri/sine plus 16 wavetables through a resonant 303 filter. Flip any track from mono squelch to 3-voice chords. Eight drum lanes — 808 and 909 synthesis or your own samples, side by side. Tune, decay, and choke each one. Sample the room — hold one key, watch the level meter, release. It's already playing on a lane. Resample yourself — bounce the live mix onto a pad and build the next layer on top. Sequence and arrange — 8 patterns of 16 steps, clone with a hold, chain up to 64 into a full song. Ready to play out of the box — the SD image on GitHub ships a five-pattern demo track and a CC0 sample pack.

description: LUX3: A Minimal Case for the Xteink X3 Credits This design was inspired by the Retro X3 Case and Xteink X4 Full Body Case . Though I designed all geometry from scratch in Fusion 360, I wanted to give credit where it's due, since the overall concept and vibe started with their work. Go check out their cases! The Pokédex style wallpaper shown in my photos were generated here . Because they only export in a size for X4 devices, I did have to expand the artwork to properly fit my X3. About the Case LUX3 is a rounded, minimalist case built specifically for the Xteink X3 e-reader. This case intentionally covers several parts of the device (reset button, micro SD card slot, and lanyard holes) to keep it looking and feeling as clean as possible (depending on feedback, Im open to making an alternative version where all of these are exposed and usable with the case on the device). The lower back portion of the case has a subtle arch/contour pattern for grip and visual interest without breaking the minimal look. It's a snap-fit case, so no adhesives or hardware is required. It's designed to clsoely hug the X3's body while still being easy to get on and off. Known Issues / Printing Notes In general, this case has a lot of tight tolerances because I wanted it to feel premium. That said, some of the tight tolerances around the button cutouts can cause issues depending on your printer's calibration. Slight scaling of certain parts (1-2%) may be needed depending on your setup. There are a lot of small details to this case that allow it to snap/fit together well, which means that it may take a few prints to get one coming out clean. Because of this, I highly recommend printing at a .1mm layer height (.4 nozel is fine). Some of the rounded parts on the front of the case can have a very slight blob effect due to how 3D printers fill tight spaces with filament. Though its expected, its not intended and I hope to resolve this in the future. A V2 may be in the works to address tolerance consistency and simplify the button cutout geometry depending on any feedback here! Assembly Guide Place and press the front buttons into the front case part. Insert the X3 screen down and then the side button with the extended lip facing down (towards the front of the device). Then slide the top back half on the case using the guide rails on the side. Finally, slide on the bottom back half until it snaps in place with the top back half. Misc. Notes The case in the photos was all printed with Bambu Labs PLA To customize colors, just add a print place to the file and print some of the part separately to mix and match different colors together Because their are small parts to print, make sure you clean that print bed before printing! Id love to hear feedback on this and how it can be improved for future versions. Thanks everyone and happy reading!

Hallo an alle die den EduColon Kapselautomaten gedruckt haben oder drucken wollen, (übrigens die Fensterteile findet ihr hier: https://makerworld.com/de/models/3020347-3d-window-parts-for-the-educolon-vending-machine#profileId-3393353 ) Mein Upgrade ist passend für: https://makerworld.com/de/models/1646388-remixed-full-vending-machine-200-scale#profileId-1740186 von Naddou oder https://makerworld.com/de/models/1258546-remixed-capsule-holder-for-200-scale-educolon?from=search#profileId-1282437 von Amenthyst3D. Ich habe ihn auch voller Freude gedruckt und musste schnell feststellen, dass ein paar Verbesserungen nötig sind um den Funktionsbereich zu erweitern, die Haltbarkeit des Materials zu verlängern und mehr Coins einwerfen zu können. Als erstes stellte ich fest, dass das innen liegende Fach, welches die Coins auffängt, ein sehr kleines Volumen hat. Die Coins an sich sind ja schon mit fast 5cm im Durchmesser und 6mm dicke recht klobig und groß. So kam es bei uns nahezu immer vor, dass schon nach etwa 5 Münzeinwürfen, der Münzausgang versperrt war. Die Münze blieb dann einfach unten stecken und es verklemmte sich entweder das Drehrad, oder die Münze blieb stecken und drehte einfach durch und fuhr noch einmal mit. Das sah dann so aus: Eine sehr ungünstige Situation, gerade weil ich es für Kinder gedruckt habe und das Drehen immer leichtgängig sein muss. Dreht man dennoch mit Gewalt weiter, so bricht die Mechanik die vom Drehrad gesteuert wird und man muss den Automaten wieder mühevoll auseinander nehmen und das Teil ersetzen. Die andere Option, wenn der Coin mehrfach seine Runden in der Mechanik dreht, ist das ebenfalls blöd, denn jedes Kind möchte ja seine eigene Freude am Münzeinwurf finden. Abgesehen davon, fand ich es auch blöd, dass ich etwa 20-25 Kugeln (5cm) effektiv in den Kugelbehälter einfüllen kann (bei mehr mischt und bewegt es nicht mehr so gut) aber nur etwa 5 Münzen einwerfen kann bevor das System ins stocken gerät. Ich wollte es nicht immer nach 5 Münzen schütteln oder ausleeren. Das macht keinen Spaß. Also öffnete ich den Automaten wieder und überlegte wie ich es Verbessern kann. Dann setzte ich mich an Fusion 360 und fing an meine Gedanken in einen Volumenkörper zu verwandeln. Mein Upgrade löst diese Probleme zuverlässig und beinhaltet: 1) Eine größere Münzauffangschale als Unterbau. Der fertig gedruckte Automat kann einfach auf das zusätzliche Fach drauf gestellt werden. Der Deckel an der Unterseite des Automaten muss geöffnet werden, er wird für diesen Unterbau nicht benötigt und kann bei Seite gelegt werden. In Verbindung mit der größeren Rutsche aus 2) fallen die Coins direkt durchs Loch nach unten in die große Auffangschale. Wie ein Abfluss. So können unendlich viele Coins gesammelt werden, das Volumen ist riesig. 2) Eine größere Rutsche zum nachträglichen Einkleben (doppelseitiges Klebeband reicht schon, oder Sekundenkleber) die einen zuverlässigen und schwungvollen Abgang der Coins gewährleistet und den Ausgang vor dem Steckenbleiben schützt. Die Coins bleiben also nicht mehr am Ausgang liegen und türmen sich dort, sondern bekommen mehr Schwung, um weiter nach hinten direkt durch die Öffnung im Boden zu verschwinden und von der Auffangschale aus 1) aufgefangen zu werden. Die Rutsche ist später von außen nicht mehr sichtbar, die Farbe ist daher unwichtig. Wichtig ist nur, dass Sie den Keil nahtlos an der Wand positionieren, es darf gerne etwas Druck bzw. Wiederstand gegen die Wand aufgebaut werden. 3) Eine Transport- und Ordnungsbox mit Deckel, passend für 20 Coins. Wer mehr Coins verstauen will, kann die Box in der Höhe skalieren. Berechnungsgrundlage ist, dass 1 Coin eine Höhe von 6mm hat. Meine Coins haben einen Durchmesser von 49mm. Sie passieren die Mechanik des Automaten perfekt und passen perfekt in die Box hinein. Jedes Fach kann, dank eines integrierten Schlitzes Coin für Coin geleert werden. Man muss nicht alle zusammen ausschütten. Die Aussparungen für die Coins haben einen Durchmesser von 52mm falls ihr etwas größere Coins habt, passen diese auch. 3 kurze Hinweise zum Drucken: - der Unterbaubehälter besteht aus 2 Teilen, die mit 4 Verbindern zusammengesteckt und an den Kanten geklebt werden müssen. Die Verbinder ermöglichen eine passgenaue Ausrichtung. Der Druck benötigt keine Stützen. - Ihr könnt auch die Füllung reduzieren, damit es schneller druckt (z.B. 5% Infill mit Gyroid, das ist stabil genug) - wartet bis das Druckbett abgekühlt ist, sonst reißt ihr euch die Oberfläche runter. Hier ein direkter Vorher und Nachher Vergleich als GIF: Mit und ohne mein Upgrade: Likes, Kommentare und Bewertungen werden täglich gelesen und beantwortet. Teilt gerne Fotos eurer Drucke. Ich sehe gerne wenn meine Profile zum Leben erweckt werden.

description: Desktop Fume Extractor Keep your workspace cleaner with this compact Desktop Fume Extractor , designed for soldering, PCB assembly, and electronics repair. Built around a standard 50 × 50 × 10 mm fan , it provides effective airflow while maintaining a small desktop footprint. The adjustable stand allows you to easily direct airflow where it's needed, and the replaceable activated carbon filter helps reduce solder fumes during everyday electronics work. Designed to print without supports , the assembly requires only a few pieces of hardware and can be completed in just a few minutes. Safety This fume extractor is intended to help reduce exposure to solder fumes by drawing them through an activated carbon filter. It is not a replacement for proper ventilation . Always solder in a well-ventilated area and follow appropriate safety practices. Features ✓ Standard 50 × 50 × 10 mm fan ✓ Replaceable activated carbon filter ✓ Adjustable viewing angle ✓ Compact desktop design ✓ Prints without supports ✓ Quick and easy assembly Print Settings Material: PLA Nozzle: 0.4 mm Layer Height: 0.2 mm Walls: 3 Top/Bottom Layers: 5 Infill: 10% Gyroid Supports: None Hardware Required 1 × 50 × 50 × 10 mm Fan ( Amazon Link ) 3 × M3 Heat-Set Inserts 1 × M3 × 10 mm Socket Head Cap Screw 2 × M3 × 6 mm Button Head Screws Activated Carbon Filter ( Amazon Link ) Assembly Assembly takes approximately 5 minutes using only a soldering iron for the heat-set inserts and a 2 mm & 2.5 mm hex driver. Step 1 – Install the Heat-Set Inserts Install the three M3 heat-set inserts into the housing. Install one insert in the side pivot hole. Install two inserts in the bottom mounting holes. Allow the inserts to cool before continuing. Step 2 – Install the Fan Place the 50 × 50 × 10 mm fan into the bottom cover. Route the cable through the rear cable opening. Ensure the airflow is directed toward the rear exhaust. Step 3 – Install the Filter (Optional) Filter needs to be cut to size, and it goes behind the fan slot. Insert the activated carbon filter into the housing. Ensure it sits flat before installing the bottom cover. Step 4 – Install the Bottom Cover Position the bottom cover beneath the housing. Secure it using: 2 × M3 × 6 mm Button Head Screws Tighten until snug. Do not overtighten. Step 5 – Attach the Stand Align the stand with the side pivot. Install the M3 × 10 mm socket head screw . Tighten until the housing pivots smoothly while holding its position. Finished Assembly Final Checklist ✅ Fan spins freely ✅ Cable is not pinched ✅ Carbon filter is seated correctly ✅ Bottom cover is fully secured ✅ Stand pivots smoothly

description: This press plate set makes a quick and easy scalloped flower dish, bowl or plate out of clay. Use the cutter to make the initial piece, the large frame to align the center and the center piece to press the clay into a foam bat. Perfect form every time! This scalloped flower press plate has a deeper inner filet to help with clay cracking when pressing. Use slow, even pressure as you press into the foam. Pottery Tip 1 - You can get a deeper plate/bowl by pressing into thicker foam. When making a deeper press, flip your piece upside down with the inner press plate still in place and set it on top of a glaze bottle or something to keep it raised until the clay has a chance to get more solid. Be sure to flip it back and remove the plate before your piece dries to prevent cracking. If you’re making multiple deep plates at one time, print multiple copies of just the inner plate so you can continue making while your finished pieces rest! Pottery Tip 2 - Use a piece of plastic sheet, like cling wrap, over your clay before cutting to get a nice, rounded edge! Keep it in place during your press to help preserve your texture. description: LoopLoom - a fully 3D printable tablet weaving loom. The goal: Long warps. Small footprint. No tools. There's no question about it: A nice wooden loom is fun to use and looks great. But it also takes up quite a bit of space, isn't exactly light, and isn't cheap either. For beginners or when you're on the go: A printable loom would be just the thing! The facts: 2,5 meter (100 inch) warp. Adjustable waving angle. Printable on 256mm bed size. The three adjustable extensions allow you to stretch up to 2.5 meters of ribbon—realistically, you can weave braids about 2 meters long. Using the two front extensions, you can adjust the angle to be steeper or flatter: You can adjust the thread tension on all three extensions. On the left side of each extension, there is a screw that you can use to loosen or tighten it. To secure the thread at the beginning, simply tie a knot in the cord and pull it through the slot from the right: If you're used to doing it this way with another frame (e.g., an "Ashford inkle loom"), you can also screw a 3mm screw into the existing hole and wrap the thread around it. When you want to store the LoopLoom, you can loosen the screw that secures the base and pull the base out. It then snaps into place—with a click—in the center of the frame, making the LoopLoom even more portable: That's exactly how the frame with the foot comes out of your printer. Apply a little pressure to the foot to remove it, slide it onto the frame from the back (there's a slot in the frame for this), and secure it with the screw that matches the frame's color: The print: 2 plates, 2 colors. Since the frame is very large, it tends to warp during printing. I’ve therefore made a few optimizations, which you can read about here . In my enclosed printers (P1S and X1C), this allows me to print the frame perfectly flat—which is important for the extensions to work properly. Either use my print profile or slice it yourself: Start with a 0.16 mm profile as a base, set the infill to 10% gyroid, and adjust the number of walls for the different parts: Cover caps: 2 Screws, base: 3 Frame: 4 Slide-outs: 5 Slide-out 3—the longest one—should be as sturdy as possible: 7 walls and 50% infill. Although I usually print with engineering filaments, plain PLA is the best choice here because stiffness is key. If you have PLA-CF, you can use it for the extensions (i.e., for Plate 2), but it’s not necessary. Here, I printed the first plate in “PLA matte dark brown” and the second in “PLA matte dark chocolate brown”: Some of the pieces on Plate 2 have changed since the photo was taken, and a shuttle has been added: If you prefer weaving shuttles that are a little bigger and fit better in your hand, here’s another model I made. If you'd prefer the foot to be a little heavier or thicker (for example, so you can wedge it between your legs on the sofa more easily), just place the foot on a suitable wooden board. Trace around it and cut it out. Screw the foot onto the board—there are already 4 holes for countersunk screws. I'll take some photos of this soon. I hope you have a lot of fun weaving—if so, I'd love to see a photo of the border, but I'd also appreciate a like, a good review, or a boost! And of course, feel free to ask questions if things aren't working out as they should. If you'd like to sell the loom, please contact me. Update 19.07.2026 I made a slight modification to slide 3; it now has a height-adjustable foot. This prevents the loom from wobbling when the slide bends upward slightly due to thread tension. You can easily reprint and replace the slide.
