#T34evolution #Contests #Hostedbycreator A small remix of @Bavaria_3DTanks's T-34 Modular Platform: https://makerworld.com/en/models/2637402-t-34-tank-magnetic-modular-platform-1-35-scale-t34#profileId-2923731 The contest hints that remixes of the T-34 should be redesigns or an evolution, instead of that I did a de-evolution . I present the T-34 Mod. 1941. What was remixed? The Wheels Using Bavaria's T-34 platform, I have done lots of changes to the model. I introduced my own road wheels which are based on the early solid-rubber wheels, these road wheels come with the tire part separate to allow the tire part to be printed in TPU, it requires 95A TPU or softer to allow the tire to stretch over the rim. However, if unable to use TPU, or if you have a AMS, there are un-separated road wheels and AMS/Multicolor road wheels respectively. Turret and Hull Panels Another add-on to the T-34 platform was the early 1941 Model turret and the F-34 cannon. These were designed by me from the ground up to represent the early model of the T-34. Tracks The tracks were designed from the ground up, now they are more realistic and accurately represent the unique design of the T-34's tracks. Recommended Print Settings Filament: I used Overture's Matte Army Green PLA for the hull/turret/wheel parts, Overture Black TPU 95A for the tires, and Bambu Lab Matte Black PLA for the tracks. Everything else: refer to Bavaria's model print settings for tips. Assembly General Glue is needed to attach the magnet mounts to the hull panels. Turret Gun is attached to the pegs in the turret. DO NOT USE GLUE AS IT IS A MOVING PART. Wheels Glue is optional when attaching the tires to the rims. Hull piece The two pieces (typically labeled “bottom hull part”) are optional and go on the bottom of the hull near the sprocket as shown. This is on a separate 3mf file for this model.

description: This is a 45-degree directional return jet designed for above-ground pools with a 32 mm water outlet, such as compatible Bestway and Intex systems. The original pool outlet sends the filtered water straight ahead. This replacement nozzle redirects the water at approximately 45 degrees, allowing the flow to be aimed downward or sideways to improve water circulation inside the pool. The model consists of two printable parts: Directional outlet nozzle Threaded retaining ring It replaces only the original water outlet nozzle. The remaining original pool fitting, seals and internal components are reused. The nozzle can be rotated before tightening the retaining ring, allowing you to choose the direction of the water flow. Compatibility Tested on a Bestway pool with a 32 mm outlet. It should also be compatible with Intex and other above-ground pools that use the same style of 32 mm return outlet, although small differences may exist between models. Please compare the original fitting and dimensions before printing. Printing Recommended material: PETG PETG is recommended because the part will be exposed to water, sunlight and outdoor temperatures. No supports required Print both parts in the orientation provided Recommended layer height: 0.20 mm Recommended walls: 4 Recommended infill: 25–40% A brim can be used if your printer has adhesion problems Print the threaded ring slowly for better thread quality Assembly Turn off the pool pump. Remove the original directional outlet nozzle. Keep the original pool fitting and rubber seals in place. Insert the printed directional nozzle. Rotate it to the desired position. Tighten it using the printed retaining ring. Turn the pump back on and check for leaks. Do not overtighten the threaded ring. Hand tightening should be enough. Important This model has been tested on my own Bestway 32 mm pool outlet. Always check the connection for leaks after installation. The model is not intended for high-pressure plumbing systems. If you successfully test it on another Bestway or Intex pool model, please leave a comment with the exact model so the compatibility list can be expanded.

Before you print: An AMS is required. You must have PETG and PLA, or any two filaments that don't stick together, or soluble support material. This boomerang does indeed work, but boomerang throwing is not easy. If this is your first time throwing this sort of boomerang, expect to take at least 1-2 hours of practice before you have even one successful catch. Printing Make sure you choose the correct file. I have made a different print profile for the left-handed version so that my signature isn't mirrored. Set the green material to whatever PETG you have, and the white material to whatever PLA you have. The bottom of the boomerang is designed to print my signature in a different colour of PETG. If you only have one colour of PETG, use the fill tool under the paint menu to make the whole boomerang one colour. Make sure your buildplate has been cleaned with soap and water, and that bed-levelling is enabled to ensure optimal adhesion. VERY IMPORTANT: While the printer is printing the purge line , start to peel it off before the whole purge line has printed . The boomerang will be printed over the purge line if it is not removed immediately, and you will have to try again. When finished printing, peel off the supports using the little tabs that stick out, and then pop out the chamber supports by poking an object through the hole on the other side with something like a screwdriver. Optional: Sand or scrape the edges and the ‘transitions’ to and from the undercut as they may have a slightly bumpy edge. Safety: This boomerang is not a toy. Treat it as a piece of sporting equipment that has the capacity to injure or even kill very young children or small animals if you throw within the vicinity of others. This boomerang can be thrown without much power, but please keep in mind that it is designed to be thrown in excess of 75mph (120km/h) and is a spinning piece of solid plastic. I do not take any responsibility for any injuries this may cause if thrown carelessly. If you are actually going to use this boomerang for fast-catch (5 consecutive throws and catches, timed), I recommend wearing safety glasses and a thick glove on your non-dominant hand. Restrain any hair that may block your eyesight and wear sunglasses if sunlight hinders your ability to see the boomerang in flight. I would recommend throwing this boomerang during wind speeds of under 10km/h, and never during wind speeds of 15km/h or more. About this Boomerang I am very proud to present this boomerang as I truly believe that it is currently my magnum opus - my best work to date. This current design has taken about 5 iterations to perfect, and is now my go-to for practicing fast-catch and endurance. Previously, I had thought it would be impossible to incorporate chambering and undercut, something that is very common on hand-made boomerangs into 3D printed boomerangs due to the limitations of supports and the very steep angles required. I worked around this by designing custom supports in my CAD software, and had them print in a filament that wouldn't stick to the main boomerang. I print my boomerangs in PETG, so PLA was the obvious choice for the support material, which ended up giving me very clean bottom surfaces. Many people would probably already have these two filaments on hand too, which is a plus. This boomerang also features a stepped airfoil on the trailing edge of each wing which was inspired by Denis Suprana's ‘Turbo’ boomerang. From my testing, I found that it reduced the likelihood of the boomerang swooping up during the end of the flight, but the exact reason for why is still unclear. Range: 19-23 metres (adjustable by twisting wings - angle of attack) Flight time: around 3.4 seconds, calculated from one of my fast-catch rounds Below is a video of the boomerang being tested, thrown by Grant Perry, captain of the Australian Boomerang team. Throwing Guide Pinch grip the boomerang as shown: Throw at shoulder height and straight forward or just very slightly up (as seen in the video). Use your wrist and the whipping motion from your elbow to give the boomerang spin. It is very important to keep the boomerang vertical, i.e. the plane of rotation is perpendicular to the ground when you throw, and never throw sidearm. If you have a weaker throw and/or there is little to no wind, throw with about 5 to 10 degrees of layover (lean the boomerang towards the right rather than releasing it completely vertical). Adjusting throwing direction for better accuracy: Like with most boomerangs, throwing 45 degrees to the right of the wind is a good starting point, but this must still be adjusted most of the time. With a fast-catch in very light wind, you can try throwing directly into the wind, or about 10 degrees to the right of it (a so-called ‘backdoor’ approach). Adjust your throwing direction with the following guide (flip left/right if you are left handed but not front/behind): Lands in front of you or to your right . Turn to the right a little bit. Lands behind you or to your left . Turn to the left a little bit. Simply repeat this until you can catch the boomerang while standing from the same spot or until you are satisfied with the accuracy. You will have to adjust this every time the wind changes direction. Enjoy the boomerang and I wish you many happy returns! Throw safely and responsibly :)

I wanted to be able to permanently mount a monitor to my 19" 45U rack. I looked at some options and they were all fairly expensive. I didn't need it to move or articulate .. I just wanted a monitor I could use if I needed to connect directly to any of the servers in my rack. This design uses 4U for the mounting plate, but this is less space than is used by a typical monitor. I used a 4U size plate because it gave me appropriate thickness to mount the monitor and access to more mounting holes and a larger mounting surface area to ensure the mount was secure. I printed this using Siraya Tech's PPA-CF Core (mostly because I wanted to try it out). The mount is actually more sturdy than the aluminum in the rack - the rack bends before the mount does if I apply force. Any material that can handle the temperatures in your server closet will work given that small monitors < 24" are generally fairly light. I would suggest ABS or ASA at a minimum since some PETG formulations and most PLA formulations may deform under load at temperatures commonly found near a network rack.

description: Click the Customize button to use this Cutter maker! Built for potters who want repeatable, precise mug sizing without performing the math themselves!! Stop eyeballing paper templates. This tool calculates the exact flat pattern for a tapered or straight-sided mug, compensates for your specific clay's shrinkage, and outputs a ready-to-print cutter - sharp blade, comfortable press rim, and built-in bracing so it holds its shape under real hand pressure. How it works Enter your target top diameter, bottom diameter, and height (or just tell it the volume you want - in mL or oz - and it'll solve the height for you, with headroom left below the rim so your coffee doesn't spill). Punch in your clay body's shrinkage percentage, and the tool mathematically "unrolls" the cone shape into the precise 2D pattern, then oversizes it so the fired mug comes out at your intended size. Features True cone-development math (not an approximation) - works for tapered mugs and straight-sided cylinder mugs alike Shrinkage compensation for any clay body (stoneware, porcelain, whatever you're working with) Set height directly, or calculate it from a target fill volume (mL or fl oz) with adjustable headroom Sharp cutting blade with a durable (non-fragile) edge, tapering up to a flared rim you can press with your palm Structural cross-ribs keep the loop rigid so it doesn't flex out of shape mid-cut Cutter has clean, rounded corners, no print artifacts Prints rim-down for the strongest bed adhesion, auto-centered and auto-rotated to fit your plate Optional bed-size check with an unmissable warning if your mug size won't fit your printer Quick start Set your top and bottom diameter and height (or switch to volume mode) Enter your clay's shrinkage % from the spec sheet Generate, print, and press into a rolled slab Trim the seam, join, and you've got a perfectly sized mug blank Want more control? Open the Advanced sections in the customizer — blade sharpness, rim grip width, rib count/bracing, and the bed-fit checker all live there. The four basics up top get you a great mug fast, but the advanced tabs are where you fine-tune it exactly to your studio and printer. Notes before you print Ignore the build plate graphic shown in the preview - it's a fixed generic size and doesn't reflect your actual printer or update with your settings. Changing a value doesn't update the model automatically - after adjusting any option, click Generate to see it reflected in the preview. Once it looks right, click Download in the top right to get your 3MF or STL. Want a real fit check for your printer? Turn on the bed-size checker in Advanced - Printer Bed Size Check - it's off by default. Print settings PETG or PLA, 100% infill on the walls (they're already thin), no supports needed. A taller cutter wall (default 20mm) makes it easier to keep your cut vertical through a thick slab. Got changes or suggestions? Want another parameter parametized? Drop me a comment below and I will see what I can do! Enjoy!

For my layout, the Z-scale version of this factory will be receiving lumber from a lumber mill down the line and producing wood-based products, such as furniture, for shipping out to market via the railroad. To see other kits in this series please visit my collection page: https://makerworld.com/en/collections/15297762-model-train-projects . I designed this model in SolidWorks inspired by an original design by a former member of our Z-scale modeling club - he did market a laser-cut wood kit for a short while (as fannocreek designs) but alas those kits are no longer available so he graciously gave me permission to craft my model as a likeness of his. Given my model is for 3d-printing, I've completely re-engineered the way that the kit is made and assembled, and I've made other design changes based on how some interior aspects of the factory would change some of the exterior appearance. And, after many failed attempts to recreate an exposed support structure under the trackside dock and front deck that would print reliably in one piece, I chose to enclose the underside of both dock and deck. Important Note: Before proceeding to print and build this kit, please note the following requirements needed to produce good results. Also, please read through the entire description to understand all of the assembly steps required. For printing, a 0.4mm nozzle and a clean build plate is required - this model profile specifically uses a 0.20mm layer layer height given that its a scaled design from the Z-scale model which requires a 0.2mm nozzle and a 0.08mm layer height (0.08 x 220/87 = 0.20229 rounds to 0.20). This kit includes both two-color and three-color prints - an AMS is required . Supplied needed: fast setting (5-10 seconds) CA adhesive; and a selection of acrylic paints / brushes for painting the model (if desired). Tools needed: a good bed scraper tool for removing some of the parts from the build plate - I found the bed scraping blade supplied with the printers by Bambu Lab to work well for this purpose (most beneficial was its thin sharp blade for lifting very thin prints . The Print Profiles - Three profiles are available for this structure kit, the profiles generally differ by single ( P1S , A1 , H2S , etc.) and dual-nozzle ( H2D and H2C ) printers, and also an A1 Mini -specific profile. Please note that all of the profiles include a number of parameter changes from the standard print profiles that probably should not be tampered with if you want good results. One of the more important profile variances is that I've significantly slowed down the nozzle speed, travel speed and acceleration to help assure the best result printing the detail features of these models - I've specifically supplied separate profiles based on direct-drive nozzle count because changing the printer of a single-nozzle profile to a dual-nozzle printer (and vice versa) may cause the speed settings to be lost in the profile. I highly recommend that you use the appropriate single or dual-nozzle profile matching your printer capability. Note: I've included X2D with the A1 profile primarily because of the build plate size … if you choose to take advantage of the auxiliary nozzle, just be aware that this model relies on being able to print some very fine detail. Important note regarding the factory name: The original laser-cut wood kit included decals for naming the factory, a choice of either “ R. L. HAYDEN FURNITURE CO. ” or “ TELLER & SONS MFG ”, the latter one being the one I'm planning to use on my Z-scale layout. For the HO-scale profiles, I've included both naming options with the “ R. L. HAYDEN FURNITURE CO. ” as the default choice - if you prefer “ TELLER & SONS MFG ” on your model, find the build plate where the wall with the name appears and deselect the named wall you don't want and select the named wall that you do want. Make sure that only one of these walls are selected for printing … if both are selected, Bambu Studio should complain and you will need to deselect one to proceed; if none are selected, you will be missing a wall in the print so make that one is selected. If you have questions about any of this, please feel free to reach out to me. One final note … you can optionally remove the name from the wall by deleting the text element, or you can attempt to change the name to something you prefer but please note that you should take care to recenter, left to right, the text on the wall after you edit the name. Also note that the text tool when used on a textured surface such as these walls can be a bit finicky with sometimes distorting the placement of individual characters so you might have to mess around with it a bit to get it to behave. I've taken some care to make sure that the text fits nicely when positioned vertically across the siding boards. And finally, most of the text fonts available will not print well at these scales which is why I've focused on the two sans-serif fonts used in the profile. Choosing Filaments - In my profiles, I've chosen to use Bambu Lab PLA Matte filaments as I prefer the surface finish over PLA Basic . With the model based on four colors as set in the profiles, all of the major elements of the model could be left as printed but there are a small number of details that I recommend be painted to help finish the model (see below for painting recommendations). I've tried to minimize the number of color changes needed on each build plate in the profiles to keep purge waste as low as possible. === ASSEMBLY INSTRUCTIONS === These diagrams provides a general overview of the kit parts. === Painting and Window Glazing Recommendations === At a minimum, I would suggest adding some diluted color washes to give a more weathered look to the structure. Before assembling the kits in the photos, I choose to paint the lower masonry block surfaces of the two white bases to help bring out the detail. I first coated the masonry surfaces with a white acrylic gesso and after that dried thoroughly, I worked it over with a thinned coat of ‘tarnished’ black, the gesso helps to create a more receptive surface for the paint on the plastic. For those interested, here is an Amazon link to the Micro-Mark Acrylic paints I've used on my models: https://a.co/d/0fMC2PB2. There are a number of details in this kit that should be painted prior to assembly. This include the two chimneys, the utility cabinet, the shipping crates, and the firebox as seem in the following photo. The firebox is an integrated feature of the middle wall and it takes a bit of extra care in painting it without getting paint on the wall siding (blue) - note that I chose to paint the lid in gray with the rest of the box in red. For the crates, I only chose to dirty them up a bit to help differentiate them from the dock color. Note: If you choose to change the filament colors to either reduce the number of filaments or simply to picking more neutral colors with a plan of painting the model, you should consider painting individual parts prior to assembly although adding weathering detail is often done with the overall model built up. Using some paint color washes can help enhance the details while also making the building not appear as it was just build yesterday :-). If you want to add window glazing (simulated window glass), I would suggest that being done either before attaching the walls to the base, or at least right after attaching the walls to the base - going beyond those steps in the assembly process will make it difficult to adding glazing. You also need to consider that if you are painting the model, care must be taken to not get paint on your window glazing so the painting versus glazing order becomes important. I'm still messing around with different techniques for glazing 3d-printed models … either using a clear film/plastic material or something like this clear adhesive by Microscale Industries ( https://a.co/d/0gy3e33L ) that can also be used to form small windows on models (this stuff can be a bit tricky to get it to work right but I've successfully used similar, unfortunately discontinued by Micro-Mark , products in the past. === Starting with some sub-assemblies === There are a number of sub-assemblies to complete prior to starting the general assembly of the kit. It is recommended that before applying adhesive, you study all of the photos closely to see how parts are supposed to fit once assembled. Once each is completed, set it aside until needed in the general assembly. The fire escape Note the alignment of the underside notches of the ladder to the support features of the wall - make sure to get the ladder in the proper orientation with the shorter piece of the ladder above the top notch and the longer piece of the ladder below the bottom notch (and extending below the wall once attached. Also take care to center the latter, left to right, on the provided supports. Note the alignment of the escape platform with the two provided wall supports centered beween the platform leg structures. The winch support beams The winch supports are two small parts that look somewhat like mini-tripods. Note the alignment of the winch support relative to the top of the door and the notch in the wall. The awning platforms with supports Note that the support legs have bumps that fit into the underside slots of the awning bases. Also note that the leg of the support is positioned closest to the thinner edge of the awning base. Key to this sub-assembly is to make sure that the supports sit flush against the surface of the base with the leg standing straight up, left to right, from the base. The larger awning platform is for the trackside dock and the smaller one is for the front deck. The clerestory Note that the four walls fit well within the inside cavity of the main roof beam base. Once they are in position with all of the wall edges lined up and with the walls firmly seated down within the cavity, add the adhesive drops where the walls meet and with a couple more at the base on the longer walls down where they meet the base, and hold everything in position, making sure not to disrupt that the wall edges appear properly aligned with no obvious gaps. The upper beam can then be added with adhesive on the small flat surfaces of the beam to glue to the inside of the end walls when set into the alignment gaps. The right-side chimney Note that the chimney needs to be inserted from the underside of the roof section and oriented with the thicker side of the chimney wedge base positioned toward the large gap side of the roof. Once you have the chimney firmly seated flush to the underside of the roof, apply some adhesive to hold it in place. The chimney wedged base serves to orient the chimney vertical once the roof is installed on the model. Now you should have the following sub-assemblies ready for use when starting the general assembly of the factory. === Assembling the factory === The base Each of the interlocking tabs on the left-side base, the trackside dock and the front deck have corresponding receiving slots on the right-side base, and for the dock and deck, also on the left-side base. Gently press each tab into its corresponding slot and work each in until its fully inserted and flush … it helps to place the assembly on a solid surface and press things down from the top but be careful to not damage any of the other features on the bases when doing this … I've strengthened the underside of the bases in the areas around the slots to facilitate pressing down in those areas. While these four parts are designed to hold together without need for gluing, you may choose to add some CA adhesive to the mating joints underneath once the parts are mated up flush together. The right-side walls Note: The key to having nice corners between walls of this model are to focus on the close alignment of each wall edge relative to the adjacent wall edge when holding them together while the adhesive takes hold. There should be no significant gaps, top to bottom, along the mating edges. Before adding adhesive to glue in any of the walls, please do a test fit to make sure that the wall edges will align nicely when finally set in place. [This actually takes a bit more effort on this HO-scale version of the model than it does on the smaller scale versions as the mating surfaces are quite a bit larger.] Start with the middle wall … note the alignment notch position where the middle should lock into place. Make sure that the wall sits flush with the side of the stairway and other vertical features of the base. Next is the back wall … apply adhesive drop to the exposed surfaces of the vertical features as well as a small drop along the inside edge of the middle wall and at points along the bottom edge … if all goes according to plan, once in place, the edge between the middle and back walls should line up very nicely. Continue with the front wall (with the name) … apply adhesive drop to the exposed surfaces of the vertical features as well as a small drop along the inside edge of the middle wall and at points along the bottom edge. Next is installing the second floor insert … note the orientation of the second floor insert and how it aligns at the top of the stairway. Apply adhesive drops at the tops of the vertical features of the base and then place the second floor insert within the structure and flush down on those features. After the floor is in place, you may choose to add some more adhesive to help secure the front and back walls to the second floor. Finally, adding the right-side wall sub-assembly with the fire escape … take care not to damage the ladder when handling this wall section. Again, apply small adhesive drops to the exposed surfaces where the wall will sit. The left-side walls Starting with the back wall, apply small adhesive drops where shown and assure that the wall is flush with the base alignment edge and vertical features once in place. Next, add the front wall ... Finally, add the left-side wall using the vertical surface of the fireplace feature for adhesive and as a supporting surface for the wall. The awnings Each awning sub-assembly has three slots that are designed to align with the three support tabs on the left-side front and back walls. To install each awning sub-assembly, gently press the slots over the corresponding tabs … make sure to not damage the awning support legs while doing this … the tabs will fit rather snugly, so take it slow as you go. I generally start with one of the end slots followed by the opposite end slot, making sure that the middle slot is in its proper place as I start to press them together. I then work each tab into the slots a little bit each at a time, rotating between them until they are all fully inserted. Place a finger inside the wall behind each tab as support while pressing the awning base flush to the outside of the wall. No adhesive is needed at this point. Repeat with the awning against the back wall, and again work each tab just a bit at a time, rotating between them until they are all finally fully inserted. Make sure that the awning bases are flush with the walls before proceeding … it may take some persuasion but do be careful to not damage anything while working them on. Now is time to install the awning top surfaces. Examine the awning surface parts closely … note that one of the long edges of each will have a complete shingle row and the other a partial one, the partial row should end up mounted close to the wall so that the complete row of shingles is exposed along the outer edge of the awning. Apply adhesive drops along the edges close to the wall and the outside edge of the awning. (If, as you move the awning surface pieces into place, a bit of adhesive gets pushed up into the crack where the awning base is pressed against the wall, that would not be a bad thing :o). Now it is time to add some adhesive to keep the awning legs in the proper place … for this, you will need either a toothpick or another way to gab a small drop of adhesive behind each of the legs where they will sit up against the leg alignment features of the dock and deck. Each leg should be positioned just in front of and centered on each alignment bump … the legs are a bit flexible and move easily at this point so dab on a small drop of adhesive just behind the lower back portion of the leg and then move it into place followed by gently pressing down on the awning while the adhesive takes hold. Do this for each leg, one at a time until you have secured all three back-side legs followed by all three front-side legs. The roof supports The left-side roof support beam fits within the notch at the top of the left-side wall and the beam support shelf of the middle wall. Once in position, make sure that the beam is sitting flush with the surfaces of the middle wall support shelf and the inside of the left-wall. The right-side clerestory sub-assembly also serves as the roof support beam for the main right-side roof sections. Apply adhesive to both ends where indicated and position the beam structure between the notches of the right-side front and back walls. Key to this step is making sure that the clesestory sub-assembly is sitting level/balanced between the walls … you should be able to judge it being level by observing how the roof support surfaces align evenly with the top edges of the walls on both sides. The roof sections For the left-side roof sections, note that the underside of each roof panel there are recessed areas that are intended to be positioned over the top edges of the walls being covered … there is no need to specifically align these recesses as the alignment of the roof sections are more dependent on getting the top edges of the roof panels snugly positioned under the beam's top finished surface as seen in the final image of this illustration. On the right side of our factory, the two main roof sections are designed to fit around the clerestory with the main roof section that has the factory chimney being mounted on the far right side. Take care to not damage the chimney when attaching that roof section. Again, take care to align the top edges of each roof section to fit snugly just “under” the top surface of the beam. Finally, attach the remaining small roof sections to the top of the clerestory structure. Some final details The left-side chimney needs to be installed using a little bit of adhesive … make sure that the lower angled surface of the chimney sits flush with the exposed portion of the beam such that the chimney sits vertical on the roof. All that remains now are the shipping crates and the utility cabinet. You can see where I've chosen to position the utility cabinet on the side of the factory, using a small dot of adhesive on the upper back of the cabinet to hold it against the wall. Shipping crate placement is up to you … here are a couple of examples where the crates have been left on the trackside dock. I hope that copies of this model find good homes on model train layouts around the world … if you are careful and patient, you should be able to produce a nice looking structure … have fun with it!

description: Shad Fishing Mold – Professional Soft Bait Mold length 66 mm Shad Fishing Mold is a professional, two-piece reusable mold designed for DIY casting of soft plastic fishing baits in a highly effective minnow/shad shape with a paddle tail. The project is optimized for smooth material flow and flawless detail reproduction, giving your DIY lures a professional, store-bought finish. 🎣 Application & Target Species These paddle tail shads are a true staple in any angler's tackle box. The classic fish-like profile paired with high-frequency tail vibrations works wonders across various fishing styles: Perch: An absolute magnet for perch. The realistic action and subtle rolling body mimic small fry perfectly. Trout: Extremely stable in the water – it works brilliantly whether retrieved slowly in search of active pike or cast into fast-flowing rivers for wild trout. Rigging Versatility: Thanks to its sleek and hydrodynamic shape, the lure performs beautifully on a standard jig head, cheburashka rig, or an offset hook for weedless presentations and Carolina/Texas rigs. 🖨️ Recommended Print Settings To ensure the mold is completely sealed and the cast lures come out smooth with a high-gloss finish, use the following settings: Layer Height: Max 0.16 mm (for premium quality, 0.12 mm is highly recommended). A lower layer height ensures a flawless surface finish inside the cavity, resulting in perfect-looking baits without visible layer lines. Infill: Min. 20% ( 25% is recommended for extra durability under clamp pressure). Wall Loops: Min. 3-4 walls to prevent liquid plastic/plastisol from seeping through the printed layers. Material: PET-G, ABS, or ASA is highly recommended due to their superior thermal and chemical resistance when coming into contact with hot casting materials (liquid plastisol is typically poured at 160–180°C / 320–350°F). Note: Standard PLA may deform over time from the intense heat of liquid plastisol. 💡 How to Use Align: Fit both halves of the mold together (the built-in alignment pins ensure a perfect, flush fit). Clamp: Secure the mold tightly using a small hobby clamp, G-clamp, or strong rubber bands to prevent any leaking along the seams. Pour/Inject: Slowly inject or pour heated liquid plastisol (soft bait plastic) into the injection port. De-mold: Allow it to cool down completely (approx. 2-3 minutes), gently open the mold, and enjoy your custom, high-catching homemade shads! If you like this project, please leave a "Like" ❤️ and share photos of your custom baits or catches in the comments!

description: Important! For optimal results, see the Customization Guide below Filament Zero The last baseplate you'll ever need. If you are doing Gridfinity, you'll need baseplates that are: standard: compatible with standard Gridfinity bins practical: reliably prints on all Bambu printers (0.4mm nozzle, PLU) strong: holds bins securely in place & stand up to 100s of bin take-outs and drop-ins If you care about maximum efficiency, or just want to save a buck, you'll need Filament Zero: First-principles, ground-up re-engineered, endgame Gridfinity baseplate system Up to 10x lighter than standard Gridfinity baseplates (0.133g/tile) Up to 12x faster than standard Gridfinity baseplates (18.8s/tile) Filament Zero comes in three models. Whatever your needs, one of these Filament Zero models is the most efficient baseplate you can print. Full stop: ultralight Net (0.133g, 18.8s/tile) semi-rigid Tape (0.295g, 33.4s/tile) rigid Beam (0.460g, 66.1s/tile) Print up to 7,500 tiles per KG at over 190 tiles per hour . Up to 2x lighter and 2.7x faster than anything else on MakerWorld (July 2026). Features Filament Zero is designed to save you money and time: Impossibly light & fast: not 0.1g more than absolutely necessary & it'll be done before you notice it started Choose from 3 strength options: flexible Net, semi-rigid Tape and rigid Beam Sparse Gridfinity - beyond impossibly light & fast: halve your print time and filament again with sparse baseplates Filament Zero lets you create any gridfinity layout you need effortlessly: Interlocking: strong baseplate interlocking system Any Custom Grid Size: set any width and length (half-unit increments) Built-In, Custom Drawer Spacers: add drawer-fit spacers to any side (mm increments) Any Custom Shape: Ls, circles, triangles, etc… Powerful Multi Baseplate Generator: all the plates you need to cover any area in one click Four Filament Zero Models Filament Zero comes in four models to meet all your baseplate needs. There are trade-offs between model weight and model strength. During design, I realized there were three main tradeoff points for various use cases. Rather than making one model to meet everybody's needs, I made three main models to address the three main optimal weight strength trade-offs. The fourth model, FZBeam+ is an interlocking vs aesthetics & time trade-off. FZ Model Quick Selection Guide There are two main decisions you need to make to choose your model: Strength? How rigid and strong do you need your baseplates to be? Flexible : FZNet+ (lightest) X-Y rigid : FZTape+ (balanced) X-Y-Z rigid : FZBeam / FZBeam+ (strongest) Interlocking? Do you prefer to have your baseplates fully interlocked? The “+” in the model name indicates interlocking. Yes: FZNet+ , FZTape+ or FZBeam+ No: FZNet+ , FZTape+ or FZBeam About the Models FZ Net+ (lightest, flexible) — Think fisherman's net. Choose this if you want the lightest, fastest option and you are going to fully fill your grid with bins. The primary structural requirement for baseplates is to hold your bins together. Net does exactly that and nothing more… at 190 tiles per hour and 7,500 tiles per kilogram . Nearly 2x the tiles per kilogram and 2.7x the tiles per hour of the lightest base on MakerWorld, of any kind. FZ Tape+ (optimal, X-Y rigid) — Semi-rigid: rigid in the X/Y plane when placed on a flat surface, flexible in Z. The best overall performance. Strong in all the ways that matter yet still unbelievably fast and lightweight to print. It's in the same weight class as the best flexible base on MakerWorld, yet is strong and prints 1.5x faster . FZ Beam (strongest, X-Y-Z rigid) — Fully rigid, strong and the most like classic gridfinity-like styling. To me, this is the most aesthetically pleasing lightweight model anywhere while also being the most efficient rigid base on MakerWorld: 1.7x more tiles per kilogram and 1.5x more tiles per hour than the previous rigid record holder. FZ Beam+ (FZ Beam + Interlocking) – For slightly more print time, but about the same weight, you can print FZ-Beam plates with full interlocking capabilities. How strong does a baseplate actually need to be? Step back and ask what a gridfinity baseplate actually does: it holds your bins in place. Once bins are seated and the plate is resting on a flat surface, the surface provides all the vertical support. Gravity holds everything down. The only job left for the baseplate is resisting horizontal forces: keeping bins from sliding apart when you push, pull, and rummage. Structurally, that's a tension-and-shear problem in the plane of the plate, not a stiffness problem. That insight is what makes the three regimes possible: Net takes the insight to its logical conclusion. Like a fisherman's net, it only resists tension. On a flat surface with bins seated, that's genuinely all you need, and it's why Net can be so radically light. The trade-off: it has essentially no rigidity of its own. It's a conforming skeleton, not a structure. Handle it empty and it flops; that's the point. Tape adds in-plane rigidity. Sitting on a flat surface, it's rigid in X and Y: bins stay locked in their grid, and the plate keeps its shape as you load and unload. It still flexes in Z, so it conforms to slightly uneven surfaces and pops out of drawers easily. For most real-world use, this is the sweet spot: everything a baseplate must do rigidly, it does rigidly. Beam is rigid in all directions, the classical gridfinity experience. It resists twisting and bending even when picked up and feels like a solid foundation in the hand. If you move plates around with bins on them, or your surface isn't flat, or you simply want the familiar feel, Beam is the one, and it's still lighter and faster than any other rigid base on MakerWorld. The progression is simple: each step up adds rigidity in a new direction, and costs filament and time. Pick the regime that matches how you actually use your grid. Aesthetics (for the few seconds you'll see it) Let's be honest: a baseplate spends its life hidden under bins. Once your grid is loaded, you'll never see it. So Net and Tape make no apologies for looking like what they are: pure function, though beauty is in the eye of the beholder. Beam is the exception. Its strength comes from triangles, arranged to maximize strength per gram as printed, and a key innovation was removing all the rounded, extended parts of the original gridfinity profile: they serve no mechanical purpose and dramatically slow down printing. What's left is a faceted, multi-triangle surface that looks almost prismatic. The goal was always strength per weight; the looks are what optimization happens to look like. The Interlock System Need your baseplates locked together? No sliding, no drifting — a single unified grid before a single bin goes down. We've got you covered. The system itself was a happy accident. In stripping out every gram of unnecessary filament, the corners emptied out since the bins never touch them. That empty corner space turned out to be the natural home for an interlocking cap. Net and Tape became interlocking the moment I designed the cap; the only real work was creating Beam+, the interlocking variant of Beam. The result: small caps that snap into the corners where plates meet, resisting both tension and shear. They print in minutes by the dozen, and every interlocking plate is compatible with every other, so you can mix and match Net+, Tape+, and Beam+ freely in one locked grid. Interlocks also unlock more advanced custom shapes: while the customizer handles basic shapes like Ls, circles, triangles etc, shapes with a holes or a complex perimeters may need to be printed in two or more pieces. The interlock system then lets you connect those parts together to form a solid whole. Filament Zero Performance Weight: Filament is Money How much filament do you need to complete your Gridfinity baseplate job? One way to answer that is to figure out the average weight per tile for a particular gridfinity base plate. Filament Zero is so light, though. (down to 0.133g/tile ), that it's hard to compare this way. Instead, I've started comparing models by how many tiles can you get out of a kilogram of filament: Tiles per Kilogram or TpKG. Speed: Time is our most precious resource I don't know about you, but I hate waiting for 3D prints to complete. To me, print speed is even more important than filament use, though the two go hand in hand. Though I aggressively optimized every print profile, I did not change the print speed settings. That means you can probably use Sport Mode or even Ludacris Mode to print these in even less time (not tested!). However, These models already print so fast that the final print time is dominated by the printer's prep time. Performance by The Numbers Models Type 4x4 print weight 4x4 print time (*) 6x6 print weight 6x6 print time (*) Tiles /kG Tiles /Hr Filament Zero Net+ flexible, interlocking 2.29g 5.5m 4.8g 11.3m 7,500 191 Filament Zero Tape+ X-Y-rigid, interlocking 4.88g 9.5m 10.6g 20.1m 3,387 108 Filament Zero Beam X-Y-Z-rigid 7.68g 17.5m 16.6g 39.7m 2,173 54 Filament Zero Beam+ X-Y-Z-rigid, interlocking 7.91g 19.6m 16.9g 43.2m 2,128 50 3DMM Baseplates v1 X-Y-Z-rigid 13.95g 16.3m 29.8g 42.0m 1,208 51 Customization Guide Your drawer isn't 4x4. Nobody's is. The whole point of gridfinity is a system that fits your space — and stock rectangular baseplates almost never do. The customizer is where Filament Zero goes from "efficient baseplate" to "the exact baseplate your drawer has been waiting for": any size, half-unit precision, spacers for a perfect friction fit, custom shapes for odd corners, even auto-generated plate sets for big areas. Beginner Customization Guide: Pick a model, Pick a size → Download & Print Start Customizing: Click “Customize” below the print profiles Select the “Single Baseplate” option Look for the customization options in the Customize panel, usually on the left. Pick your Filament Zero Model: In the Customize panel, the Model dropdown chooses which base style to build: Beam — rigid, classic feel (choose Beam+ if you plan to interlock multiple plates) Tape+ — semi-rigid: holds bins firmly, flexes to lift out of drawers Net+ — ultralight and flexible: absolute minimum filament and print time Set your size: Under Grid , set columns (squares wide) and rows (squares deep). A gridfinity square is 42mm, so a 4x4 plate is 168x168mm. Generate: Click “Generate” and after few moments, you'll see your model in the preview. Download: See the Download and Print Guide below That's it. A custom-sized baseplate in under a minute, no modeling required. Parametric Model Maker Download & Print Guide Question: “Why are my custom FZ prints way slower and use way more filament than claimed?” Answer: The MakerWorld Parametric Model Maker doesn't support all the print-profile controls Filament Zero needs. Here's how to use the customizer AND get FZ's full performance: Customize & Export you Filament Zero Baseplate(s) as STL Customize as you like (Beginner Customization Guide above or Features Guide below) Click Download (top right) When it asks for 3MF vs STL: Select STL! Download and Open Matching Filament Zero Base Print Profile On this page, select one of the base profiles that match your model choice (Net+, Tape+, Beam or Beam+) Click “open in Bambu studio” to download and open it. Delete the existing objects (Edit → Delete All) Set the Printer to match your Printer Save (optional): You can re-use this file and skip Step 2 in the future. Import your Custom STL into the optimized Filament Zero Print Profile Add in your custom STL (File → Import → STL - or just drag the file into Bambu Studio) IMPORTANT if your STL has more than one baseplate: Click the “Split to Objects” icon (with your STL selected) then press “A” to auto-arrange objects across all plates (see Multi Baseplate Print Prep below) NOW you can print with maximum efficiency. I wish this was easer. You should be able to just download the 3MF and have it work perfectly. I'll be petitioning MakerWorld to better support advanced 3MF print profiles in the Parametric Model Maker. Features Guide Sparse Gridfinity Bigger project? Bigger savings. Sparse mode removes inner geometry, creating 84x84mm cells wherever they fit — halving material and doubling print speed on top of everything above. For larger gridfinity layouts, and especially larger trays, this is all you need. Net+ in sparse mode approaches 20,000 standard squares per kilogram and nearly 500 squares per hour . But the sweet spot is Tape+ at 7,692/kg and 271/h: the extra rigidity is the right compromise for a sparse layout while keeping incredible efficiency. Run a few test prints and experiment with your layout. Model with Sparse Layout Type 6x6 print weight 6x6 print time (*) Tiles /kG Tiles /Hr Filament Zero Net+ Sparse flexible, interlocking 1.9g 4.6m 18,848 473 Filament Zero Tape+ Sparse X-Y-rigid, interlocking 4.7g 8.0m 7,692 271 Filament Zero Beam Sparse X-Y-Z-rigid 8.8g 15.4m 4,110 140 Filament Zero Beam+ Sparse X-Y-Z-rigid, interlocking 8.9g 17.2m 4036 126 3DMM Baseplates v1 X-Y-Z-rigid 29.8g 42.0m 1,208 51 Reduce your print times and filament even further with Sparse Gridfinity Drawer Spacers Nobody likes a gridfinity that slides around the drawer. And nobody likes printing separate spacers that pop out, drift, and rattle either. Print your spacers as part of your baseplate : add them to any of the four sides, in 1mm increments, for a snug fit that locks your whole grid in place. Add spacers to any side in MM increments Custom Shapes Drawers aren't always rectangles. Corners, notches, angled walls — real spaces have odd shapes, and your baseplate should fit them. Remove squares from the left and right of any row, in any configuration, to create nearly any shape you need. And if the shape configurator can't do it, split it in two: print two plates and join them with the interlock system. Create Custom Shapes by Removing Squares Multi Baseplate Generator Covering a whole drawer, shelf, or workbench? Skip the math. Instead of counting gridfinity squares, just enter your layout's width and depth in millimeters and Filament Zero generates exactly the baseplates you need. Pick your printer from the list and it automatically knows your build plate size — so usually it's just: pick your printer, pick your model, set your area, go. Fine-tuning options are there when you need them. Filament Zero already saves you printer time; this saves your time too, and if you're printing a lot of gridfinity, total time saved is what actually matters. Automatically generate all the plates you need for your area. Just specify the width and depth in MM, FZ takes care of the rest. Multi Baseplate Print Prep After you imported your customized, multi baseplate STL into the optimized print profile, it'll look like the screenshot below. There is an icon on the top with an “O” in it. That's the “split to objects” icon. Click it: Select “Split to Objects” Once you've split it into objects, press “A” and Bambu Slicer's auto-arrange will optimize your plates: Press “A” to auto arrange *: Times are based on the Bambu Slicer A1 “Model printing time” for 6x6 baseplates, 0,4mm nozzle.

description: Meet Wheely , probably the cutest little starter robot you'll print this week. It’s designed to be super beginner-friendly, making it a perfect weekend project to get into robotics without the usual wiring headaches. This project is a mashup of a few designs I love. It’s a remix that combines the modularity and style of CUBY , the fun community spirit of Otto DIY , and some clever mechanical ideas from Winchy . Weekend project You won't need to waste days of printing time or a whole spool of filament for this one. It's an incredibly optimized print that only uses 82 grams of filament! In just 3 hours and 44 minutes you will be building the robot ready to start playing. Servos For the wheels you will need 2x 9g Continuous Rotation Digital Servo-360°. Instead of using standard DC motors I decided to build Wheely around servo motors. Servos are way easier to wire up, plug in, and program. If you are just starting out or building this with kids, this setup will save you a lot of frustration. The Remote Control: The controller layout is very intuitive. Each joystick directly controls one servo, giving you easy, tank-like steering control. Speed & Power: In the default code, I have programmed the servos to run at 50% power. This keeps the movements smooth, quiet, and perfect for driving around a desk. However, if you want more speed, you can easily modify the code to unleash 100% of their power. Controller and control scheme At this moment you can use the CyberBrick Official Standard Remote or other controller that uses the same wiring.

Fully printed system to make plaster moulds. This produces a 3-part mould to cast round ornaments with a pumpkin design. This print has been scaled to 112% to account for clay shrinkage, which should give a final ornament size of 6.5cm diameter with most casting slips. If you want it smaller/larger than 6.5cm, scale every piece of the print. With any fully 3D printed mould, you’ll benefit from using a release agent on the base plate surface. I use a generic mouldmaker’s soap, but any product designed for plaster release should be fine. It needs around 375ml of plaster, and you can calculate the weight of water and plaster needed with this tool: Plaster Calculator You can get a much better cast surface, even if your plaster mix is full of air bubbles, by using a paintbrush to dislodge any trapped air from the surface. I would suggest that you pour plaster until the ornament surface is covered but it isn’t completely full, then get a relatively small paintbrush and move it around in the plaster so that you’re brushing all of the details on the base plate surface. This will dislodge air bubbles, and once dislodged they’ll float upwards. Once you’ve finished this, pour in the rest of the plaster. If you manage to avoid adding more air as you do it (just brush gently), you’ll eventually remove all the bubbles from the surface and get a perfect cast. This uses the updated 3 part mould design, which is compatible with other updated 3 part moulds but not the original ornament moulds. This new design has slots added to the back to allow the mould to bend slightly when releasing the plaster, making the process much easier. This version has an additional larger slot in the print with a removable insert to stop plaster from leaking during casting. Remove the insert once you're ready to demould the plaster, then the added flexibility will allow the print to pop right off!

description: I picked up embroidery this year and every hoop I bought had the same problem: a metal screw sticking out of the edge, right where my thread wants to travel. It snagged on every pass. So I went looking for a hoop without one. Amazon, Etsy, the craft store. It does not exist. Spring hoops have fixed tension. Press-fit hoops do not adjust. Every adjustable hoop on earth puts the screw on the edge. So I moved it. On this hoop the entire tension mechanism lives in a small bridge behind the frame. The outside edge is completely smooth. You still tighten it clockwise like any hoop, you still get fine control (about 3 turns per millimeter), but there is nothing for your thread to catch on. Ever. Four oval sizes (60x80 up to 140x200 mm). All the hardware tucks completely inside. Prints without supports. Round sizes coming soon. WHAT YOU NEED PER HOOP (not included, standard hardware-store parts): 1x M4x30 socket head cap screw 2x M4 hex nuts a 3mm allen key (for assembly only) Any brand works, metric sizes are standard. Use socket head cap screws and plain hex nuts, not button-head screws and not nylon lock nuts. Always print knobs two at at least .16 high quality, .12mm is best PRINT: No supports, anywhere. Do not rotate parts. PETG recommended for inner rings (they flex when you mount fabric). 0.2mm rings, 0.12mm knobs. Snap the mouse ears off the knob after printing. description: HALO GP — MotoGP Desktop Companion Case Always know when the next session starts. No apps, no aggressive ads, no searching. Born from the foundations of Halo F1 . What is Halo GP? Halo GP is a sleek, always-on desktop companion for MotoGP fans. Built around the JC4827W543 , an ESP32 all-in-one board from Guition with a 4.3" capacitive touch display. It sits on your desk and gives you everything you need about the current MotoGP season at a glance: 🏁 Session times for the next race weekend, automatically converted to your local timezone 🏆 Drivers' championship standings , updated live 📋 Session results: qualifying, race and sprint at the moment they're published 📰 Latest MotoGP news headlines , fetched directly from the web (experimental, only english for now) 🌙 Night mode with configurable time window and brightness 🌍 Many languages : English, Italian, Spanish, French, Dutch, German and counting… No subscription. No app. No aggressive ads. Just plug it in and glance at it. About this case This is the official case for the Halo GP project. It's designed to be simple to print, simple to assemble, and good-looking on a desk. The case is a two-piece snap fit : the front and back halves slide-in together and hold the board securely with no screws, no glue, and no inserts. Disassembly takes seconds if you ever need to reflash or tinker. Designed specifically for the JC4827W543 board with its integrated 4.3" capacitive touch TFT display. Print settings Setting Recommendation Material PLA or PETG Layer height 0.2 mm Infill 15–20% gyroid Supports Yes Brim Not necessary Print time is approximately 3 hours on a typical FDM printer. No post-processing needed beyond removing the supports. Getting started with Halo GP Print this case Flash the free firmware directly from your browser (no drivers, no software) at halof1.com (select Halo GP FW) On first boot, connect to the Halo-MotoGP Wi-Fi hotspot from your phone or PC and enter your home Wi-Fi credentials Snap the case shut and put it on your desk That's it. The whole setup takes under 5 minutes. Hardware you'll need 1× JC4827W543 board with capacitive touch ( you can buy it from Aliexpress from this link ) 1× USB-C cable and a phone charger to power it Important Before You Assembly: This is the items you should receive when ordering the board. The black thing on the left is a WiFi antenna with an Ipex connector. It is very important you connect it on the back of the board, otherwise it will not get a stable connection on the WiFi. If you don't receive an antenna with your board, you can buy any Ipex Antenna from Aliexpress, Amazon, Temu, … To install the antenna, simply align it on the connector on the corner of the main chip, then press firmly. It should slot into place and stay attached. Once you place the screen into the case, simply bend the antenna to fit it in the free space at the top. Common Troubleshooting: Connect to the PC via a USB A → USB C cable, USB C → USB C cables usually don't work. Check that your cable is a data cable, otherwise you won't be able to upload the firmware. Once the firmware is uploaded you can use a power only cable to power it, if you prefer. To flash the firmware connect to halof1.com and connect your board to the PC. Go to the “Install Firmware” section and press “Connect”, then select your device's COM port from the dialog and proceed with the installation wizard. description: 🎤 VocalAIR™ – Adjustable Vocal Resistance Warm-Up Trainer Your voice is an instrument. Just like any instrument, it performs best when it's warmed up properly. After a week of prototyping, testing, refining, and obsessing over tiny details, I designed this adjustable vocal resistance trainer to provide consistent back pressure for humming, lip trills, and vocal exercises. Whether you're a singer, voice actor, public speaker, or simply someone who wants a healthier, more controlled warm-up, this tool is designed to become part of your daily routine. Unlike fixed-resistance designs, this model features 4 adjustable airflow settings , allowing you to gradually increase or decrease resistance depending on your exercise or comfort level. ✨ Features 🎚 4 Adjustable Airflow Levels Dial in the amount of resistance that feels right for your warm-up. Perfect for different vocal exercises and experience levels. 👄 Lip Retention Bump A subtle raised feature on the mouthpiece helps keep the device comfortably positioned during use without feeling intrusive. 🔑 Built-In Lanyard Loop Clip it onto your keys, backpack, microphone case, or gig bag so it's always ready before rehearsals or performances. 🧩 Simple Two-Piece Design Prints quickly. No supports. No AMS required. ⚙️ Precision Engineered Designed in Fusion 360 with extremely tight tolerances for a satisfying, secure sliding mechanism. 🖨️ Recommended Print Settings For the intended fit and feel: Recommended Layer Height: 0.08 mm Produces the smoothest slider action and most accurate fit. Acceptable Layer Height: 0.12 mm Still works well if you prefer a faster print. 🧵 Material Recommendations The main body looks fantastic in carbon fiber composite materials , but there is one important recommendation: Print the slider from a NON-carbon-fiber material such as standard PETG. Carbon fiber filaments are slightly abrasive. While a carbon fiber slider will still function, the carbon fibers rubbing against each other create noticeably more friction, resulting in a rougher sliding action. For the smoothest, most satisfying movement: Main Body → Carbon Fiber Composite (optional) Slider → Standard PETG (recommended) 🔧 Assembly Assembly only takes a few seconds. Print both pieces. Apply a thin coat of food-grade lubricant to: the inside slider track both sides of the slider A food-safe lubricant designed for meat slicers or food-processing equipment works perfectly and is inexpensive online. Using a small paintbrush makes application quick and even. Although the device will function without lubrication, it was intentionally designed with very tight tolerances. Lubrication transforms the movement from slightly grippy into a smooth, crisp, satisfying click between airflow settings. 📥 Installing the Slider Insert the slider with the wide, flat end first. Once fully installed, the retention feature locks it into place so it cannot accidentally fall out during use. This is intentional. If you ever need to remove it: Move the slider to Setting 4 Pull upward on the thumb tab Push forward until it clears the retention bump Removal requires a little force by design to prevent accidental disassembly. ❤️ Designed With Care This wasn't modeled in an afternoon. It represents roughly a week of design iterations, print testing, tolerance adjustments, and refinement to achieve a smooth mechanism, reliable fit, comfortable ergonomics, and an enjoyable user experience. Every revision taught something new, and the final design reflects countless small improvements that most people will never notice—but will absolutely feel when using it. ⭐ If You Enjoy It... description: For cleaning the condensate tray at the bottom of the Midea PortaSplit. Earlier manuals recommend cleaning the condensate tray with AC cleaning tabs. However the PortaSplit doesn't really come with an ideal location to put these tabs - one might be able to squeeze them in behind the plastic to the left and right of the slot where you can reach the condensate tray from, but I was worried that vibrations might carry the tab out of there. Putting the tabs directly into the reservoir makes them dissolve far too quickly. The purpose of this model is to try to keep the tab above the standing water level, so the tab is never fully submerged. Instead the condensate can drip onto the tablet, and (ideally) drain from the holder immediately. Parametric Electronics Panel Generator Create fully customized front panels for electronics projects directly in MakerWorld’s Parametric Model Maker. This generator combines a configurable base plate, component-specific cutout presets, fan openings, mounting holes and optional labels in one single OpenSCAD file. It is designed for control panels, power supplies, workshop equipment, enclosures, test stations, model-making projects and other custom electronics applications. Customizable panel The base panel can be adjusted to fit the required enclosure or installation area. Available panel settings include: panel width and height panel thickness rounded corners upper edge chamfer optional raised border four optional mounting holes optional countersinks manual or automatic cutout arrangement The model is centered around the origin and has a completely flat underside for easy printing. Up to 10 configurable cutouts The panel supports up to ten independently configurable component positions. Each cutout can be: enabled or disabled positioned individually rotated freely arranged automatically in a grid combined with mounting holes combined with anti-rotation holes combined with side locking reliefs labeled separately Selecting None disables the corresponding cutout. Included cutout types The generator includes basic geometric openings as well as presets for common electronic components. Available types include: round hole slot rectangle rounded rectangle USB-A USB-C RJ45 toggle switch rocker switch potentiometer rotary encoder display standard fan sizes custom fan The component presets use different starting geometries and optional secondary openings. Manual dimensions can still be used when a specific component differs from the preset. Because component dimensions vary between manufacturers, the actual part should always be measured before printing the final panel. Fan cutouts and ventilation grills Fan cutouts include the central airflow area and the corresponding mounting-hole pattern. Available fan options include several standard sizes and a fully customizable fan type. Different ventilation styles can be selected: open circle cross radial slots honeycomb concentric rings The grill rotation, bar width, opening size and mounting-hole dimensions can be adjusted. Individual component labels Every cutout can receive its own text label. For each label, the following can be configured: label text engraved or raised style position above, below, left or right text size text depth or height distance from the component additional X and Y offset independent text rotation The label is positioned relative to the associated component and moves together with it when the cutout is repositioned. Typical labels include: POWER USB NETWORK DISPLAY FAN INPUT OUTPUT RESET VOLUME ON / OFF All component labels can also be disabled globally. Optional panel title A separate title can be added to the complete panel. The title can be placed at the top or bottom and can be either engraved or raised. Possible applications include: CONTROL PANEL POWER SUPPLY FAN CONTROLLER TEST STATION WORKSHOP CONTROL BATTERY MONITOR The title size, depth, edge distance, position and rotation can be adjusted independently. Automatic layout When automatic layout is enabled, all active cutouts are placed in a configurable grid. The user can define: number of columns horizontal spacing vertical spacing complete layout offset Individual cutout dimensions and rotations remain active, while their manual position values are ignored. Typical applications The generator is suitable for: electronics enclosures control panels bench power supplies workshop machines fan controllers test equipment Raspberry Pi and microcontroller projects audio equipment vehicle and camper installations robotics and model making custom switch and connector panels Printing The panel is designed to print with its flat rear side directly on the build plate. In this orientation: the chamfer faces upward countersinks face upward engraved labels remain visible raised labels are printed on top supports are normally not required For mechanically loaded panels, use a suitable material and sufficient wall thickness. Important note The included presets are intended as practical starting points. USB modules, RJ45 sockets, switches, displays and other components are not fully standardized between manufacturers. Always measure the actual component and verify: main opening dimensions mounting-hole spacing locking tabs panel thickness requirements required printing tolerance

Fully printed system to make plaster moulds. This produces a 3-part mould to cast freestanding ornaments with a snowman design. This print has been scaled to 112% to account for clay shrinkage, which should give a final ornament size of 8.5cm height with most casting slips. If you want it smaller/larger than 8.5cm, scale every piece of the print. With any fully 3D printed mould, you’ll benefit from using a release agent on the base plate surface. I use a generic mouldmaker’s soap, but any product designed for plaster release should be fine. It needs around 375ml of plaster, and you can calculate the weight of water and plaster needed with this tool: Plaster Calculator You can get a much better cast surface, even if your plaster mix is full of air bubbles, by using a paintbrush to dislodge any trapped air from the surface. I would suggest that you pour plaster until the ornament surface is covered but it isn’t completely full, then get a relatively small paintbrush and move it around in the plaster so that you’re brushing all of the details on the base plate surface. This will dislodge air bubbles, and once dislodged they’ll float upwards. Once you’ve finished this, pour in the rest of the plaster. If you manage to avoid adding more air as you do it (just brush gently), you’ll eventually remove all the bubbles from the surface and get a perfect cast. This uses the updated 3 part mould design, which is compatible with other updated 3 part moulds but not the original ornament moulds. This new design has slots added to the back to allow the mould to bend slightly when releasing the plaster, making the process much easier. This version has an additional larger slot in the print with a removable insert to stop plaster from leaking during casting. Remove the insert once you're ready to demould the plaster, then the added flexibility will allow the print to pop right off!

description: I only just realized my new motherboard only has two fan headers but my case has six fans. I went online and found some 1-3 splitters for $5 a piece! I figured it's just wires, plastic and crimp pins so I should be able to make my own splitter cables for a few cents. I already have the wire and a bunch of male and female dupont pins along with a cheap crimper so all I really need is the 3D printable male and female housings. I looked online and none really looked good to me so I designed my own. All parts are printed with a 0.2mm nozzle to ensure the tiny features come out correctly. Then all you need to do is crimp the pins onto wires, insert into the holes in the correct orientation and with all wires inserted use tweezers to insert the locking tab which wedges in to prevent the pins from pulling back out. It may be necessary to put a tiny bit of super glue to lock the tab in place long term, but friction was enough to hold mine. Parts should be printed with PETG or better yet ABS.

A very compact gas canister stand for uneven ground when camping. It fits directly inside a Sea to Summit X-Cup, under your gas canister, when stored inside your cooking pot (e.g., a Toaks 750ml). I always carry my collapsible X-Cup under my gas canister to prevent rust rings inside my cooking pot, but also because I like to have a coffee while eating breakfast on the trail. description: I recently bought a Unifi Travel Router and wanted to make a shell for it to prevent it from becoming scratched up. Most of what I could find online were storage/travel cases which were used to only store the router, but I wanted something more akin to a phone case that would be permanently on it, so that I could throw it into a backpack, cable bag, etc… and reduce the chances of the white plastic becoming scratched and scuffed up. Also helps in case you accidentally tug the power cable and it falls onto the floor, etc… I have left the case mostly open to allow for better heat dissipation, and the case is reversible meaning you can install the router in either direction (front or back) depending on where you prefer the screw holes. This decision was made mostly because I wanted the design to be more open and wasn't sure how to design the back ideally. Requires 4x M3x10mm screws to close the case, and the screws are threaded directly into the plastic - please don't overtighten these. I might add a version that uses threaded inserts but for the time being I don't think this is necessary as it isn't load-bearing in any capacity. All ports are fully accessible, the power port and tethering port are both recessed - you can still use the little USB-C plug that came in the tethering port, however this would likely be difficult to remove. Both ethernet ports are fully accessible as the recess allows the ethernet cover to be lifted up as usual.

model_name: SSX23 / MK23 Airsoft Holster – With Rotary Mount
description: Description This is a durable, modular holster designed specifically for the SSX23 / MK23 airsoft pistol platform. The design focuses on secure retention, smooth draw, and adaptability through a rotary mounting system. The holster is built from three main components: a base, a trigger gripper mechanism, and a connector with a rotary mount. A spring-loaded trigger gripper ensures reliable retention and consistent return pressure, while the integrated rotary mount allows flexible positioning for belt or gear setups. A metal-reinforced M5 nut is embedded directly into the connector during printing, ensuring long-term strength at the rotation joint. The trigger system uses a 4 mm × 15 mm compression spring for smooth and controlled operation. This design is optimized for strength, usability, and easy assembly with common hardware. Hardware Required 2 × M3 x 20 Torx screws (trigger gripper assembly) 1 × M5 nut (embedded during print of connector) 1 × 4 mm × 15 mm compression spring 3D printing settings Printing Instructions / Settings Material: PETG or ABS (recommended for strength and impact resistance) Layer Height: 0.2 mm (recommended) Walls / Perimeters: 4 Infill: 35% (gyroid or grid recommended) Supports: Only if your slicer requires them for overhangs Orientation: Print parts flat as designed for maximum strength Assembly Notes (Manufacturing Guide) The connector part must be paused during printing to insert the M5 nut. Ensure it is fully seated before resuming the print. The trigger gripper attaches to the base using two M3 screws and is spring-loaded using the included compression spring. The connector is permanently bonded to the base using epoxy or strong plastic adhesive for maximum durability. Ensure all moving parts are free of debris before final assembly.

I created an all‑direction protector for TinyWhoop. It is available in two sizes: a 130 mm type and a 160 mm type. By mounting this 360° protector parallel and level to the aircraft’s center axis, acro‑mode flight becomes possible. Because the weight increases, the operating difficulty becomes slightly higher, but since the guard is installed, I believe the likelihood of damage is reduced. The structure has moderate flexibility, helping protect the FC and the frame. It can also run along the ground. The weight is approximately 16 g for the 130 mm type and about 20 g for the 160 mm type, so it is recommended for use with 0802 motors or larger. Print Parts 1–3 in PETG, and Parts 4–5 in TPU. For assembly, 3 mm acrylic rods are required, which can be purchased inexpensively at home improvement stores. For the 130 mm type, use six rods cut to about 75–80 mm and one rod cut to about 130 mm. For the 160 mm type, use six rods cut to 100 mm and one rod cut to 160 mm. Adjust the lengths as needed depending on the six rods placed around the circumference. Please make sure the six rods around the circumference are all the same length. After forming the circular shape with these six rods, determine the final length of the center acrylic rod. Cut the center rod slightly longer at first, then trim off the excess after test‑fitting to avoid mistakes. After printing the parts, the protector can be assembled by simply snapping the pieces together. Parts 3 are mounted to the canopy.Secure them with cable ties and insert the center acrylic rod through the cut‑out center section. Instead of Parts3, you can also drill a 3.5 mm hole in the genuine C03 canopy and use it that way (see photo 15).This one was more stable. Parts 5 function as a stopper to keep the aircraft centered.Please leave a slight gap between Parts 3 and Parts 5. The alignment may shift due to crash impacts. Adjust the horizontal alignment using Parts 3, and fine‑tune the front‑rear tilt by changing the battery position. The 130 mm type is intended for 65‑size frames, and the 160 mm type is intended for 75‑size frames. However, by adjusting the length of the acrylic rods, a 75‑size frame should also fit in the 130 mm type. After connecting the side parts with the six round rods arranged around the circumference and assembling them into a spherical shape, insert the aircraft through the gaps between the pillars and then attach the center shaft. Sufficient space is provided for easy access to the battery as well. If you have any questions, feel free to leave a comment. description: Parametrische Universal-Adapterplatte Diese vollständig anpassbare Adapterplatte verbindet zwei unterschiedliche Befestigungs- beziehungsweise Lochbilder miteinander. Sie eignet sich ideal, wenn vorhandene Bohrungen weiterverwendet werden sollen, das neue Bauteil jedoch andere Befestigungspunkte besitzt. So können beispielsweise Sensoren, Kameras, Displays, Elektronikmodule, Netzteile, Gehäuse, Halterungen oder kleine Geräte montiert werden, ohne neue Löcher in eine Wand, Maschine oder vorhandene Konstruktion bohren zu müssen. Zwei unabhängig einstellbare Lochbilder Die Adapterplatte besitzt zwei getrennt konfigurierbare Lochbilder: Lochbild A – vorhandene Befestigung Dieses Lochbild wird passend zu den bereits vorhandenen Bohrungen eingestellt, beispielsweise an einer Wand, einem Gehäuse, einer Maschine oder einer bestehenden Halterung. Lochbild B – neues Bauteil Das zweite Lochbild wird passend zu dem Bauteil eingestellt, das auf der Adapterplatte montiert werden soll. Beide Lochbilder können unabhängig voneinander angepasst, verschoben und gedreht werden. Dadurch sind auch versetzte oder unterschiedlich ausgerichtete Befestigungen möglich. Anpassbare Lochanordnung Für jedes Lochbild kann separat gewählt werden zwischen: deaktiviertem Lochbild einer einzelnen Bohrung zwei Bohrungen in einer Reihe einem rechteckigen Vierlochbild Die horizontalen und vertikalen Abstände lassen sich unabhängig einstellen. Eine Zweierreihe kann durch Drehen des Lochbildes auch vertikal oder diagonal ausgerichtet werden. Runde Bohrungen oder Langlöcher Jedes Lochbild kann wahlweise mit normalen runden Bohrungen oder Langlöchern erzeugt werden. Langlöcher bieten zusätzliches Montagespiel und sind besonders praktisch, wenn vorhandene Lochabstände nicht exakt bekannt sind oder das montierte Bauteil später noch ausgerichtet werden soll. Einstellbar sind unter anderem: Durchmesser der Bohrungen Gesamtlänge der Langlöcher Ausrichtung der Langlöcher Drehung des gesamten Lochbildes horizontale und vertikale Position Die Ausrichtung der Langlöcher kann unabhängig von der Drehung des Lochbildes verändert werden. Optionale Schraubensenkungen Für jedes der beiden Lochbilder können optional Senkungen aktiviert werden. Dadurch können geeignete Schraubenköpfe bündig oder nahezu bündig in der Oberseite der Platte sitzen. Die Senkungen werden nur auf der Oberseite erzeugt. Die Unterseite der Adapterplatte bleibt vollständig flach und kann direkt auf dem Druckbett platziert werden. Optionaler mittlerer Ausschnitt Zusätzlich kann ein mittlerer Ausschnitt aktiviert werden.
