!!!!! Hinweis bitte vor dem Drucken die kompette Beschreibeung lesen !!!!! Dieses Getriebe ist Teil eines Projektes aus der Vorlesung Konstruktionslehre IV aus unserem Studium. Ich habe das Getriebe zusammen mit @dontbanme , @Scheppa , @silas_irgendwas und zwei anderen Kollegen entwickelt. Wir haben dies zusätzlich zu der Ausarbeitung abgegeben und sind mächtig stolz darauf. Es ist ein wunderbares Anschauungsmodell, welches weiter optimiert wurde als die ursprüngliche abgegebene Version. Hier die wichtigsten Infos zum Getriebe: - das Planetengetriebe ist Teil eines Antriebstranges einer Presse. Um das Getriebe herum befindet sich noch ein deutlich größeres Schwungrad, sowie eine Kupplung. - ich habe das Getriebe komplett aus PLA gedruckt, wie es sich mit anderen Materialien verhält weiß ich nicht - ich habe einen P1S von Bambulab und sehr feine Einstellungen gewählt. Ob das notwendig ist, weiß ich nicht. Das Ergebnis lässt sich aber auf jeden Fall sehen - ich würde das Getriebe nicht skalieren, da sich sonst Abstände zwischen Lager und Welle proportional erhöhen, diese jedoch aufeinander abgestimmt sind - Für ein komplettes Getriebe muss man die Platten 1-3 und 4 oder 5 drucken. Die Platte 4 enthält einen Ständer mit Fläche für ein Schild (Siehe in der pdf), die Platte 5 ein Ständer ohne Fläche für ein Schild. - nach meiner Farbkodierung ist: weiß die Antriebswelle, schwarz der Abtrieb von Planetenträger, grau das Gehäuse, rot die Zahnräder, grün die Lager und gelb der Stopfen bzw. die Schrauben - ich habe folgendes geklebt: die Stifte in das Gehäuse, den Stopfen in das Gehäuse, die inneren Lager, direkt am Gehäuse - die Deckel können auf das Gehäuse geklebt werden, dann kann das Getriebe jedoch nicht mehr auseinandergenommen werden. Damit das Getriebe trotzdem zusammenhält ist die Klammer da. Diese kann von unten auf das komplette Gehäuse geschoben werden - die Kleinen Lager gehen lassen sich nur sehr schwer in die Zahnräder pressen. Dafür diese vorsichtig mit etwas diese in die Zahnräder schlagen, bis die Lager deutlich unter der Kante des Zahnrades sind - der Deckel vom Planetenträger hat extra eine Aussparung, sodass man ein Zahnrad sieht. Die „Schrauben“, welche Wirklichkeit nur Stifte sind, gingen bei mir sehr schwer. Wenn ihr das Getriebe wieder gut aufmachen können wollt, diese am besten ein wenig kleiner Skalieren und evtl. an den Deckel vom Planetenträger kleben - das angehängte pdf enthält die Beschriftung (52mmx22mm), ich habe dies auf Papier (DIN A4) ausgedruckt, welches man als Aufkleber verwenden kann. Es lässt sich aber auch mit normalem Papier ausdrucken und aufkleben - das ganze Getriebe mit Gestell braucht ca. 130g Filament - ich habe für die Stützen unter dem Gehäuse ein paar Schichten Support for PLA verwendet. Wenn kein Support for PLA Filament vorhanden ist dies einfach zu PETG ändern. Das funktioniert genauso. (Wenn das Getriebe aus PETG gedruckt wird dann zu PLA wechseln) Daher kommen auch ein paar wenige Filamentwechsel. Wer dies möchte einfach das Profil normale Stützen drucken. Ich habe insgesamt 5 Modelle gedruckt bis das Getriebe die finale Version hattte. Viel Spaß damit! english version: This gearbox is part of a project from the “Design Engineering IV” course in our degree program. I developed the gear together with @dontbanme , @Scheppa , @silas_irgendwas and two other colleagues. We submitted this in addition to our term paper and are incredibly proud of it. It’s a wonderful demonstration model that has been further optimized beyond the original version we submitted. Here’s the key information about the gearbox: - The planetary gearbox is part of a press’s drive train. Surrounding the gearbox is a significantly larger flywheel, as well as a clutch. - I printed the gearbox entirely out of PLA; I don’t know how it would behave with other materials. - I used a Bambulab P1S and selected very fine settings. I’m not sure if that was necessary. In any case, the result is definitely impressive. - I wouldn’t scale the gearbox, as doing so would proportionally increase the distances between the bearings and the shaft, which are designed to be precisely matched. - To build a complete gearbox, you need to print plates 1–3 and either 4 or 5. Plate 4 includes a support with space for a label (see the PDF); plate 5 includes a support without space for a label. - According to my color coding: white is the drive shaft, black is the output shaft of the planetary carrier, gray is the housing, red is the gears, green is the bearings, and yellow is the plugs or screws - I glued the following parts in place: the pins into the housing, the plug into the housing, and the inner bearings directly to the housing - The covers can be glued to the housing, but then the gearbox can no longer be taken apart. The clip is there to keep the gearbox together anyway. It can be slid onto the entire housing from below - The small bearings are very difficult to press into the gears. To do this, gently tap them into the gears with a small tool until the bearings are clearly below the edge of the gear. - The cover of the planetary carrier has a special cutout so you can see a gear. The “screws”—which are actually just pins—were very difficult for me to insert. If you want to be able to open the gearbox easily again, it’s best to scale these down slightly and possibly glue them to the cover of the planetary carrier - The attached PDF contains the label (52mm x 22mm); I printed this on paper (DIN A4), which can be used as a sticker. However, you can also print them on regular paper and stick them on. - The entire gearbox with the frame requires about 130g of filament. - I used the Super Cool Track Pro plate for the housing and the Textured PEI Plate for the rest. That’s how it’s set up. If you use different plates, be sure to take this into account! - I used a few layers of “Support for PLA” for the supports under the housing. If you don't have “Support for PLA” filament, simply switch to PETG. It works just the same. (If the gearbox is printed in PETG, switch to PLA.) That's why there are a few filament changes. If you don't want those, just change the support settings in the slicer back to normal supports. I printed a total of 5 models before the gearbox reached its final version. Have fun with it!

A simple educational electromagnetic motor powered by a battery, copper coil, and magnet. Perfect for learning the basics of electricity, magnetism, and motor mechanics. Designed as an easy beginner electronics project with a clean 3D printed base. How to Build: This simple electromagnetic motor works by using a battery, a copper wire coil, and a permanent magnet to create rotational movement. First, bend two paper clips so they can hold the coil while still allowing it to spin freely. Attach the paper clips to the battery or the 3D-printed holder using electrical tape, making sure they are stable and properly aligned. Next, create a coil by winding insulated copper wire into a circular shape with around 6–10 turns, leaving two wire ends sticking out on each side. Carefully remove the insulation from the wire ends: only strip the insolation from one site this is impotent if done on both it wont function. This allows the electric current to switch on and off during rotation, which keeps the motor spinning. Place the coil into the paper clip supports so it can rotate with minimal friction. Then position a permanent magnet directly underneath the coil. Once the battery is connected, give the coil a small push with your finger. The magnetic field generated by the current inside the coil interacts with the permanent magnet, causing the coil to continuously rotate and creating a simple electric motor. A simple gear set I created for a maker day event at the library. I would have preferred to just use something that was already out there, but as is typical for me, I began to want certain features / tweaks, so I just made my own. These were modeled in TinkerCAD using the gear generator shape. I wanted: something small and simple and lite for kids a grid / board that supports a large number of combinations of gear connections a way to drive the gears without turning them by hand an indicator for direction they were turning Ended up with: 5mm spaced grid board Works with 10T, 12T, 18T, 20T, 21T, 24T, 30T, 31T, 40T gears (most perfectly, some combinations have a tiny spacing error) Small hole direction indicator Handle / driver PDF activity for kids (8+) I initially didn't want to use pegs and fully open pegboard holes because I wanted the gears to be standard with hole in the center and no attached peg. So I initially started with a true board of pegs for gears to slip onto, but then realized I would be very limited with gear placement without some deep hubs on the gears to clear the peg heights. So then I moved onto a design with gears that slotted onto removeable pegs with separate c-clips to keep them on (like @osamutake models). The pegs screwed into slots on the board and then c-clips locked the gears onto them. This worked, but then I realized it wasn't so simple for kids, and the print resolution would have to be very fine to ensure threads were clean and c-clips were strong enough for kids to not break them. Kids screwing pegs in and out of the board and snapping c-clips into place, especially if the prints weren't perfectly clean, was going to be a problem.. So finally I reluctantly accepted a pluggable gears design into a holed pegboard as posted (similar to design by @Ioannis Tsar). The grid spacing evolved from 10mm to 5mm to support more gears. Also evolved from a hexagonal shape to conserve space and keep diagonal distances equilateral, but then the 5mm hypotenuses worked even with small spacing errors, so kept the grid shape for simplicity. The handle didn't work great and could be redesigned. This was my 3rd design, but still not driving the gears as well as hoped. Could definitely benefit from redesign. I had to print about 100 pieces of everything (sans 40T gears), so needed fast prints. Profile defaults to Random seam so seam is less of a hurdle. A grid bound at 0% sparse infill, draft 0.24mm layer print worked fine for me for my event. Gears were printed with 10% infill. A few posts snapped if kids were rough, so consider higher infill for longer lasting model. Sanding posts definitely helps but is time consuming. I would only recommend if you wanted to keep the kit around for a long time. If it's a one-off event, the gears work fine once snapped in and turned a bit.

3D Printing and Assembly Instructions for the C60 (Buckminsterfullerene) Model Print the parts and assemble them into a C60 (Buckminsterfullerene) model. The completed model consists of 60 carbon atoms (balls) connected by 90 bonds (rods) , forming a structure that resembles a soccer ball with 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons . The model is printed from two build plates: Rod Plate: Contains 18 rods . Print this plate 5 times (90 rods total). Ball Plate: Contains 15 balls . Print this plate 4 times (60 balls total). For the model picture shown here, PLA Silk Silver was used for the rods, while PLA Black was used for the carbon atoms (balls), creating an attractive contrast that highlights the molecular structure. Once all parts are printed, simply snap the rods into the balls to assemble the C60 molecule. The assembly process is fun, educational, and makes an excellent STEM activity for students and children while demonstrating the unique geometry of one of the most famous carbon molecules.

I wanted to electroplate my models and investigated online for suiting models. Found none that I was happy with. So I decided to design and build my own. The design consists of three main parts: 1) the motor assembly 2) the controlbox 3) the arc bridge assembly The motor assembly is designed so it can easily be fitted on different sized arc bridges, because not all containers have the same width/height requirements. I will share the dimensions of the current container i used, orderable off amazon. If you have another container, I will share the SCAD file as well, so you can easily adapt the width to your needs. Keep in mind that the min dia is always the width of the motormount plate and standoffs to the side of the container. The motor assembly itself houses the stepper (28BYJ-48) and the ULN2003 motor driver board. The controlbox has a couple of easy to acquire and solder components: an ESP32 board (i used a SEED XIAO ESP32-C6, very small board), a LM2596 buck converter, a rotary encoder (KY-040) to control the speed, a battery and an on/off switch. I will share the scheme here as well. The ESP firmware will also be shared (rename the main.c.txt to main.c) IMPORTANT NOTE; make sure to trim your buck convertor to 5v before connecting anything to it, otherwise it may be set too high and you will fry your electronics The arc bridge is pretty straightforward; it clamps on to the side of the container (dont overdo it, just keeps it from moving around) and comes with a nut to secure the motor assembly in place. I also designed a model hook that allows a straight copper wire down into the bath, by easily sticking the wire in from below, where it exits on the side and you can loop it around the rough thread of the hook. this is a 10/10 connection to your model. Moreover; this allows you to prep and test your hookup before you connect it to the hook of the rotary and allows for multiple models to be prepared in parallel. In functional terms; the device is powered either through usb or through a 9v block in the compartment of the control box, it's wired to prefer the USB power when available. The movement is started by pushing in the rotary encoder button, that controls start/stop movement. then turning the knob controls the speed of movement. The movement is designed as an oscillator; it turns 1,25 times and then reverses that movement. This is to make sure your connecting wire (to the negative lead) doesnt get looped (ruining your electrical connection). I added the whole setup in one .3mf on two plates. enjoy and let me know if you have questions or are happy with your build !

This is my Astronomy Without Borders Onesky 130F5 upper tube assembly. I found two major deficiencies with the original upper tube assembly. The sloppy threads in the helical focuser, that does not have adequate rigidity The finicky secondary mirror collimation The sloppy threads in the original helical focuser is well known with kludgy fixes like wrapping the threads in Teflon tape or using grease on the threads… But the bigger problem was the thin plastic cantilevered design. If you tried using any moderately heavy eyepieces the weight was cause it to sag and vibrate intolerably at higher magnifications, making planetary observing incredibly frustrating. And for some reason that I can not imagine, people making these entry level telescopes put the spring between the secondary mirror and the hub thingy. When you loosen the locking screw the whole thing just goes wherever it wants and makes collimation a total pain. Also, having the whole assembly on the one round rod made one more axis it could rotate on and need adjusting. Very annoying. In this upper tube assembly, the whole things is printed thick and solid, allowing for the mounting of a full size Crayford focuser. This upper assembly is very solid and has very little deflection. It uses a four vane spider, and I relocated the spring to the top side of the hub so it's in a push/pull orientation. Now when you loosen the center screw a turn or two, the spring holds the mirror mount against the three screws so you can actually see what effect your adjustments have on your collimation. As an added benefit, the holes for the strut rods are much deeper, which leaves a lot less unsupported rod length further increasing stiffness. And finally, I rotated the focuser around a bit for easier seated observing. IMO, the stock orientation seemed better for standing and hunching over the telescope. Now the focuser is at a 45° angle which I think offers better ergonomics. There are a couple of compromises though. First, it makes the telescope very top heavy. I had to slide the dovetail all the way as far as it can go, and it's still not 100% perfectly balanced but it's good enough. And second, the large Crayford sticks out axially further than the original focuser, requiring the use of 22mm spacers limiting how far the telescope extends to achieve focus. This is the focuser: https://agenaastro.com/gso-crayford-focuser-reflector-telescope-dual-speed-eaf-1-25.html Use the 176mm base curvature option. The design also utilizes this dovetail mounting shoe https://a.co/d/0iBxRjiH It is designed for m6 screws but I wanted to only use M4 on this design so I made this insert that allows the use of two M4 x 16mm countersunk head screws.` The designed it to use 4mm heat set inserts. https://a.co/d/0dv4AGsl Finally, I purchased this red dot finder scope https://a.co/d/04XIdzyd My only criticism is that even on the dimmest setting it's still pretty bright. I printed all the parts in ABS at 0.16mm layers, 6 wall loops, 20-25% gyroid infill with 3 fill lines. PETG or either ABS or PETG CF would also be nice, but I didn't have that and the normal ABS seems plenty stiff enough. This print requires minimum supports. I would not print in PLA, as it will warp if left in a hot car. I flocked the inside of the telescope tube and shroud, and painted the inside of the upper tube and spider in Musou black paint. https://a.co/d/06kpUJR0 https://a.co/d/05EYCLqY When assembling the strut rods into the upper tube assembly, it's a snug press fit and might require some persuasion with a plastic tipped hammer. The ends of the tubes must be flush with the bottom of the counter-bores. A keen eye will notice the end screws are missing on my telescope. I lost one somewhere along the way but I made the counter-bores a little too tight and makes installing the screw difficult. I fixed this on the uploaded model. I contacted Celestron and Skywatcher for replacement screws but neither were any help, so I'm on my own to find a suitable substitute but it seems like an odd thread. The tube extension fits into a groove and is fixed in place with CA glue. The shroud snaps in firmly, glue is optional. I used a soldering iron set to 280-290C to set the threaded inserts. All finished I could not be happier with the performance of the 'scope. It focuses fast and easy, especially with the Bahtinov mask. The 10:1 micro adjust is a dream. Collimation is easy and holds solidly. Vibrations are minimal and settle quickly.

description: DESCRIPTION ----------- A three-stage rubber band motor that stores and releases energy through a sequence of rack-and-pinion stages. When the first rubber band contracts, it pulls its rack and turns the gears. Once that stage is fully contracted, a lever trigger releases the second stage, and the same hand-off then fires the third. The complete run lasts about five seconds and is satisfying to watch in motion. This design explores a way to store more energy in rubber bands by chaining stages instead of relying on a single band. The lever-trigger approach works well here, though other methods (for example bevel or worm gears) could also be used. In theory the same idea can be extended to any number of stages, which makes the model a useful base for anyone who wants to understand the mechanism and improve on it. ASSEMBLY NOTES -------------- Assembly needs care so that every trigger and lever engages correctly. A practical approach is: 1. Get the first stage to reliably trigger the second. 2. Glue that hinge in its exact best position once it works. 3. Then set up and tune the third stage the same way. 4. The axle is made of several parts that fit together inside the middle of the pinion gears. Photos of the fully assembled machine are included to show how the finished model should look.

The Basics: This print is a Ranque-Hilsch Vortex Tube (RHVT) cooler or Maxwell Demon's tube, a remarkably simple device that mysteriously separates compressed air into hot and cold streams without any moving parts or electricity. The physics of this phenomena have been a long-running subject of scientific investigation and remain unsettled to this day. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vortex_tube Default Print Setup: 0.2mm nozzle preferred for flow dynamics and accurate threads All tolerances are setup for Bambu Labs PETG Basic The Minutia: The design being shared is modular to allow interchanging of internal components for optimal nozzle, vortex and tube diameter geometries. Various vortex generator nozzles and hot pipe divergers with part numbers are included for the user to experiment with. Recommended starting configuration is: Vortex Generator: RF1006-00D-0909 Hot Tube Diverger: RF10-15D Hot Tube Throttle Valve: Close fully and unscrew ~ 3.5x turns Once assembled per the diagram below, simply inject compressed air via the ¼" NPT inlet and appreciate the almost instantaneous separation of hot and cold air from the ends of the device. Feel free to experiment with the included generators, divergers and throttle valve settings to optimise cold vs. hot air fraction for a given inlet air pressure. Notes: Vortex Generators and Hot Tube Divergers are denoted with LF and RF to indicate “low flow” and “regular flow” and are intended to be paired together. RHVT's are capable of generating extremely hot and cold temperatures (-50 ° C to 200 ° C) far beyond the capability of regularly used materials so brittle and melting failures are quite possible depending on how you configure the device and the duration of use. Due to the many factors affecting print strength, it is left to the end user to assess what air pressure can be safely used without compromising the device. I have routinely used pressures up to 60psi on PETG Basic without any failure.

Mostly meant as static/display pieces for now, not functional parts — more updates coming as the series progresses. ⚠️ Scale Warning: The uploaded models are scaled at 1.5x by default. Because the blades are thin and have complex curved/overhanging geometry, print quality can vary a lot depending on your printer and nozzle size. If you're using a standard 0.4mm nozzle, you may need to scale the model up further to keep the blade walls and edges printing cleanly — check your slicer's wall count and thinnest wall warnings before printing, and scale up if needed rather than printing too small. By default, the blade thickness is 1.2mm (in the uploaded version) — take that into account when setting your number of walls.

description: 36:1 Dual-Stage Planetary Gearbox for NEMA 17 This is a functional 36:1 dual-stage planetary gearbox designed for a NEMA 17 stepper motor. It was developed as a joint reducer for my base-actuated robotic arm, but it may also be useful for other low-speed rotary mechanisms, positioning systems, and experimental robotics projects. This design is the result of a long process of printing, measuring, disassembling, redesigning, and testing. It was not created using nominal CAD dimensions alone. The final geometry was repeatedly adjusted according to the actual behavior of FDM-printed mechanical parts, including: Bore shrinkage Extrusion and outer-wall spread Temperature-dependent dimensional changes Bearing and shaft press fits Deformation caused by assembly pressure Gear-tooth contact Wear during initial running-in One of the most important features is the lower hub of the central sun gear. It was designed as the primary alignment reference between the motor shaft and both planetary stages. Even accurately modeled gears can develop noise, vibration, uneven wear, and backlash when the sun gear is loose, tilted, or eccentric. For this reason, the shaft interface, bearing support, gear clearances, output structure, and six-point fastening system were developed together as one complete mechanical assembly. The gearbox may feel slightly tight immediately after assembly. During controlled low-speed running-in, microscopic high points on the printed tooth surfaces gradually wear away, allowing the gearbox to reach a smoother and more stable final operating clearance. Running-in should only remove minor surface irregularities. Severe binding, tooth skipping, concentrated heating, or large plastic fragments indicate a printing, dimensional, or assembly problem. Demonstration Video https://youtube.com/shorts/FVjSa3sgb2A Main Specifications Gearbox type: Dual-stage planetary gearbox Total reduction ratio: 36:1 Motor interface: NEMA 17 Output method: Upper ring-gear output Main output bearing: 35 × 47 × 7 mm Recommended material: PETG or another strong, dimensionally stable material Intended use: Robot arms and low-speed rotary mechanisms Backlash: Very low perceptible backlash during manual testing Quantified backlash: Not yet measured using calibrated equipment Required Hardware M3 × 20 mm hex socket screws: 6 M3 heat-set inserts, 5 mm height: 24 M3 × 8 mm countersunk hex screws: 6 35 × 47 × 7 mm bearing: 1 M3 × 12 mm countersunk hex screws: 6 M2.5 × 7 mm countersunk hex screws: 6 NEMA 17 stepper motor: 1 Hex-drive screws are recommended for all connections. Important Printing Instructions Use a Brim on All Parts Except the Sun Gears and Planet Gears A brim is strongly recommended for all printed parts except the sun gears and planet gears . This includes: Housing parts Ring gears Output components Bearing retainers Motor-mounting parts Covers and other structural components The brim helps provide: Reliable bed adhesion A stable and flat bottom surface Accurate alignment between stacked housing parts Proper bearing and heat-set insert seating Reduced corner lifting and warping The flatness of the housing, ring gears, and output components directly affects the alignment of both planetary stages. Even a small amount of warping may cause uneven rotational resistance, bearing misalignment, or periodic binding. A brim is not recommended for the sun gears and planet gears because removing it may damage the lower tooth edges or alter the critical tooth geometry. Remove all brims carefully without damaging the bottom reference surfaces. Use the Manufacturer-Recommended Bed Temperature Always use the normal bed temperature recommended for the selected filament. Do not unnecessarily increase the bed temperature to improve adhesion. Excessive bed temperature may cause elephant-foot deformation, which can: Enlarge the lower edges Distort screw-clearance holes Affect bearing and insert locations Prevent stacked parts from seating flat Change the alignment of the planetary stages The first layer must adhere securely without being excessively compressed or spread outward. Use a Strong Material A mechanically strong and dimensionally stable material is strongly recommended. PETG was used during development, but another properly calibrated high-strength material may also be suitable. The selected material should provide: Strong layer adhesion Resistance to cracking Reliable bearing retention Reliable heat-set insert retention Adequate wear resistance Low long-term deformation under bolt pressure and mechanical load Different materials may produce different dimensions, tooth clearances, friction, and running-in behavior. Test the fit carefully before completing the full assembly. Correcting Tight Tolerances When the printed clearances are slightly too tight, first check: Flow ratio First-layer compression Bed temperature Nozzle temperature XY compensation Hole compensation Actual printer dimensional accuracy If excessive material flow or thermal spreading appears to be the cause, printing at a slightly lower nozzle temperature may improve the fit. Reduce the temperature only in small increments. Do not lower it so far that layer adhesion or mechanical strength is reduced. Never Scale or Modify the Model Do not scale the model or change its geometry to correct a fitting problem. Scaling or reshaping the components changes critical mechanical relationships, including: Gear-tooth thickness Gear pitch geometry Planetary center distances Ring-gear engagement Bearing seats Shaft alignment Motor mounting positions Fastener spacing Output concentricity Even a small dimensional change may prevent the two planetary stages from meshing correctly. Do not modify: Gear profiles Gear center distances Bearing locations Shaft interfaces Alignment surfaces Overall component proportions Printing errors should be corrected through printer calibration, flow adjustment, temperature adjustment, first-layer calibration, and appropriate hole compensation—not by changing the model. Assembly Instructions and Precautions Tighten every six-screw pattern gradually in a diagonal sequence. Do not fully tighten one screw before installing and partially tightening the others. Uneven tightening may distort the housing or shift the planetary stages out of alignment. Use moderate hand pressure. Excessive tightening may: Deform the printed housing Distort the bearing seat Misalign the planetary stages Damage or rotate the heat-set inserts Increase rotational resistance Distort the output ring gear If an M3 clearance hole prints too small, carefully open only that clearance hole using a 3.0 mm drill bit so that the screw passes through freely. Do not drill: Heat-set insert holes Bearing seats Sun-gear or planet-gear bores Motor-shaft interfaces Precision alignment surfaces The 3.0 mm drill should only be used on holes intended to provide free passage for an M3 screw. Press the 35 × 47 × 7 mm bearing into the housing evenly through its outer ring. Do not hammer the bearing into place, and do not transmit the insertion force through the inner ring or rolling elements. Before applying an external load: Rotate the gearbox by hand in both directions. Check for hard stops or periodic binding. Operate the motor slowly without load. Run the gearbox in both directions. Inspect the teeth and remove loose wear debris. Confirm that the bearing and housing remain properly seated. Increase the load gradually only after smooth operation is confirmed. Stop operation immediately if you observe: Severe binding Tooth skipping Sharp periodic impacts Concentrated heating Large plastic fragments Cracked gear teeth Bearing movement Shaft slipping Rapidly increasing backlash Development Background This gearbox was developed using a printer that I have repaired, modified, and studied for a long time. A newer machine could have produced prototypes faster, but learning the limitations of an imperfect printer taught me how printed parts actually change between CAD, printing, press fitting, assembly, wear, and real operation. I repeatedly printed and measured parts to understand: How internal holes shrink How external surfaces spread How temperature changes the final dimensions How press fitting deforms printed components Which interfaces must remain completely rigid Which microscopic tooth irregularities may safely wear away How initial running changes the final operating clearance The final design represents the complete process: Printing → Measurement → Dimensional correction → Assembly → Running-in → Final operating clearance This is not simply a generic planetary gear set placed inside a housing. The shaft alignment, bearing support, output structure, six-point fastening, gear clearances, and running-in behavior were developed together through repeated physical testing. The precision of this gearbox did not come from a perfect machine. It came from understanding the machine’s limitations and designing around them.

Atmos Mk 1.2 The Atmos Mk 1.2 is a compact 3D-printable model rocket designed for use with Estes E16-6 and E16-8 motors . It features a dedicated electronics bay that can fit a Raspberry Pi Pico/Pico 2 , GY-BME280 pressure sensor , and a 3.7V LiPo battery , allowing makers to add custom flight computers, altitude logging, and other experimental electronics. Designed with accessibility and customization in mind, the Atmos Mk 1.2 can be printed using a wide range of common 3D printing materials. Whether printed in PLA for easy prototyping, PETG for added durability, or other materials for specialized builds, the design can be adapted to suit different launch goals. The Atmos Mk 1.2 is a platform for makers, students, and rocketry enthusiasts who want to explore 3D printing, electronics, and experimental flight systems in a compact and reusable rocket design. Flight Notes Stability margin: Approximately 1.7 calibers . Estimated altitude: Typically reaches 800–1,000 ft (240–305 m) , depending on launch conditions. Flight history: Successfully tested over 3 flights (with a 4th planned) with E16-8 estes rocket motors, demonstrating reliable performance and durable construction, you could use f motors but i wouldn't go below 15N of force engines to ensure safe liftoff. MiniMoto Educational Drivetrain V1 (Competition Edition) A compact, fully functional educational drivetrain designed to demonstrate how power travels from the engine to the wheels. This model was designed for the Thangs "Keeping Busy - Toys & Projects" contest as a hands-on teaching tool that lets you see the internal workings of a vehicle drivetrain instead of hiding everything inside a transmission case. The assembly includes a working engine, selectable transmission, driveshaft, open differential, and rear axle. Every major component is removable, making it easy to understand how each system works individually and how they work together as a complete drivetrain. Whether you're learning about gear ratios, differential operation, or simply enjoy mechanical engineering, this model was built to make those concepts easy to visualize. As a bonus, assembling small mechanical models can be a relaxing way to focus your attention and take your mind off the day... unless you're fighting with a stubborn 3D printer. Apology I messed up. In my frantic rush to finish this model before the contest closed, I made the holes on the engine frame too big or too small the axles could slip out of the holes, and the control shaft wouldn't fit. This has since been fixed in a new file labeled "Frame_Fixed", but I had to delete the original model, already uploaded (and downloaded by 5 people) so I could add them. If you see double, this is the right one. I apologize for any confusion this caused and can only hope that you will be understanding of my situation. If you catch any more mistake I made, Please write a comment, I will try my best to fix them. Thank you. Features Working inline engine Selectable transmission with multiple gear ratios Functional open differential Rear axle and wheel assembly Modular design for easy assembly and maintenance Designed for education, demonstration, and display Parts Included Main Frame Front Axle Rear Axles Engine Frame Crankshaft Connecting Rods (x4) Piston Heads (x4) Transmission Control Shaft Transmission Frame Transmission High and Low Gears Transmission Power Shaft Transmission Shift Collar Transmission Transition Gear Ring Gear Spider Gears Wheels (x4) Tires (x4) Hardware Required None. The model is designed to assemble entirely from printed parts. Assembly Notes Most components use snap-fit / press-fit features designed to simplify assembly and reduce the need for hardware. (Glue may be required) Take your time during assembly and test-fit moving parts before fully snapping components together. Depending on your printer's tolerances, light sanding or minor cleanup may improve the fit of gears and shafts. Assembly instructions are at : https://thangs.com/designer/MINIMOTO_LAB/3d-model/MiniMoto%20Educational%20Drivetrain%20V1-Fixed-1571745 Tires and Rims are included but not required. Design Notes This project was designed to be both educational and enjoyable to assemble. Rather than hiding the drivetrain inside a solid body, the frame intentionally leaves the moving parts exposed so the complete path of power can be followed from the engine, through the transmission, into the differential, and finally to the wheels. The goal was not to create a scale vehicle, but to create an interactive model that makes mechanical concepts easy to see, understand, and demonstrate. Future Versions Possible future improvements include: Larger chassis Suspension Steering Additional gear ratios Improved engine detail A boxer engine More realistic vehicle layout Feedback If you print this model, I'd love to hear how it went! If you have suggestions, discover a bug, or come up with an improvement, please leave a comment (and maybe a remix). Your feedback will help make future versions even better and will help MiniMoto_Lab continue creating educational mechanical models for the community. Thanks for downloading, and happy printing!

Chomp vive en las Placas Quietas de Zoora, donde el suelo cambia de sonido con cada paso. Camina con cuidado, porque sus pisadas son tan fuertes que siempre teme mover algo sin querer. Una tarde vio tres piedras claras colocadas en línea. Intentó rodearlas para no tocarlas, pero resbaló un poco y apoyó las patas justo encima de las tres a la vez. Entonces pasó algo extraño: la piedra vibró bajo él y, por un instante, apareció completa la línea que antes parecía quedar abierta en el gran círculo del camino antiguo . Así Chomp entendió una parte del misterio. La línea no estaba rota ni faltaba un trozo: simplemente solo se completaba cuando alguien presionaba los tres puntos al mismo tiempo. Desde entonces, Chomp ya no intenta esconder sus pasos. Ahora sabe que su fuerza no siempre complica las cosas; a veces también puede ayudar a resolverlas. Moraleja: A veces, eso que creías un problema es justo lo que hacía falta.

Update: keychain versions added on Plate 2 of each print profile! Rainbow trout are a member of the salmon family distinguished by dark green, pink, and white coloration with black spots. Originally native to to the Pacific basin, including eastern Russia, the Aleutian islands, Alaska, western Canada, and the west coast of the United stated, they have been introduced to many other waterways worldwide. In the US in the 1800's a government stocking program started stocking these prized game fish in lakes, rivers, and streams across the country. For this reason, rainbow trout are typically the first trout caught by young anglers (myself included). Rainbow trout come in many forms and subspecies. steelhead are a type that will live out at sea but return to the streams they were born in to spawn. Redbands are subspecies set apart by the vibrant red coloration of their lateral line. Palamino, golden, or banana trout are gold in color but still keep their pink lateral line. This subspecies originated from a single color mutation discovered in a West Virginia hatchery in 1955 that is still propagated to this day. These cold water fish usually weigh between 1-5lbs. This model is the newest edition to my articulated fish collection. Same interlocking scales, same assembly, same swimming motion. The fish were designed to fit on a single A1-mini plate, but can be scaled up as large as you want. These fish are colorful and for 3D printing that means there's going to be a lot of purging and filament swaps. To reduce the number of swaps, I've included a non-spotted version to eliminate an additional color change on almost every layer. Just use a thin paintbrush and black acrylic paint to paint the dots on the model after printing. Advantage: less waste, no bleeding of black into white Disadvantage: acrylic paint is water soluble so the dots could be washed off. I hope you enjoy your new fishy friend, happy printing (and fishing)!

About Models: These models are designed to represent real animals as naturally as possible, with focus on accurate size, shapes, proportions, colors, fine details, and natural movement or pose. Some models include articulated, hinge, or flexi parts for motion and flexibility, while others are non-articulated and focus on realistic appearance. Some parts, such as legs, can be carefully adjusted with gentle heat for a more natural pose, but too much heat can damage or deform the model. Print: All settings are pre-configured and optimized for a balance between detail, print time, strength, functionality, and easy support removal. I recommend printing the models at their original scale. Scaling down may cause issues such as fused moving parts, small hinges not working correctly, or fine details not printing properly. Difficulty Guide: The difficulty icon is a general overall guide and may vary depending on your printer, filament, slicer settings, calibration, and experience. It mainly reflects print complexity, filament changes, possible waste, fine details, support use, and support removal. Multicolor prints may create more waste on single-nozzle AMS or AMS Lite systems, such as A1 with AMS Lite, compared to dual-nozzle or lower-waste systems like X2D or H2C. Level 3 / Supports: For higher difficulty models, especially Level 3, I recommend using Support Material for PLA. It can make support removal much easier, cleaner, and safer for delicate parts. This is especially helpful when the model has many supports, thin details, legs, antennas, or other fragile areas. Note / Handling: Some models may have very small hinge parts or delicate thin areas, such as legs, antennas, tails, or other small details. On some models, these parts may disconnect or break more easily if handled roughly. Please handle the models with care. They are not intended for aggressive play, but rather as educational models, display pieces, or gentle collectible toys. Durability may vary from model to model. Some models are stronger and may be suitable for careful play, while others are more delicate and better suited for display on a shelf. Articulated / Hinge Versions: For models with moving parts, hinges, or flexi sections, please open the included 3MF file, ideally in Bambu Studio. Exporting to another slicer may cause hinge problems. My hinges are created and tested by me, usually designed to print without supports, and are added this way so they can be moved, adjusted, customized, or removed when scaling the model down. STL / 3MF Note: STL files are usually provided without moving parts. The prepared articulated or hinge version is inside the 3MF file. This helps avoid problems with small scaled-down models, where moving parts, gaps, or hinges may fuse or fail. If needed, you can remove the hinges and print the model as a solid version. Safety Notice: Some models may have sharp edges or small parts. Avoid printing them too small and do not leave children unattended with them, as there is a choking risk. If you adjust parts with heat, always proceed carefully and use heat gently. Support / Links: I truly appreciate every comment, rating, or photo of your print it really motivates me to keep creating. Entonces siguió ese eco hasta un claro de piedra. Allí entendió una parte importante del misterio: los caminos que Tambo y Fenn habían descubierto no solo llevaban al mismo centro… ese centro también respondía , como si fuera el corazón del camino antiguo. Desde entonces, Rory ya no ruge para demostrar lo fuerte que es. Ahora ruge para recordar que incluso lo más poderoso sirve mejor cuando ayuda a orientar a los demás. Moraleja: La verdadera fuerza no está en hacer más ruido, sino en saber para qué la usas.

description: About Models: These models are designed to represent real animals as naturally as possible, with focus on accurate size, shapes, proportions, colors, fine details, and natural movement or pose. Some models include articulated, hinge, or flexi parts for motion and flexibility, while others are non-articulated and focus on realistic appearance. Some parts, such as legs, can be carefully adjusted with gentle heat for a more natural pose, but too much heat can damage or deform the model. Print: All settings are pre-configured and optimized for a balance between detail, print time, strength, functionality, and easy support removal. I recommend printing the models at their original scale. Scaling down may cause issues such as fused moving parts, small hinges not working correctly, or fine details not printing properly. Difficulty Guide: The difficulty icon is a general overall guide and may vary depending on your printer, filament, slicer settings, calibration, and experience. It mainly reflects print complexity, filament changes, possible waste, fine details, support use, and support removal. Multicolor prints may create more waste on single-nozzle AMS or AMS Lite systems, such as A1 with AMS Lite, compared to dual-nozzle or lower-waste systems like X2D or H2C. Level 3 / Supports: For higher difficulty models, especially Level 3, I recommend using Support Material for PLA. It can make support removal much easier, cleaner, and safer for delicate parts. This is especially helpful when the model has many supports, thin details, legs, antennas, or other fragile areas. Note / Handling: Some models may have very small hinge parts or delicate thin areas, such as legs, antennas, tails, or other small details. On some models, these parts may disconnect or break more easily if handled roughly. Please handle the models with care. They are not intended for aggressive play, but rather as educational models, display pieces, or gentle collectible toys. Durability may vary from model to model. Some models are stronger and may be suitable for careful play, while others are more delicate and better suited for display on a shelf. Articulated / Hinge Versions: For models with moving parts, hinges, or flexi sections, please open the included 3MF file, ideally in Bambu Studio. Exporting to another slicer may cause hinge problems. My hinges are created and tested by me, usually designed to print without supports, and are added this way so they can be moved, adjusted, customized, or removed when scaling the model down. STL / 3MF Note: STL files are usually provided without moving parts. The prepared articulated or hinge version is inside the 3MF file. This helps avoid problems with small scaled-down models, where moving parts, gaps, or hinges may fuse or fail. If needed, you can remove the hinges and print the model as a solid version. Safety Notice: Some models may have sharp edges or small parts. Avoid printing them too small and do not leave children unattended with them, as there is a choking risk. If you adjust parts with heat, always proceed carefully and use heat gently. Support / Links: I truly appreciate every comment, rating, or photo of your print it really motivates me to keep creating. ZH： 去年我乘坐过一次阿拉斯加航空的 737 MAX 9，不过这次体验有点一言难尽，因为航司把原本计划执飞的带翼梢小翼的 737-900——我订票时特意选的、并且真正想坐的机型——换成了 MAX 9。听起来是一次升级，但多亏了美国航司幽默的维护水平，机舱内饰的状态实在拉跨（好多座位的皮都裂开了）。最终我还是决定制作 MAX 8，主要是因为关于这个机型的资料和参考图片更多。 EN: I included two print profiles: Blank: A single-color version of the model. I recommend referencing photos of a real Lion Air 737 MAX 8 to determine the most accurate decal size for your print. Bring the raw energy and intensity of ancient battles to your shelf with this highly detailed, dynamic statue of a running Spartan warrior. Carefully sculpted to capture every muscle, the texture of the armor, and the dramatic flow of his cape, this model is designed to be a striking centerpiece for your home decor or miniature collection. Note on scaling: The model is highly detailed, so you can scale it up for an even more impressive display piece, but be careful if scaling down too much, as the sword and cape edges might become too fragile.

description: Hello All, So, I felt like insects were underrepresented in the series, and even more so, stick bugs are underrepresented in the insect world! So I present this wonderful little guy. Notes: He is by definition a bit fragile. He is a stick bug after all!, but in all seriousness, the supports should be removed with care, especially on the antennae. The leaves are optional. There are holes for them, but they're so small, I basically just put a dab of glue and they stuck there. Anyway, if you decide to print/assemble this one, just be ready to have some patience with the parts. One more thing: MAKE SURE you put the legs/tail together and put them inside the robe, BEFORE you put the robe together. Basically put the legs/tail in to one half of the robe, then put the robe connectors in, add your glue and then close it all together with the other side of the robe. If you don't do this, you probably won't be able to get the legs/tail in afterwards. Hope you like it! description: Slogan: Deine eigene schwimmende Black Pearl! (Wasserdicht nach Druck, aber Trimmung erforderlich) Einführung: Dies ist nicht irgendein Schiff. Dies ist die legendäre Black Pearl , das schnellste Schiff der Karibik, inspiriert von den Filmen! Ich habe sie mit höchster Detailtreue nachgebildet. Das Besondere: Dieses Modell ist darauf ausgelegt, wasserdicht zu sein und tatsächlich zu schwimmen! Aber wie bei jedem legendären Schiff gibt es einen Haken, eine Herausforderung, die nur die tapfersten Baumeister meistern können. Die Merkmale: Höchste Detailtreue Schwimmfähig Wasserdichtigkeit Die Herausforderung: Aufgrund der hohen Detailtreue und der unterschiedlichen Gewichtsverhältnisse des 3D-Druckmaterials im Vergleich zum "echten" Schiff ist die Black Pearl im Wasser extrem kopflastig und instabil. Ohne Anpassung wird sie sofort umkippen. Du musst sie ausbalancieren! Schritt-für-Schritt-Anleitung zur Trimmung: Gewichtsanbringung: Um sie aufrecht zu halten, musst du Gewichte an der Unterseite des Rumpfes anbringen. Du kannst kleine Bleikügelchen, Metallplättchen oder Angelblei verwenden. In unserem Beispielbild haben wir kleine Gewichte am Kiel angebracht, um den Effekt zu zeigen. Feinabstimmung: Experimentiere mit der Position und der Menge der Gewichte. Füge kleine Mengen hinzu und überprüfe, wie sich das Gleichgewicht im Wasser ändert. Perfekte Stabilität: Das Ziel ist es, den Metazentrum/Schwerpunkt so zu justieren, dass das Schiff aufrecht im Wasser schwimmt, ohne zu kippen. Dies ist eine echte Ingenieursleistung! Der “Kleine Fehler” PS: Ich habe einen winzigen, aber deutlichen Fehler in das Modell eingebaut. Schau genau hin. Kannst du ihn entdecken?. Schreib deinen Tipp in die Kommentare! Dies ist ein Projekt für Fortgeschrittene, das Geduld und Präzision erfordert. Aber das Endergebnis ist es wert! Hast du das Zeug dazu, die Black Pearl zu meistern?

description: The Breach Gate Ruins is a dark fantasy terrain set designed for 28–32mm heroic scale tabletop games, RPG encounters, skirmish games and ruined city battlefields. The set is built around a large ruined magical gate / portal as the main centerpiece. Around it, the terrain includes ruined wall sections, cracked stone floor tiles, crystal clusters, barricades, a ritual altar, a broken statue and a small Breach Spawn marker. The design is inspired by a shattered fantasy city torn open by magical corruption. Broken masonry, cracked stone, arcane details and jagged crystal growths create a strong “Breach” atmosphere while keeping the pieces usable as tabletop terrain. The parts are separate individual terrain pieces. They are not mechanically connected, not stackable and do not use alignment keys. This allows the models to be placed freely and rearranged for different tabletop layouts, scenarios and encounters. Designed for FDM 3D printing and scaled for common 28–32mm heroic scale miniatures. Set includes: 01 – Breach Gate / Portal 02 – Ruined Wall Section A 02 – Ruined Wall Section B 03 – Cracked Floor Tile A 03 – Cracked Floor Tile B 04 – Crystal Cluster A 04 – Crystal Cluster B 04 – Crystal Cluster C 05 – Barricade / Debris A 05 – Barricade / Debris B 06 – Ritual Altar 07 – Broken Statue 08 – Breach Spawn Marker Scale: Designed for 28–32mm heroic scale tabletop miniatures. The terrain is scaled to work with common fantasy miniatures and standard tabletop bases. The proportions are slightly heroic and oversized where needed, so details remain readable and durable when printed on an FDM printer. Contest theme fit: This terrain set is designed around the idea of a ruined city broken apart by a magical breach. The portal, corrupted crystals, cracked stone floors, ritual altar and ruined walls are intended to create a cohesive dark fantasy battlefield that supports actual tabletop play instead of being only a display piece.

description: I actually wanted to upload this on friday. Today its Monday. Yet I decided to publish this “Boat” earlier to honor Sam Neill who played Red Octobers XO Vasili Borodin in The Hunt for Red October (and of course in honor of Sean Connery, one of the greatest actors of all time). The Typhoon class (Project 941 Akula) is the largest submarine ever built and one of the most iconic symbols of the Cold War. Designed as a nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine (SSBN), the Typhoon combined immense size with exceptional endurance and survivability. Its distinctive twin-pressure-hull design and massive missile compartment made it unlike any other submarine ever constructed. The class gained worldwide recognition through Tom Clancy's novel and the film The Hunt for Red October , becoming one of the most recognizable submarines in naval history. This detailed 1:350 scale model faithfully captures the unique proportions and unmistakable silhouette of the legendary Typhoon class. Assembly is very easy. Stick the two parts together and put them on the socket. Only thing actually requiring glue is the label which should be glued to the socket. Printing recommendations You can use the standard 0.2mm preset. Support is required for most parts. Hull parts are be too large for smaller printers, but everything should be downscalable if you want to. Twisted by divine punishment, their once-proud elven form is fused with the body of a monstrous spider, creating a relentless hunter driven by hatred, fanaticism, and the will of Lolth. Long flowing white hair frames the Drider's cold expression as it lunges forward with blade drawn, ready to strike prey that has wandered too deep beneath the world. The transition between humanoid torso and arachnid body is sculpted seamlessly, emphasizing the unnatural curse that created the creature. Intricate details cover every surface, from finely textured armor and flowing garments to segmented spider legs, chitinous plates, and the swollen abdomen. The dynamic pose gives the impression of constant movement, as if the Drider is silently advancing across cavern walls before launching a deadly ambush. The rocky Underdark base completes the scene with rough stone and cavern debris, perfectly suited for encounters deep below the surface. A Drider knows no mercy. Only devotion to Lolth... ...and the hunt. ✨ Key Features Drider inspired by Monster Manual 2024 Dynamic pose with drawn blade and advancing spider stance Detailed fusion of dark elf torso and monstrous spider body Flowing white hair and finely sculpted drow features Intricate chitin, armor, and segmented leg textures Scenic Underdark rocky base 🎨 Great for Painting Perfect for deep purples, obsidian blacks, dark crimson fabrics, pale lavender skin, and glossy spider chitin. Brown trout are another common species of trout targeted by anglers, and the newest flexi model in my collection. Originally native to Europe, western Asia, and northern Africa, this species has been transported worldwide to such a degree that it is one of the top 100 invasive species in the world. With such a wide dispersal, many forms and subspecies have formed ranging in appearance and behavior. Some are anadromous meaning they swim out to sea to spend most of their lives, returning only to spawn. During spawning season, males develop a kype, or hooked bottom jaw to help them fight other males for breeding territory. While this characteristic is not unique to this species, it's something I wanted to include in the model to capture the appearance of trophy brown trout caught by anglers. Large specimens can reach 40 lbs and 31 inches. Brown trout are generalist predators meaning they'll eat a wide array of bugs, invertebrates, frogs, and even mice. This model uses interlocking scale units to swim and is printed in 2 halves, aligned with the registration pin and secured by glue on the flat faces. The model prints in 4 colors so it is printable with 1 AMS. Keyring versions are also available on plate 2 of each print profile. The fish were also designed to fit on a single A1-mini plate, but can be scaled up as large as you want. Like my Rainbow Trout model I've provided a separate print profile that removes the fish's spots to reduce purge, the spots can then be painted on with acrylic after printing. Happy printing (and fishing)!

description: This latest addition to the collection is easily one of my favorites. Eddie Van Halen revolutionized rock guitar playing, and his primary weapon of choice was the Frankenstrat (also known as "Frankenstein" or "Frankie"). Hand-built by Eddie in his garage in the mid-1970s, this DIY masterpiece forever changed instrument design and birthed the modern "Superstrat". Below is a little bit of history on this remarkable guitar. Technical Specifications & Assembly The Body & Neck: Eddie bought an unfinished Northern Ash Strat-style body and a maple neck from Charvel/Boogie Bodies for around $130. He purposely chose a body with a cosmetic wood knot because it was cheaper. The Electronics: He used a hammer and chisel to carve out the bridge cavity to fit a high-output Gibson PAF humbucker taken from an ES-335. He screwed the pickup directly into the wood and simplified the wiring to a single master volume knob. He even labeled the volume knob with a dial that said "Tone". The Dummy Elements: To confuse competitors and copycats, he installed a non-functional neck single-coil pickup and a broken 3-way selector switch into the middle slot, neither of which were actually wired to anything. The Tremolo System: Originally built with a standard Fender tremolo, Eddie worked closely with inventor Floyd Rose in 1980 to implement the revolutionary Floyd Rose dual-locking tremolo. This allowed Eddie to perform his signature, pitch-dropping "dive bombs" without falling out of tune. The 1971 Quarter: Eddie famously screwed a 1971 quarter directly into the guitar's wood underneath the back of the bridge to act as a physical stop, preventing the tremolo from pulling up. Evolution of the Iconic Paint Job The Frankenstrat's aesthetic evolved over time using strips of masking tape and layers of standard spray paint: Black and White (1977–1978): The original coat was painted black. Eddie applied masking tape lines and sprayed over it with white paint. When the tape was peeled away, it left a striking geometric design. This version is featured on the cover of the 1978 debut album Van Halen . The Red Overwrite (1979): As other guitar manufacturers began copying his black-and-white design, Eddie decided to change it. He re-taped the body and sprayed it with red Schwinn bicycle paint To make this model complete. description: Take the Guesswork Out of Building a 40K Battlefield 40K 11th edition introduced some really cool predetermined battlefield layouts that show you exactly how to set up the battlefield and what terrain goes where. They didn't do a great job sharing the dimensions of the terrain pieces and figuring out what terrain to use can be surprisingly confusing. There are countless terrain models available, but figuring out which pieces you actually need, what sizes they should be, and how everything fits together on an 11th Edition battlefield can become a project of its own. This collection was created to simplify that entire process. I carefully studied the battlefield layouts shown in the 40K app, determined the different terrain footprints and sizes needed to recreate them, and designed a complete, coordinated set that allows players to print everything required for a functional battlefield in one place. Instead of downloading unrelated models from multiple creators and hoping they work together, this set provides a clear starting point for new players and a convenient, consistent battlefield system for experienced players. Also, I included A1 Mini Print Profiles as well, so the game has never been more accessible. What’s Included The complete collection includes: Battlefield terrain footprints Light terrain features Dense terrain features Standard objective markers Central and expansion objective markers Deployment zone markers Coordinated pieces designed to work together as one battlefield system The terrain footprints clearly define each terrain area, while the light and dense terrain pieces provide the physical structures needed to make the battlefield easy to understand and play on. The objective and deployment zone markers make setup faster and reduce the need to repeatedly measure important locations before every game. AB, CD, EF, and GH Dense Terrain The dense terrain pieces were specifically designed and marked to correspond with the AB, CD, EF, and GH terrain categories shown in the battlefield layouts within the 40K app. This makes it much easier to identify which dense terrain piece belongs in each location when setting up a battlefield. Rather than comparing several similar-looking pieces, estimating dimensions, or trying to determine which terrain feature matches each layout position, simply select the appropriately marked AB, CD, EF, or GH model. This labeling system helps make battlefield setup faster, clearer, and more approachable—especially for players building their first complete terrain collection. Designed for Fast, Reliable Printing Every part of this collection was created with practical 3D printing in mind. The main design goals were: Fast print times Low filament use High printing success rates No support material required Simple, reliable geometry Easy battlefield setup Clear and consistent terrain sizes Minimal preparation after printing All models were designed to print without supports and can be used immediately after removing them from the build plate. There should be no support removal, complicated assembly, or extensive cleanup required. Print the pieces, remove them from the plate, and place them directly on the battlefield. These models are intended to be accessible to newer 3D-printer owners and players who may be building their first complete 40K battlefield. They are functional gaming pieces first. Not overly complicated display models that require days of printing, large amounts of filament, or extensive post-processing. Recommended Printing Approach For the clearest gameplay experience, I recommend printing the footprints, light terrain, and dense terrain in different colors . Using separate colors makes it easier to quickly tell which terrain category a piece belongs to and helps reduce confusion when applying terrain rules during play. This is especially helpful for newer players, teaching games, or anyone trying to make battlefield interactions more intuitive at a glance. For example, using one color for footprints, another for light terrain, and another for dense terrain can make it much easier to determine which terrain rules apply when models move into, through, or around a terrain feature. A Complete Starting Point for New Players This set is especially useful for someone who has recently started playing 40K and is asking: What terrain do I need? How large should each terrain area be? Which pieces are light terrain and which are dense terrain? Which dense terrain piece corresponds with AB, CD, EF, or GH? How do I reproduce the battlefield layouts shown in the app? How many objective markers do I need? Where should deployment zones and objectives be placed? The goal is to remove as much uncertainty as possible so you can spend less time researching terrain and more time printing, painting, and playing. Modular and Easy to Customize The pieces can be printed as a complete matching set or mixed with terrain you already own. Terrain footprints can also be used with ruins, buildings, rock formations, industrial structures, or other decorative terrain placed within the marked areas. This makes the system useful even as your terrain collection grows. Print the included terrain for a quick, lightweight battlefield, or use the footprints and markers as the foundation for a more detailed custom table. Additional Helpful Models Along with this terrain set, you may want something for quick measurements between models. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or produced by Games Workshop. Battlefield requirements, event standards, and tournament interpretations may vary, so always confirm the requirements of your local gaming group or event organizer. Brook trout are vibrant and beautiful members of the salmon/char family native to the eastern United States and Canada. They hold significant ecological significance and are designated as the state fish of 5 states (Pennsylvania, Virginia, Michigan, New Hampshire, and New York)! Due to their sensitivity to pollution, they are a great indicator species, meaning that waterways and environments able to house them are very healthy. Before introduction of brown trout and rainbow trout. the brook trout were the only trout species targeted by anglers for the first 100 years of the United State's history. For both of these reasons, Brook trout are seen as a symbol of pristine North American wilderness. These fish hold special meaning to me too. As a kid my grandfather would take me to small streams in northern Pennsylvania to catch them. Each time I caught one I was surprised at just how vibrant they were, even if they were only 3-4 inches long. Those experiences really made me love being in nature and fishing, which has inspired all of my articulated fish models. So I'm dedicating this model to my grandfather, Wayne. Keyring versions are also available on plate 2 of each print profile. The model was designed to fit on the A-mini but can be scaled up as large as you want it! As mentioned before, Brook Trout are very colorful fish which means a lot of filament swaps in 3D printing. The base model is painted in 6 colors and requires 2 AMS units. I used black as the base color, but a dark-olive color would more closely match the real thing. To get around these requirements though, I've also provided a print profile with only the basic black, white, and orange coloration. For that print profile the yellow squiggles and red and blue spots are left out and can be painted on in acrylic afterwards. In my opinion, the painted blue and red dots stood out more when painted on rather than printed on. The only downside to acrylics paint is it's water solubility so the color could be washed away or smear if the model gets wet. However you decide to print/paint this model, I hope you enjoy your new fishy friend! Happy printing (and fishing)!

About Models: These models are designed to represent real animals as naturally as possible, with focus on accurate size, shapes, proportions, colors, fine details, and natural movement or pose. Some models include articulated, hinge, or flexi parts for motion and flexibility, while others are non-articulated and focus on realistic appearance. Some parts, such as legs, can be carefully adjusted with gentle heat for a more natural pose, but too much heat can damage or deform the model. Print: All settings are pre-configured and optimized for a balance between detail, print time, strength, functionality, and easy support removal. I recommend printing the models at their original scale. Scaling down may cause issues such as fused moving parts, small hinges not working correctly, or fine details not printing properly. Difficulty Guide: The difficulty icon is a general overall guide and may vary depending on your printer, filament, slicer settings, calibration, and experience. It mainly reflects print complexity, filament changes, possible waste, fine details, support use, and support removal. Multicolor prints may create more waste on single-nozzle AMS or AMS Lite systems, such as A1 with AMS Lite, compared to dual-nozzle or lower-waste systems like X2D or H2C. Level 3 / Supports: For higher difficulty models, especially Level 3, I recommend using Support Material for PLA. It can make support removal much easier, cleaner, and safer for delicate parts. This is especially helpful when the model has many supports, thin details, legs, antennas, or other fragile areas. Note / Handling: Some models may have very small hinge parts or delicate thin areas, such as legs, antennas, tails, or other small details. On some models, these parts may disconnect or break more easily if handled roughly. Please handle the models with care. They are not intended for aggressive play, but rather as educational models, display pieces, or gentle collectible toys. Durability may vary from model to model. Some models are stronger and may be suitable for careful play, while others are more delicate and better suited for display on a shelf. Articulated / Hinge Versions: For models with moving parts, hinges, or flexi sections, please open the included 3MF file, ideally in Bambu Studio. Exporting to another slicer may cause hinge problems. My hinges are created and tested by me, usually designed to print without supports, and are added this way so they can be moved, adjusted, customized, or removed when scaling the model down. STL / 3MF Note: STL files are usually provided without moving parts. The prepared articulated or hinge version is inside the 3MF file. This helps avoid problems with small scaled-down models, where moving parts, gaps, or hinges may fuse or fail. If needed, you can remove the hinges and print the model as a solid version. Safety Notice: Some models may have sharp edges or small parts. Avoid printing them too small and do not leave children unattended with them, as there is a choking risk. If you adjust parts with heat, always proceed carefully and use heat gently. Support / Links: I truly appreciate every comment, rating, or photo of your print it really motivates me to keep creating. The model fits naturally into crusader strongholds, shattered shrine districts, devastated defensive lines or war-torn imperial cities and helps create a more immersive and believable battlefield. The scenic woodland base features moss-covered stones, roots, and forest debris, completing the illusion that the Dryad has stepped directly from the heart of an untouched grove. A Dryad rarely seeks battle. She offers peace first. Die natürliche Gehbewegung und die leicht nach vorne geneigte Haltung vermitteln den Eindruck einer realistischen Transportszene. Die schwarze Sackkarre transportiert eine rechteckige Holzkiste mit angedeuteten Verstärkungsbändern. Die Figur eignet sich ideal für Güterbahnhöfe, Lagerhäuser, Fabriken, Laderampen, Speditionen oder andere realistische Alltagsszenen auf der Modellbahnanlage. Kleidung, Sackkarre und Holzkiste sind fein modelliert. Die natürlichen Proportionen, realistische Stoffstrukturen sowie die stimmige Körperhaltung sorgen für einen hochwertigen und authentischen Gesamteindruck. Die dynamische Laufbewegung verleiht der Figur eine glaubwürdige und lebendige Präsenz in jeder Transport- oder Verlade-Szene. Gedruckt in neutralen Hautfarben und anschließend individuell nach Wunsch bemalbar. Die Figur kann optional auf eine Scheibe oder einen Sockel geklebt werden. Auf eine feste Bodenplatte wurde bewusst verzichtet, um maximale Gestaltungsfreiheit zu ermöglichen. Universalsockel findet Ihr in meinem Profil. Hinweis zu den Stützstrukturen: Je nach Druck können sich die Stützen teilweise etwas schwer lösen lassen. Es empfiehlt sich, die Stützen vorsichtig nach unten abzuziehen. Bitte nicht seitlich hebeln, da dabei feine Details beschädigt werden könnten. Hinweis zur Nachbearbeitung: Scharfe Kanten und kleine Unebenheiten können nach dem Druck vorhanden sein. Weitere Figurenmodelle sind geplant und werden schrittweise veröffentlicht – passende Zubehörteile und Szenenelemente sind bereits in Arbeit 😊 Mehr Modelle findest du in meinem Profil.

description: Bring iconic battlefield communication infrastructure to your Star Wars: Legion tabletop with this detailed Geonosis Comms Tower terrain piece. This model is designed as a tall sci-fi communications tower inspired by the harsh military architecture of Geonosis. The piece combines a strong vertical silhouette with clean panel lines, antenna details, reinforced support structures and a compact tactical footprint, creating a dramatic mix of command relay, battlefield outpost and thematic terrain. It works perfectly as line-of-sight blocking terrain, objective scenery, mission target or a striking centerpiece for desert and outer-rim battlefields. Its tall shape makes it especially useful for Star Wars: Legion , where terrain height, cover and objective placement can have a major impact on the flow of the game. The design fits naturally into Geonosis-themed boards, Separatist installations, Republic invasion zones or any arid sci-fi battlefield and helps create a cinematic tabletop experience. For easier printing and handling, the tower is split into two main sections at the middle. Both parts are designed to fit together with a simple plug connection, allowing for straightforward assembly after printing while keeping the overall structure tall and impressive on the table. All my models are real test prints, not just digital renders. I always try to find the best balance between print time, level of detail and filament usage, so the terrain looks impressive on the table without becoming unnecessarily difficult or wasteful to print. I also put a lot of effort into optimizing the files, removing print issues and making the models as user-friendly as possible. My goal is to offer terrain that prints cleanly, feels solid, and can be used straight from the printer or painted with simple drybrushing techniques. Designed with FDM printing in mind, the piece is suitable for PLA filament printing and looks great in simple grey material without any color changes. The finely sculpted fur, powerful musculature, and flowing tail emphasize both speed and strength, while the scenic rocky base reinforces the creature's natural hunting grounds without distracting from its imposing stance. A Displacer Beast rarely attacks head-on. It circles. It confuses. description: About Models: These models are designed to represent real animals as naturally as possible, with focus on accurate size, shapes, proportions, colors, fine details, and natural movement or pose. Some models include articulated, hinge, or flexi parts for motion and flexibility, while others are non-articulated and focus on realistic appearance. Some parts, such as legs, can be carefully adjusted with gentle heat for a more natural pose, but too much heat can damage or deform the model. Print: All settings are pre-configured and optimized for a balance between detail, print time, strength, functionality, and easy support removal. I recommend printing the models at their original scale. Scaling down may cause issues such as fused moving parts, small hinges not working correctly, or fine details not printing properly. Difficulty Guide: The difficulty icon is a general overall guide and may vary depending on your printer, filament, slicer settings, calibration, and experience. It mainly reflects print complexity, filament changes, possible waste, fine details, support use, and support removal. Multicolor prints may create more waste on single-nozzle AMS or AMS Lite systems, such as A1 with AMS Lite, compared to dual-nozzle or lower-waste systems like X2D or H2C. Level 3 / Supports: For higher difficulty models, especially Level 3, I recommend using Support Material for PLA. It can make support removal much easier, cleaner, and safer for delicate parts. This is especially helpful when the model has many supports, thin details, legs, antennas, or other fragile areas. Note / Handling: Some models may have very small hinge parts or delicate thin areas, such as legs, antennas, tails, or other small details. On some models, these parts may disconnect or break more easily if handled roughly. Please handle the models with care. They are not intended for aggressive play, but rather as educational models, display pieces, or gentle collectible toys. Durability may vary from model to model. Some models are stronger and may be suitable for careful play, while others are more delicate and better suited for display on a shelf. Articulated / Hinge Versions: For models with moving parts, hinges, or flexi sections, please open the included 3MF file, ideally in Bambu Studio. Exporting to another slicer may cause hinge problems. My hinges are created and tested by me, usually designed to print without supports, and are added this way so they can be moved, adjusted, customized, or removed when scaling the model down. STL / 3MF Note: STL files are usually provided without moving parts. The prepared articulated or hinge version is inside the 3MF file. This helps avoid problems with small scaled-down models, where moving parts, gaps, or hinges may fuse or fail. If needed, you can remove the hinges and print the model as a solid version. Safety Notice: Some models may have sharp edges or small parts. Avoid printing them too small and do not leave children unattended with them, as there is a choking risk. If you adjust parts with heat, always proceed carefully and use heat gently. Support / Links: I truly appreciate every comment, rating, or photo of your print it really motivates me to keep creating.
