description: DISCLAIMERS This is a fairly invasive modification. It requires drilling eight 3 mm holes into the acrylic top cover and replacing two of the factory screws on the side of the machine with longer ones. If you are not comfortable making these modifications, I recommend not attempting this. I do not take responsibility for any damage that occurs during the installation or use of this model. If I encounter any issues myself or someone reports any, I will try to release an updated version with a fix or, if that is not possible, I will remove the model to prevent further problems. Please watch the video to see the installation process and the finished result. Somebody will most likely come up with a more elegant or more secure solution in the future. I simply wanted to give this idea a try. I do not recommend printing these parts in PLA or PETG. In the video I used PLA only because I was prototyping. I later replaced every part with PA612-CF. A rigid, temperature-resistant filament is highly recommended. You will need several M3 screws in different lengths. The design is fairly forgiving in some areas, so multiple lengths can work. Below I have listed the sizes I used, along with alternative recommendations based on my testing. I also recommend keeping the parts in their supplied/uploaded print orientation for printing. They were arranged specifically to maximize strength by avoiding weak layer line orientations. All of the strength settings have been tested my be. I do not recommend reducing the amount of walls, top/bottom layers or infill percentage. Increasing is fine. Different infill pattern should also be fine. The model consists of: A - 2 hinge assemblies (2 parts each) B - 2 backplates C - 2 side reinforcements D - 1 middle reinforcement Only minimal supports are required. The holes are intentionally designed with very tight tolerances. In most cases you will need to use the screws themselves to thread the holes slightly during assembly. This is intentional to eliminate unnecessary play. If your printer struggles with dimensional accuracy, you can carefully open the holes up using a 3 mm drill bit. Step 1 Assemble the hinges. Refer to the photos for the correct orientation. The two hinge halves fit together tightly. Each hinge requires: 1 × M3x40 mm screw 1 × M3 nut The screw direction does not matter as long as it passes completely through the hinge and is secured with the nut. Step 2 Remove the factory screws from the toolhead communication assembly. Insert the assembled hinges by pushing the locating pins into the holes where the factory screws were removed. Make sure the pins are fully seated. You may need to twist or wiggle the hinge slightly while pushing it into place. If the pins are excessively tight, lightly sand or shave them until they fit. Secure each hinge with a screw, but do not fully tighten them yet. On my printer, an M3x40 mm screw was almost a perfect fit if you want it to sit flush from the inside (see the video, XXXX timestamp). I personally used M3x45 mm screws and secured them with a nut on the inside. Step 3 Place the top cover back on the printer and make sure it sits straight, flush, and pushed as far toward the hinges as possible. Flip the hinges upward so they sit flush against the cover. Install the mirrored side reinforcements onto the hinges. Each reinforcement only fits on one side. With the reinforcements installed, you can rotate the hinges slightly left or right to fine-tune their position. If the hinges move too freely, lightly tighten the screws from Step 2. The goal is for the side reinforcements to sit perfectly flush against the walls and corners of the top cover. Repeat on the opposite side. Once you are satisfied with the alignment, use the eight mounting holes in the hinges to mark the drilling locations on the acrylic cover. Take your time during this step. This is the point of no return. Up until now, every modification has been completely reversible. Step 4 Remove the top cover and place it on your work surface. Using a 3 mm drill bit, drill all eight marked holes. After drilling, remove all burrs and debris. Step 5 Install the screws into the backplates. Top holes: M3x20 mm Bottom holes: M3x10 mm for flush fit. Longer screws will work but reduce the opening angle. The 12 mm screws will protrude slightly and slightly reduce the maximum opening angle of the lid. If you want the cover to open a little farther, use M3x10 mm screws instead. Longer screws can also be used if you prefer a smaller opening angle. There is some room for personal preference here. Insert the screws through the acrylic from the inside until the backplate sits completely flush against the inside wall of the cover. Repeat for the opposite side. Step 6 Remove the hinge assemblies from the printer (see Step 2). Slide the hinges onto the screws protruding from the backplates. Because of the tight tolerances, you may need to rotate each screw gradually with a screwdriver instead of simply pushing the hinge into place. Step 7 Secure the lower four screws (two per hinge) with nuts. Install both side reinforcements, then place the middle reinforcement across the top. Secure the remaining four screws with nuts and tighten everything firmly. Step 8 Flip the hinges outward and reinstall the entire assembly onto the printer. Guide the two locating pins back into the holes from Step 2. Having a second person helping makes this step much easier. Once both pins are fully seated, close the cover and reinstall the side screws from Step 2. Tighten everything completely. Installation is now complete. A few things to keep in mind When closing the cover, you may occasionally need to wiggle it slightly so the two locating pins slide back into the frame correctly. If everything was aligned properly during Step 3, the cover should sit just as flush as it did before the modification. Do not slam the cover open or closed. Do not place objects on the open cover in the opened state. I have no idea how durable the acrylic will be over time. It is not particularly thick, and additional weight or force could cause it to crack. I also do not recommend leaving the cover open on the hinges for extended periods. Open it only when needed. Think carefully before deciding whether this modification is right for you. Finally, I cannot guarantee that every current or future Creator 5 will be manufactured identically. Small design changes may occur without notice, so fitment could vary between machines. description: A1 Vibration Damping Pods Inspired from the use of damping in the A2L. These mount to the brace that connects the X-axis to the Z-axis screws instead of the gantry. The mount is the point were any vibrations and or resonance would travel to the print head via the X-Axis – this way both X and Z axis have damping. Plus, space on my gantry is at a premium! French Riviera premium. I used Iron Sand (Iron Filings) - available on Amazon, or anywhere you buy your overpriced scientific supplies - as the damping material. I don't have the equipment, nor interest to do a bunch of testing to say how effective these may be in this application on this device. I have seen varying guides of how to calculate damping material v’s object mass. This is just the direct application of theory. Feel free to test and comment with your results below. * Assembly- Fill each compartment to approximately ¾ full. I used a hobby syringe. Make sure to fill them equally so they weigh the same on each side! Use a scale to weigh each compartment as you fill them. Mine weighed 57grams each, once filled. Your results may vary. but, if they weigh the same as mine we can be twinzies. Seal each compartment by gluing a plug in the fill port. Or fill each port with a glue plug. Insert into X-axis brace from the top. Will be a snug fit by design. Grunting and cursing may ease the process. Make sure they sit all the way down. My brackets had some significant burrs, so you may need to de-burr or perform some fitment of the Pods. Insert clip from below. Or lower the printer onto the clip. Secure bottom and pod together with the M3x6 button head coarse thread screw. Tighten until something snaps! Here we are again, 3D printing enthusiasts! It's mid-2026 and, after more than a year, I'm back with a new version of the "Great Calibrator," thanks to the success of previous versions. The model has undergone a redesign, losing some of the components that had been added to the main model over time and acquiring new ones (few, but effective). But the most impressive aspect is its compactness, precision, and ease of reading the tests, all while, of course, providing a good amount of stress to both your printer's steppers and nozzles, as well as the filament you're testing. Use is as simple and intuitive as ever: once printing is complete, let the print bed cool completely , then fold it and remove the main base. If your printer (or filament, or both) are already well calibrated, you'll notice that many parts will remain attached to the bed or will move away from it without remaining connected to the main base. This should (definitely) happen for the hinge and the bolt, as well as (probably) for the pins with the widest tolerance. Pins 3 and below may require a little pressure on the top. Caution: Don't use excessive force or tools to force a pin out. The goal is to read the tolerance allowed by the printer/filament combination under the conditions you printed under. An extreme unsuccessful print A successful print Let's review the model's components. Walls: The walls surrounding the main base should measure 0.8 mm , consisting of two 0.4 mm walls (the width of the standard nozzle). Turrets: As in previous versions, there are two turrets with a suspended sinusoidal upper part for support testing. You can therefore easily distinguish which method you prefer based on the results obtained. NOTE: There are two versions: the standard single-material version and the dual-material version that uses PETG and PLA for support separation. You'll notice some differences… Bridges: The bridge test is always present (the one on the far left with slopes of 45°, 60°, and the dreaded 75°) which, in theory, shouldn't pose any problems for your printers. I remind you that a "bridge" is a joint distance between two support points , and the different slopes are supported by two side walls. Half-bridges: Just like the bridges, to their right, at the center, you'll find the slopes for testing a half-bridge . What is it? Very simple, it's an overhang supported by a support on only one side , and the Great Calibrator gives you the ability to check the results for both sides. Overhang: A classic among classics, located to the right of the half-bridge, it has always been the biggest problem for a 3D printer: the "suspended" filament, meaning it's printed in "air" without any support. It depends on the extrusion capacity, filament cooling, rigidity, and the airflow system to your nozzle. The slopes don't change, but the 75° slope is more or less where the limit of what a filament printer can achieve stable overhanging ends. To verify them, it's not only important to note whether the lower part is aligned and not "spaghetti-like," but also to verify that the upper part can be completed with a good-looking top surface. Blades: The so-called "blades" have always been a distinctive feature of the Great Calibrator , as they allow for verification, and therefore adjustment, of the complexity of an extrusion balanced between thicknesses and spacing. These "blades" have a thickness that, from top to bottom, gradually decreases from 1.2 mm to a minimum of 0.4 mm (standard nozzle), with minimum distances that also decrease ( down to 0.05 ). The last distance may not be read at the slicer level, unless corrections are made or extrusion is somehow forced. This test (slicer stress) can therefore be verified already during the slicing phase without having to force printing in priority (the parameters provided with the model ensure that the last two blades are joined). Stringing stress cones : Here's another classic, placed in the center of the base, with the peculiarity that has always distinguished the Great Calibrator : the cones are not parallel to each other and not all perpendicular to the base. Obtaining a clean, smooth slin, complete cones, and no stringing will depend greatly on the quality of the filament, the extrusion temperatures, the quality of the nozzles, and so on. As you can see from the images, I managed to achieve excellent results with a simple A1 and a basic PLA filament from Bambulab . M-K-Nick : It's not the name of a rapper or a DJ, but the name of the "mechanical" innovation of the calibrator. Its shape and thickness are very unique and were specifically designed to be "easy" to print. The result should be a piece with properties that are elastic enough to be removed from the base without any effort (if your fingers aren't very fine, try using a simple tweezers, but don't force it. It should come out easily, despite the mechanical "block" caused by its particular shape). Bolt with its Nut: Here it is again, the essential bolt for testing the nut printed in the base circle. A well-calibrated printer should not cause any problems, so the nut should be easily screwed and unscrewed onto the bolt. The thread is standard, but the tolerance is approximately 0.2 mm between each wall, resulting in a total tolerance (circumference) of 0.4 mm. Som e problems may arise from the overhang required by creating the nut thread and/or the bolt itself . Parallelepiped dimensions : The block, as you can easily see, should measure 50 mm wide and 10 mm high and deep. Take the measurement, avoiding getting too close to the Base. Hinge: The other mechanical part of the Great Calibrator is this sort of "3-plate hinge" that can be used to test the possibility of performing some "on-plate direct printing" operations on mechanical parts. The plates that make up the hinge must be able to release with minimal effort and, once released, after a few bends to the left and right, they should have a fluid movement. Finally, don't forget the writing on the base, which must be perfectly legible: “ THE GREAT CALIBRATOR V1.0 BETA 04/2026" (yes... exactly, I started redesigning it in April lol)”. Try it, send me the print results and let's compare them. Together, we'll find solutions to the most common 3D printing problems and, above all, let's make "THE GREAT CALIBRATOR" a unique and indispensable model for all enthusiasts. model_name: Light and Fast Dual AMS Mount for H/X/P Series
description: I wanted a mount that didn't take too long to print or require too much material so I designed a mount that utilizes the weight of the AMS itself to help the mount clamp against the machine and keep the structure light. Unfortunately, the machines are not exactly the overall dimensions that Bambu cites. To accommodate this, the structure is broken into pieces that can be connected at various lengths to accommodate various printer sizes. This also makes them compatible with various models of Bambu machines. I also managed to fit all the parts in a single X/P series bed. H2C/H2S/H2D P2S X1C /X1E P1S/P1P AMS 2 AMS (3 Cavity) AMS (5 Cavity) Verified X X X X X Compatible X X Incompatible Note for High Temp Users: High temp printing with chamber heating will heat the printer glass beyond the glass transition temperature of PLA. This will cause warping of the structure. Please print the mount from a high temp plastic if you plan on printing chamber heated materials. If you only print PLA, this should not be an issue. Here is how the structure works: AMS weight hanging over the edge of the machine pushes down, forcing supports to pivot around the edge of the machine. Supports are retained by central tension member, which drives force into the side of the machine. Forces driving into side of machine increase friction between support and machine, improving grip. Small nubs on the central support posts retain both AMS units against each other, and prevent them from moving when the printer shakes. Size the frames so they are snug to the machine. If the notches only allow a slightly loose or slightly tight fit, choose the tight one. Once the weight of the AMS is loaded on top, any bowing in the structure will flatten out. The assembly utilizes toothed connections which are finely tuned to slide together and retain themselves with the layer lines of the print. If parts are too tight, they can likely be tapped together with a hammer without issue, just dont expect to get them back apart. If too loose, you can scale just the tensioning rods (the thin rectangular parts) to 101% to get a tighter fit. This gif shows the assembly process:

description: The YAPR™ (pronounced "YAP-er") — Yet Another Purge Receptacle Featuring BinLock™ push-button locking technology Not being completely satisfied with the first purge bin I ever printed, I set out to design (overengineer?) my own after getting the A2L. I wanted a purge bin that looked like it belonged on the printer , stayed exactly where I put it, and came off with a simple button press—without magnets, awkward removal angles, or extra hardware. I was tired of: Awkwardly angling or shifting the purge bin to remove it every time I emptied it (and sometimes spilling purge in the process) Constantly nudging the bin back against the printer because it would slowly vibrate away after a print or two Small pieces of purged filament finding their way between the bin and the printer Liners that frequently broke or cracked and needed to be reprinted The YAPR is a push-button A2L purge (or poop!) bin that locks securely in place, prints mostly in place, and requires no magnets or extra hardware . Designed to be the last purge bin you'll ever need to print. Features Easily attaches and detaches using exclusive BinLock™ push-button technology—no bin gymnastics required Securely locks in place and won't slowly vibrate away from the printer Matching side contour helps prevent stray filament from falling between the bin and the printer Contoured to match the printer's lines for a clean, OEM-inspired appearance Prints mostly in place with only a small amount of support beneath the button Available in three sizes: Slim (100mm wide — best for tight spaces), Standard (125mm wide — the daily driver), and Wide (150mm wide — ideal for heavy AMS printing and lower maintenance) Optional liner fully protects the bottom of the bin (unlike many liners with fully cut-out patterns) while also helping reduce purge rattling Won't block your printer's ventilation ports Angled bottom makes it easy to grab those last stubborn pieces of purge Assembly Notes This is specifically designed for the A2L only. For the easiest assembly, assemble within two hours of printing. The BinLock™ mechanism is intentionally designed with a tight initial fit and has a short break-in period. It will become noticeably smoother with use. If the button doesn't move smoothly after pressing it several times, grasp it with pliers and work it in and out a few times. The additional travel and force help speed up the break-in process. Instructions Choose your preferred size, print the bin , peg , and peg cover , then remove the small amount of support beneath the button. If using the optional liner, print the matching size in PETG (or PLA if you primarily print PETG). Press the BinLock™ button (located on the bottom right of the bin) several times to begin the break-in process (The first press requires a fair amount of force, so using two thumbs while bracing the bin against a countertop or table is recommended.) Hold the BinLock™ button down and rub a crayon over the small internal slide (see the second to last model photo for the exact location). While this may seem like an unusual step, it is important for smooth operation of the BinLock™ mechanism. The next few assembly steps are a little tricky—but thankfully, you only need to do them once. Turn the peg cover upside down with its tallest side facing you. Insert the peg upside down so the shortest side of the peg's triangular base faces to the right. The angle of the peg should *not* match the angle of the peg cover. Please see the last model photo for up close pictures. Without disturbing the peg, and with the longest side of the peg cover facing you , insert the peg and cover together into the bin until the cover snaps into place. Turning the bin upside down during this step usually makes assembly easier, and engaging the snap-fit may require a firm push. With the bin upright, press the BinLock™ button several more times. You should notice the peg moving slightly with each press as the mechanism continues to break in. If the button mechanism isn't working correctly, the peg may not be fully seated. Grip the peg firmly with pliers, pull it straight out with steady force (the peg and cover will come out together), then repeat the installation process. Connect to printer Hold the BinLock™ button. Slide the bin fully against the rear frame and side of the printer. Release the button to lock the bin in place. Disconnect from printer Hold the BinLock™ button. Pull the bin straight toward you. Print one. Lock it in. Forget about it.

Hallo Druckfreunde, heute gibt es einen Silica-Gel-Behälter für das AMS-HT . Alle Behälter, die ich bis jetzt gefunden habe waren mir einfach zu klein und dadurch ineffektiv. Mit dieser Box, mit Zusatztank, ist das jetzt kein Problem mehr. ;-) Die Box ist schnell und druckerschonend gedruckt. Wer möchte kann die Wandstruktur im Slicer anpassen. Hier wird das Infill ohne Boden- und Deckschichten gedruckt. Je nach verwendeten Trocknungsmittel und persönlicher Ausrichtung kann hier experimentiert werden. Ich empfehle, den Behälter mit ASA zu drucken. Getestet habe ich auch mit PLA und PETG. Im Prinzip funktionieren die Filamente auch. Seid euch aber bewusst, dass das AMS-HT im Trocknungs-Modus Temperaturen bis 80 Grad erreichen kann. PLA gibt da schnell auf und ihr dürft sämtliche Gelkugeln aus dem AMS fischen. Aber jeder, wie er will…. Getestet habe ich die Box auch mit einer vollen Filamentrolle von Bambu Lab. Sollte es Probleme mit der Passung oder Reibung an der Spule geben - lasst es mich wissen!!! Hier einige Vorteile dieses Modells: ein Behälter hat eine Druckzeit von ca. 2 Stunden benötigt wenig Filament und ist leicht für den Drucker zu bewältigen druckbar mit einer oder zwei Farbe für den Zusammenbau wird kein Kleber benötigt (mit Kleber hält es aber besser) die Wände werden als Infill gedruckt, somit sind diese voll anpassbar , wer will kann sich hier austoben Montagehinweis: der Druck liefert folgende Teile theoretisch hält das Modell ohne Kleber - es ist aber sicher nicht verkehrt, welchen zu nutzen fangt mit den Seitenteilen an - einfach in einander stecken dann die Böden einschieben ( hier kein Leim benutzen ) - Achtung, die Größe varriert! dann kann die Rückwand im hinteren Behälter eingebracht werden (etwas mehr Kraft ist anzuwenden) der Rand sollte nicht überstehen und der untere Teil in der Behälterführung verschwinden jetzt die beiden Behälter zusammenfügen - hier kann etwas Kleber verwendet werden achtet auf die Ausrichtung! Glückwunsch, du hast es geschafft!!! Jetzt noch mit Silika-Gel füllen und ab ins AMS-HT. ( Vielleicht gibt es später noch eine Befüllhilfe - mal sehen ) Viel Spaß beim Drucken und lasst Fotos in den Komentaren da!! Es gibt auch Trocken-Boxen fürs AMS und AMS 2 Pro.

description: AMS HT Side Mount für Bambu Lab H2 Serie Diese Halterung ermöglicht es, das AMS HT seitlich am oberen Rahmen eines Druckers der H2-Serie zu befestigen. Dadurch kann TPU direkt über die Bypass-Öffnung des AMS HT zum Druckkopf geführt werden. Der große Vorteil dieser Positionierung ist der extrem kurze und nahezu geradlinige Filamentweg. Das reduziert den Wiederstand beim fördern des Filaments auf ein Minimum und verbessert insbesondere den Druck mit sehr weichen TPU-Filamenten, die empfindlich auf lange oder stark gekrümmte Filamentwege reagieren. Zusätzlich kann das AMS HT während des Drucks weiterhin als Filamenttrockner genutzt werden. So bleibt das TPU während des gesamten Druckvorgangs trocken, was die Druckqualität zusätzlich verbessert. Einfache Konstruktion Die Halterung besteht aus drei Steckteilen, die ohne Schrauben oder weiteres Montagematerial zusammengesteckt werden. Diese Bauweise bietet mehrere Vorteile: Sehr einfacher und zuverlässiger Druck. Durch die modulare Bauweise, kann der Halter durch austauschen des Hakens auch für andere Druckermodelle genutzt werden. Nur eines der drei Bauteile benötigt eine winzige Stützstruktur. Die Halterung lässt sich jederzeit wieder zerlegen und dadurch besonders platzsparend verstauen. Hinweis: Je nach verwendeten Material und Kalibrierung des Druckers und Filament, kann es sein, dass die Steckverbindung schwergängig ist. Versuche nicht die Teile mit Gewalt zusammen zu stecken! In diesen Fall ist es hilfreich die Steckverbinder mit etwas Schlafpapier nach zu arbeiten. Etwas Gleitmittel wie Balistol oder WD40 kann ebenfalls helfen. Einfache Montage Für die Montage muss lediglich der Glasdeckel des Druckers entfernt werden. Anschließend wird die Halterung einfach über den oberen Rand des Druckers gesteckt. Das AMS HT wird danach nur auf der Halterung abgestellt - ganz ohne zusätzliche Befestigung. Druckprofile Für dieses Modell stelle ich 2 Druckprofile zur Verfügung: Profil 1 - H2D / H2C Dieses Profil ist ausschliesslich für den H2D und H2C vorgesehen. Das Bauteil wird aus PETG gedruckt, während die Interface-Schichten der Stützstrucktur aus PLA bestehen. Profil 2 - H2S Dieses Profil ist speziell für den H2S erstellt. Hier werden sowohl das Bauteil als auch die Stützstruktur aus demselben Material gedruckt- in meinem Fall PETG Halter für P2S & X2D Hier geht es zum AMS HT Seitenhalter für den P2S und X2D: https://makerworld.com/de/models/3075472-ams-ht-tpu-side-mount-for-p2s-x2d#profileId-3462867 Bis auf den Haken zum einhängen am Drucker sind die Teile für P2S/X2D und H2-Serie identisch! Durch austauschen des Hakens, kann man somit eine Halterung für verschiedene Druckermodelle nutzen. Falls dir das Modell gefällt, freue ich mich über einen Like, einen Download, einen Boost und natürlich über Fotos deiner Drucke! Viel Spaß beim Drucken!

description: One print. Ten common failure checks. Every test labels what to inspect and what to adjust next. Most calibration prints tell you that something is wrong. Print Doctor helps you understand what the failure means and what to try next. This is a single connected diagnostic print containing ten purpose-built tests. Each card includes: The print symptom A labelled failure point showing where to inspect Three likely slicer or printer adjustments Geometry designed to make that problem easier to see Print it with your normal material profile, leave supports off, and let the model reveal where the profile needs attention. The small connecting tabs keep everything together during printing and can be snapped afterward if you want ten individual reference cards. The cute cat-shaped Print Doctor header, mushroom cooling test, and elephant-foot paw make it friendly enough to keep beside the printer instead of hiding it in a drawer. Included tests Under-extrusion — thin-wall frame and narrow ribs reveal gaps, weak strands, and missing sections. Over-extrusion — labelled 0.20, 0.40, and 0.60 mm gaps show when excess flow begins fusing nearby features. Poor pressure advance — repeated sharp corners expose corner bulges and line thinning. Stringing — four separated spires create travel moves at different heights. Weak bridging — unsupported 8, 16, and 24 mm spans reveal sagging bridge undersides. Cooling issues — three mushroom caps use increasingly demanding overhangs. Z-seam quality — a smooth thin-walled cup makes seam zits, gaps, and inconsistent starts visible. Elephant foot — the paw specimen sits directly on the build plate so first-layer flare remains visible. Layer adhesion — three labelled bend paddles help reveal splitting between layers. Inconsistent wall thickness — circular, square, and hexagonal walls provide multiple surfaces to measure and compare. How to use it Slice the model with the profile you actually want to diagnose. Keep supports disabled; the unsupported features are intentional. Print the complete kit flat in its supplied orientation. Follow each raised WATCH label and inspect the indicated feature. Use the three adjustments printed on that card as your troubleshooting shortlist. Change one setting at a time and reprint when necessary. The printed suggestions are starting points, not absolute rules. Material condition, hardware, motion settings, and slicer behavior can produce similar-looking symptoms. Recommended print settings Material: PLA is recommended for the first diagnostic print Nozzle: 0.4 mm Layer height: 0.20 mm Walls: 2 Infill: 15–20% Supports: Off Brim: Off when possible, because a brim can hide elephant-foot behavior Orientation: Print flat exactly as supplied Profile: Use your normal profile rather than a specially tuned calibration profile Model dimensions Footprint: 203.8 × 180.2 mm Maximum height: 22.2 mm Assembly: One connected, manifold print with optional breakaway cards The full kit fits a typical 220 × 220 mm build plate. Confirm the slicer's skirt, purge line, and machine-specific exclusion zones before printing.

model_name: Snapmaker U1 + Sunlu Filadryer S4 Feeder Adapter
description: Humidity, my worst enemy… Snapmaker sent me the U1, and unfortunately, I'm not able to get good prints with printers that have open-air spools (because of the humidity at my location). So I looked for the best way to deal with it, and none of the projects I found were good enough. The closest one used a Sunlu Filadryer S4, so that was my baseline to start this project: Snapmaker u1 + Sunlu Fliladryer S4 Setup Compact setup Air-tight (at least as much as the original S4) It has the feeders as close as possible to the spools → Easier loading and unloading This is a DIY project, so you will need some tools and materials: M3 x 6 Screws, 4 of them with nuts and washers 2 x PTFE connectors. The ones that allow the 4 mm PTFE tube to pass through Drills (3.5 mm for the screws, and one for the size of your PTFE connectors) Extra PTFE tubes (4 mm OD, 2.5 mm ID) to replace the ones that go from the original feeder location to the back of the printer. Feeder extension cable. This might be the trickiest. They can be found as GH1.25 or JST GH1.25. Be sure they are 15-pin and male-female configuration. The length depends on your setup; measure both sides from the feeder's original location to the back of the Sunlu S4. I recommend 50 cm. I'll leave some links in the comments. I don't have measurements of the process, because I did it on the go and wasn't planning to upload it anywhere. But I have some pictures taken from the video I recorded: Depending on your setup, you would want to place the S4 on the right or the left of the U1. Therefore, you need to install the feeders on the side of the S4 that faces the back (as shown in the pictures above). You need to measure the distance between the feeder inputs, and drill the holes in the S4 to install the PTFE connectors. Then, assemble the feeders in the printed holder, and place it with the holes aligned to the filament input. Mark the Holder holes, and drill the 3.5 mm holes for the screw assembly. Assemble it, place the numbers from the inside, and then the funnels (optional, but recommended) Then, place the U1 and S4 in the final position, measure, cut, and install the PTFE tubes from the printer to the feeder. Don't make them too short or they might bend; leave some extra for them to wiggle around with smooth curves. That's about it. PTFE Clips Helps prevent PTFE tubes from rubbing against the top glass These lightweight PTFE tube clips are designed to help keep the tubing from wearing on the upper glass panel on enclosed Bambu Lab printers. They have been tested on the Bambu Lab X2D and are designed for standard 4 mm PTFE tubing , so they may also fit other compatible Bambu Lab models. Why I designed them As the toolhead moves around the printer, the PTFE tubes naturally twist, bend and change position. Some tube-management solutions hold multiple tubes tightly together to create a neater appearance. While this may look tidy, it can also introduce unnecessary tension, stress or twisting into the tubing as the toolhead travels. These clips are designed to support each tube individually. This helps reduce wear on the PTFE tubes from the top glass while still allowing the tubes to move as designed. Key features Helps prevent PTFE wear from rubbing on the top glass Designed for standard 4 mm PTFE tubing Tested on the Bambu Lab X2D Allows each tube to move independently Applies only light tension to the tubing Lightweight and low profile Quick snap-on installation No tools or printer modifications required Small and fast to print How many should I use? I currently use four clips , which provides good support and separation. More clips can be installed if additional support is required, but avoid using so many that the tubing becomes stiff or restricted. Recommended print settings These were successfully printed using: Layer height: 0.16 mm Walls/perimeters: 3 Bed temperature: 60°C Part cooling fan: 0% for the first 2 - 3 layers, then a maximum of 25% Brim: Not required Supports: Not required Keeping the cooling fan low helps prevent these small parts from cooling too quickly, warping or lifting from the build plate. Material recommendations PLA is suitable for normal use where the heated chamber is not being used. For printers operating with a heated chamber, use a more temperature-resistant material such as: PETG ABS ASA Another suitable heat-resistant filament PLA may soften or deform when exposed to elevated chamber temperatures for extended periods. Installation Carefully snap each clip over a PTFE tube. Position the clips along the tubing where support is required. Move the toolhead through its full range of travel. Check that each tube can still bend and move freely. Reposition or remove clips if any tension or restriction is present. Important notes These clips are intended to gently guide the PTFE tubes, not lock them rigidly in place. After installation, confirm that: The tubes still move freely The clips do not contact the cable chain The tubing is not stretched, kinked or twisted The toolhead can reach the full build area The clips remain clear of all moving components Compatibility Tested on: Bambu Lab X2D Tube size: 4 mm PTFE Other models may be compatible but have not yet been tested Support the design

description: Tired of small, overflowing purge bins, this modular flexible tube allows you to route waste directly into any container for uninterrupted long-term printing. description: This is a simple magnet fit tolerance test kit for common round magnets used in 3D printed projects. Instead of guessing the perfect hole size for your magnets, print the test strip that matches the magnets you have, press your magnets into the different holes, and choose the fit that works best for your printer, slicer settings, filament, and material. The kit includes separate test pieces for: 3×2 mm magnets 4×2 mm magnets 5×2 mm magnets 6×2 mm magnets 8×2 mm magnets 10×2 mm magnets Each size is a separate part, so you do not need to print the whole kit. Just print the strip for the magnet size you actually have. Each strip includes multiple hole diameters around the nominal magnet size, with the tolerance clearly labelled above each hole. For example, the 6×2 mm strip tests hole sizes from 5.95 mm to 6.25 mm. The magnet pockets are designed for 2 mm thick magnets. The back of each pocket is intentionally thin so the magnet can be pushed back out after testing. Why use this? Magnet fit can vary a lot depending on: Printer calibration Filament type Material shrinkage Nozzle size Slicer settings Hole compensation settings Whether you want a press fit, loose fit, or glue-in fit For best results, print the test strip in the same material you plan to use for your final project. For example, if your finished part will be PETG, print the test strip in PETG. If your final part will be ABS, print the test strip in ABS. Included sizes 3×2 mm magnet test Tests: Ø2.95, Ø3.00, Ø3.05, Ø3.10, Ø3.15, Ø3.20, Ø3.25 4×2 mm magnet test Tests: Ø3.95, Ø4.00, Ø4.05, Ø4.10, Ø4.15, Ø4.20, Ø4.25 5×2 mm magnet test Tests: Ø4.95, Ø5.00, Ø5.05, Ø5.10, Ø5.15, Ø5.20, Ø5.25 6×2 mm magnet test Tests: Ø5.95, Ø6.00, Ø6.05, Ø6.10, Ø6.15, Ø6.20, Ø6.25 8×2 mm magnet test Tests: Ø7.95, Ø8.00, Ø8.05, Ø8.10, Ø8.15, Ø8.20, Ø8.25 10×2 mm magnet test Tests: Ø9.95, Ø10.00, Ø10.05, Ø10.10, Ø10.15, Ø10.20, Ø10.25 Printing notes These are quick, simple prints and should not need supports. Recommended settings: Layer height: 0.16 mm or 0.20 mm Walls: 2 or more Infill: 10 to 20% Supports: No Brim: Not usually needed Orientation: Print flat on the build plate Material: Use the same material you plan to use for your final magnet project For the most accurate results, avoid scaling the model. 1 colour or 2 colour printing This model can be printed in either one colour or two colours . For a simple print, use one colour. The labels are still useful as raised or engraved text. For better readability, print the text in a second colour. A dark base with light text works especially well. How to use Choose the test strip that matches your magnet size. Print it in the material you plan to use for your final project. Press your magnet into each labelled hole. Find the fit you prefer. Use that hole diameter in your own CAD model. A tighter fit may work well for press-fit magnets. A looser fit may be better if you plan to use glue. Notes If you need a different magnet size, leave a comment. I can make additional sizes if people would like them.

description: X2D Auxiliary Fan Duct The Bambu Lab X2D auxiliary fans can direct a significant amount of cool air across the left and right edge of the build plate. For materials such as PLA, and particularly PETG, this concentrated airflow may contribute to uneven cooling, edge lifting, corner warping or reduced first-layer adhesion on some models. These deflectors redirect the auxiliary fan airflow upward and away from the print bed, helping prevent the fans from blowing directly across the edges of the print while still allowing air to circulate inside the chamber. Why I designed these I began experiencing prints lifting primarily along the edges closest to the auxiliary fans, which indicated that the concentrated airflow across the front of the build plate was contributing to uneven cooling. Although auxiliary-fan values can be adjusted within the filament and process profiles, the commanded settings do not always appear to remain in effect during printing. In some situations, the printer’s internal control logic applies its own auxiliary-fan behaviour and overrides the values defined in the slicer. This means the fan may continue operating at a higher speed than expected, even after the cooling profile has been adjusted. Because the underlying firmware-controlled behaviour is not currently exposed as a separate user-adjustable setting, it can be difficult to reliably prevent direct airflow from reaching the front edge of the print bed. These deflectors provide a mechanical solution by changing the direction of the airflow itself. Rather than attempting to reduce or disable the fan electronically, they redirect the output upward and away from the build surface while still allowing air to circulate within the chamber. Key features Redirects auxiliary fan airflow upward and away from the build plate Helps reduce concentrated cooling along the edges of the print area May help reduce edge lifting and corner warping Maintains airflow inside the printer rather than completely blocking the fans Installs without permanent modification to the printer Can be easily removed when not required Designed as separate left- and right-hand deflectors Compatibility These deflectors have currently only been tested on the Bambu Lab X2D. Should fit P2S right side Aux Fan They are designed specifically around the X2D auxiliary fan outlets and surrounding clearances. Compatibility with other Bambu Lab printers has not been confirmed. Installation Fit each deflector over its corresponding auxiliary fan outlet, ensuring it is fully seated and secure. The outlet should face upward and inward, redirecting the airflow away from the surface of the build plate. After installation: Check that both deflectors are securely fitted. Confirm that neither deflector contacts the build plate, toolhead or any moving component. Manually move the toolhead throughout the complete build area. Run the printer’s normal homing or movement checks before beginning a print. Do not begin printing until full toolhead and build-plate clearance has been confirmed. Print settings The included print profile is the profile I used successfully for these parts. Recommended starting settings: Layer height: 0.16 mm Walls/perimeters: 3 Supports: Not required Brim: Painted on edges only to prevent lifting Orientation: Print in the supplied orientation The parts should be allowed to cool before removal from the build plate to avoid distortion. Material PLA is suitable for testing and general use. PETG, ABS or ASA may provide improved temperature resistance for long-term use inside the enclosed printer, particularly when printing materials that require elevated chamber temperatures. Important notes These deflectors change the direction of the auxiliary fan airflow. They do not provide electronic control over fan speed. Cooling requirements vary depending on: Filament type Model geometry Print speed Chamber temperature Bed temperature Auxiliary fan speed These parts are intended as a practical airflow-management accessory, not as a guaranteed fix for every adhesion or warping issue. Bed cleanliness, first-layer calibration, filament condition and suitable temperature settings should still be checked.

description: I created this low-profile, high-flow X2D downward-facing exhaust adapter for a compact air filtration unit. (I will be posting the full unit on MakerWorld soon as well!) I printed and tested some of the other low-profile exhausts on MakerWorld, but they either restricted the airflow too much or didn't fit my specific use case. To ensure optimal performance, I simulated the airflow of my model in SOLIDWORKS Flow Simulation (visible in the attached images). While it’s obviously not perfect given the tight space restrictions, it's the absolute best path for the air to travel. Note that the simulation was ran quite conservatively at around 25 CFM, whereas the real-world airflow of the final design is closer to 45-65 CFM (depending on fan speed). The indentation within the exhaust is for you to fit some vacuum foam to ensure air tightness ONLY if you want to, works perfectly fine as is. The total clearance length required from the back of the printer to the exhaust is around 12.5 cm. It is available in all the common exhuast sizes, if you need any specific size do let me know. I printed in a abs/asa mix. Try not to print in pla since the exhaust gas is hot. PETG should be fine. It should also work with P2S, i don't have the printer so if anyone tried it please do let me know. I'd appreciate it if you could leave reviews on how the exhaust functions so I can improve on it further as well.

description: Snap-On Remix for Fixed-End Spool Holders A snap-on remix of David D.'s Hanging (Pendulum) Filament Guide, a weighted arm that hangs on your spool holder and keeps light tension on the filament path from external spools, so the line can’t drift off the spool and tangle. His original closed eyelet is the right design when you can slide it onto the rod from one end, and it comes in three eyelet sizes (26, 36, and 46mm). If your spool rod is removable, go print his version. But some holders have fixed ends with flares or caps, like the Bambu X2D stock top mount, and nothing threads onto those. This version converts the 26mm eyelet to a C-clip that snaps onto the holder radially and stays put. The Engineering The opening size is not a guess. The gap is a 90 degree segment sized from bending strain math for a C-ring flexing over a 26mm shaft. Peak strain during snap-on lands around 1.4 percent, comfortably inside PETG’s working limit. Rounded entry bulbs on the tips guide the shaft in and spread the ring smoothly. The gap is also rotated 60 degrees off the arm centerline, so the load path never rests on the opening. It goes on with a firm push, a positive click, and swings freely as a pendulum. Tested on an X2D stock top holder and others (as seen in the photos) in PETG HF. Bonus: Light Spool Keeper Many fixed-end holders are graduated, widening toward the flared end. Because this clip fits snugly instead of loosely, it doubles as a spool keeper: it blocks the spool from walking outward off the end while still penduluming freely guiding your filament with ease. Material Matters Print this in PETG, ASA, or ABS. The snap fit depends on flex. PLA has roughly half the strain tolerance, so it will probably survive a couple installations, but repeated cycles with PLA will likely cause stress cracking, and matte PLA is even worse. I haven't tested PLA to failure on this, so YMMV, but I'd just use PETG or something with better strength and flex than PLA. ⚠️ IMPORTANT PRINT NOTE Use 4 or more wall loops (the profile has this set). The ring works as a spring and needs solid perimeters in the bending section, not sparse infill. Everything else stays at defaults. The plate includes mirrored left and right arms, plus the original design’s small locking pins as an optional backup if the detents ever wear. The original designer reports the detents holding fine on their own and that has been true for me as well, but they're there if you need them.

description: Bambu A1 and A2L Swiveling PTFE Tube Guide - Parametric, with Print-in-Place Ball Joint A small ask : if you print this and find it to your liking, please rate my model. Ratings contribute to model visibility. Thank you ! If you've ever glanced over mid-print and noticed your drybox or your AMS Lite slowly sliding toward the print bed - pulled there by a taut filament tube - this one's for you. PTFE tube management is one of those details that seems trivial until it isn't. A loose or unsecured tube puts real tension on whatever it's attached to: a desktop spool holder, an AMS Lite, or a drybox on a shelf. Some existing guides rely on a dovetail joint or a friction fit that works fine in theory - until the repeated motion of printing slowly works the joint loose, and by the time you notice something is wrong, your setup has already been dragged somewhere it shouldn't be. I learned this the hard way so I designed my own. My design uses a fully print-in-place ball joint: it articulates freely so the tube always follows the print head without resistance, but the ball is physically captured inside the housing - there's no clip, no friction fit, nothing that can pull apart under load. The lever is printed horizontally so its strength doesn't rely on layer adhesion at all. And the C-clip uses a carefully angled opening that holds the tubes in place during normal use. Fully Parametric Configure four values to match your setup: Guide placement - top of the printer (usually for external spools) or towards the front (usually for a side-mounted AMS Lite) Guide diameter - size the C-clip to your tube count and diameter Lever length - a short lever works for most prints; increase it if you frequently print very tall models and need more slack Ball joint offset - position the guide towards the front, center, or back of the top bar Pre-configured standard variants are published alongside this model, so if your setup is typical you can go straight to printing without touching a single parameter. Printing note After printing, gently move the lever in the joint until it becomes loose and starts swiveling. Longer lever variants require a small horizontal bridge support under the lever. The included print profiles handle this automatically. Happy printing !

model_name: Will it stick? Adhesion / Warping Torture Test
description: Everyone runs their own warp/adhesion tests. Nobody else ever learns from them. Every time someone figures out whether a filament sticks to a plate, that answer stays in their head, and the next person burns time and filament rediscovering it. You end up getting people in discord or reddit or forums having their own tiny bit of anecdotal evidence, and everyone cargo cults it. Will It Stick fixes that: print one standard model, report what happened, and your result joins a free, searchable matrix of build plate × filament × surface prep results at willitstick.fyi . Because every data point comes from this exact model, results are directly comparable across plates, materials, and brands; one shared test instead of a thousand private ones nobody can see. One short print, three answers 1. First-layer adhesion: did the first layer grip without sliding or lifting? 2. Warping: are the corners and long edges still flat when the print finishes? 3. Ease of removal : does it release cleanly once cool, without damaging the plate? Your result feeds the community adhesion matrix at willitstick.fyi ; crowdsourced, like-for-like data on which filaments stick to which build plates, with which surface prep. Every result comes from this exact model, so combos are actually comparable. Submitting takes about two minutes and no account: snap one photo, record pass/fail for the three checks at https://willitstick.fyi/submit . Full protocol (with photo examples) at https://willitstick.fyi/how-to-test ⚠️ Because this model is deliberately brutal, a failure doesn't mean your plate or filament is bad! It's a way to compare plate performance with evidence instead of feels. Print Settings: A 3mf for OrcaSlicer 2.4.1 is available in “Download STL/CAD files” Layer Height 0.2mm Walls 4 Top Layers 2 Top Shell Thickness 0.4mm Bottom Layers 2 Sparse Infill Density 50% Sparse Infill Pattern Aligned Rectilinear Infill/Wall Overlap 20% Example results: printed with (extremely warp-prone) Bambu Lab PA6-GF The forbidden dorito: A much more slight warping failure (glue helps!): And a perfect pass: There's also useful overview information for each plate in the database! btw, the firethorn is the only plate so far that didn't warp with Bambu PA6-GF without glue . description: Give your Bambu Lab printer a retro gaming makeover! I couldn't find a PS Vita inspired screen cover for my X2D or P2S, so I decided to design one myself. The goal wasn't just to make something that looked similar, it was to capture the proportions, spacing and overall feel of the original handheld while making it work naturally with the printer's touchscreen. The printer's display is slightly larger than the PS Vita's, so I chose to keep the bezel true to the console's proportions rather than shrinking the design and throwing off the iconic look. The result is a bezel that feels instantly recognisable while making the printer screen look like it was always meant to be there. The bezel simply snap-fits over the existing display with no modifications required. To maintain the authentic proportions of the original unit, the screen is intentionally tilted slightly upwards to provide enough clearance for the printer door to open. If you prefer to mount your screen flush against the printer, this design may not be suitable. However, I personally keep my screen slightly offset from the unit, so this has never been an issue for me. You still retain almost the full range of movement only the final portion of travel, when the screen is pushed completely flush against the printer, is lost. For me, preserving the correct proportions was well worth the small compromise. The shoulder buttons and camera lens are designed to be printed in a transparent filament for the best appearance, but they can also be printed in any colour you like. Whether you're a PlayStation fan, a retro gaming enthusiast or just want to personalise your printer, this is a fun little project that adds plenty of character without affecting everyday usability. description: X2D Support Test – Multi-Material Support Benchmark Dieses Modell wurde speziell entwickelt, um die Qualität von Supportstrukturen und Multi-Material-Drucke objektiv zu bewerten. Durch die verschiedenen Überhänge, Aussparungen, Brücken und Kontaktflächen eignet sich der Test hervorragend, um die Druckqualität unterschiedlicher Materialkombinationen zu vergleichen und optimale Einstellungen für saubere Support-Oberflächen zu finden. Was wird getestet? Oberflächenqualität über Supportstrukturen Maßhaltigkeit kritischer Geometrien Qualität von Überhängen und Brücken Trennbarkeit der Supports Einfluss verschiedener Interface-Materialien Druckzeit und Materialverbrauch Vorteile von Multi-Material Supports Durch die Verwendung eines separaten Support-Interface-Materials lassen sich deutlich sauberere Unterseiten und Kontaktflächen erzielen als mit Supports aus dem gleichen Material. Besonders bei anspruchsvollen Überhängen können dadurch: glattere Oberflächen bessere Maßhaltigkeit weniger Nacharbeit einfachere Supportentfernung erreicht werden. Empfohlene Druckvarianten Variante 1 – Nur Support-Interface in anderem Material (empfohlen) Hier wird das Modell und die eigentlichen Supportstrukturen mit dem Hauptmaterial gedruckt. Lediglich die Support-Schnittstellen (Support Interface Layers) werden mit einem zweiten Material erzeugt. Beispiel: Modell: PLA Supports: PLA Support Interface: PETG Diese Methode bietet in der Regel das beste Verhältnis aus Druckqualität, Materialverbrauch und Druckzeit. Variante 2 – Komplette Supports in anderem Material Alternativ können sowohl die Supportstrukturen als auch die Support-Schnittstellen vollständig aus einem zweiten Material gedruckt werden. Beispiel: Modell: PLA Supports + Interface: PETG Diese Variante kann die Trennbarkeit weiter verbessern, erhöht jedoch den Materialwechsel erheblich. Wichtig: Durch die vielen Werkzeugwechsel zwischen den Materialien verlängert sich die Druckzeit deutlich und es entsteht zusätzlicher Materialabfall durch Spülvorgänge. Für die meisten Anwendungen ist daher Variante 1 die sinnvollere Wahl. Empfohlene Materialkombinationen PLA ↔ PETG PETG ↔ PLA ASA ↔ Support Material ABS ↔ Support Material Viel Spaß beim Testen! Teile gerne deine Ergebnisse, Einstellungen und Materialkombinationen in den Kommentaren, damit andere Nutzer von deinen Erfahrungen profitieren können. Hinweis Die Vorschaubilder und Darstellungen in diesem Eintrag wurden mithilfe von KI-generierten Grafiken erstellt und dienen ausschließlich der Veranschaulichung des Druckkonzepts. Das tatsächliche Druckergebnis kann je nach Drucker, Material und Einstellungen abweichen.

description: Flashforge Creator 5 Pro Spool Holder Adapter – Clog & Layer Shift Fix Overview This model is a slip-on cylindrical adapter / extension sleeve designed specifically for the stock spool holder on the Flashforge Creator 5 Pro . The main purpose of this part is to widen and smooth out the original holder's surface. The factory Flashforge spool holder is quite narrow and features open slots/holes; as a result, certain filament spools — especially reusable refill spools / master spools with internal locking tabs or ridges — can catch, drag, or get completely stuck. This friction restricts smooth filament feeding, triggering false "clog" errors and causing frustrating layer shifts mid-print. By sliding this sleeve over the original arm, you create a perfectly smooth, continuous surface with an optimal diameter. model_name: Tilted Low-Profile TPU Assistant Mount (X2D / P2S)
description: Staffa Compatta, Inclinata e Ribassata per TPU Assistant (Compatibile con Bambu Lab X2D / P2S) Ho progettato questa staffa per la mia X2D (essendo al 100% compatibile anche con il modello P2S ) con un obiettivo principale: migliorare radicalmente l'orientamento dei tasti del TPU Assistant per renderli finalmente visibili dal davanti, ottimizzare la direzione del tubo in PTFE verso l'AMS HT ed eliminare una volta per tutte la necessità di scollegare i tubetti durante l'uso quotidiano o l'essiccazione. Le caratteristiche principali di questo design: Gestione lineare del tubo (Nessun bisogno di scollegare nulla): Molti progetti online richiedono di scollegare il tubo in PTFE dall'AMS HT quando il TPU Assistant non è in uso, ad esempio per inserire il tappo di sigillo e avviare la funzione di essiccazione dell'Hub. Questo spesso comporta il dover riporre il tubetto rimosso per non perderlo. Con questa configurazione, grazie alla distanza ridotta e all'allineamento, non è mai necessario scollegare il tubo . Il condotto rimane stabilmente al suo posto e sigillato, semplificando i passaggi: basta spingere il filamento dall'AMS HT direttamente nel TPU Assistant e si è pronti a stampare. Inclinazione ed Ergonomia dei Tasti: La staffa è posizionata più in basso e inclina il TPU Assistant verso lo sguardo di chi si trova davanti alla stampante. In questo modo la pulsantiera e i LED di stato sono facilmente visibili e comodi da raggiungere direttamente dal fronte. Geometria del percorso posteriore e specifiche tubi: Essendo una staffa ribassata, la distanza geometrica verso l'ingresso della stampante aumenta leggermente rispetto alla configurazione standard, richiedendo un percorso totale fisso di 200 mm . Nota per la community: Bambu Lab raccomanda solitamente 160 mm, ma non c'è assolutamente da preoccuparsi per il caricamento . Il sistema del TPU Assistant è infatti progettato per funzionare ufficialmente anche sulla H2D , che è una stampante molto più grande della X2D e ha un percorso interno del filamento nativamente molto più lungo. Visto che il sistema gestisce quel tragitto maggiore senza problemi, i 4 cm esterni in più introdotti su questo setup vengono digeriti dall'estrusore in totale sicurezza. Per installare il sistema avete due opzioni precise: Setup Diretto: Vi servirà uno spezzone di tubo in PTFE tagliato esattamente a 200 mm . Con Adattatore 4-in-1: Se utilizzate un connettore 4-in-1 come il mio (lungo circa 6 cm), dovrete compensare la misura tagliando il tubetto in PTFE a 140 mm (140 mm + 60 mm = 200 mm). Design Essenziale: La struttura è pensata per essere il più compatta e leggera possibile, riducendo la quantità di filamento necessaria e i tempi di stampa. 🔄 IMPORTANTE: Calibrazione post-installazione Come raccomandato dalle linee guida ufficiali Bambu Lab, dopo aver installato la nuova staffa e posizionato il tubo da 200 mm (o 140 mm con adattatore), è fondamentale lanciare la calibrazione del modulo . Questa procedura serve a far leggere al sistema la nuova lunghezza del percorso, misurando l'attrito per calibrare al millesimo la forza della spinta automatica. 👉 Potete seguire la procedura ufficiale passo-passo a questo link della Wiki Bambu Lab: Guida alla Calibrazione del TPU Assistant . 🛠️ Note di Stampa e Tolleranze Materiale di Test: Il progetto è stato sviluppato, stampato e testato in PETG . Nota sulle tolleranze: L'asola di incastro per il TPU Assistant è calibrata in modo preciso sul PETG. Se decidete di stamparlo in PLA o ABS/ASA, tenete conto che il diverso ritiro termico dei materiali potrebbe influire leggermente sulla tolleranza dell'incastro (potrebbe risultare impercettibilmente più stretto o largo). description: This is a dedicated mount that uses the A1 mini's Z-axis cover to attach the BMCU 370C to the right side of the printer. Most existing mounts position the BMCU behind the printer, feeding the PTFE tube from the rear toward the front. However, if your setup has limited rear clearance, this can create an excessively tight bend in the PTFE tube. To solve this problem, this mount routes the filament from the right side of the printer toward the left, allowing the PTFE tube to follow a smoother, more natural curve even in tight spaces. After testing several designs, I found that positioning the filament path at approximately a 45° angle while placing the BMCU slightly farther from the printer provided the best tube routing. description: *** Update *** Upon request, I have made it so you are now able to print this Poop Chute and Dumpster for the A1 and A1 Mini printers. I added a new Clip to the existing Chute. You now just need to select the correct plate that matches your printer and you on your way. So funny story. I love printing things. Therefore I have a lot of plastic waste from poop to supports etc…. A while ago my husband says “your going to need a dumpster for all that plastic”. Then my neighbor noticed the several bags of plastic “poop” I have and said the exact thing. And only when my nephew comes over and says the same thing once again I thought to myself, I need to make a little dumpster to catch all the poop my printer makes. I pictured the Home Alone 2 movie where the house Kevin rigs up has a chute outside the window going into a dumpster. So that's where the idea for project came from. There are tons of “poop” bins and baskets for the other printers but I wanted to make one for my new Bambu Lab A2L printer. She's a beast. Very detailed and prints well. I love it. It does shake the house though being a large sized bed slinger. I have been printing on silent mode to calm it down in most cases. This took me a week to create. A little longer than usual but I needed to get the tolerances perfect. My main goal was to make it reliable and easy to print. That was the challenge. I tried several ways to get the chute to print as one piece but it never worked out. So clip or bracket that connects to the printer is separate and has to be glued to the chute. I did make a connection socket so the two fit together perfectly so all is needed is a drop of cyanoacrylate glue (Super Glue) or something similar on each edge of the connection opening and hold it in place for the appropriate time (depending on your glue). I have printed 19 sets of the chute and bracket and glued them together successfully with no problem. Supports were absolutely necessary to accomplish my goal. I tried to keep the settings simple but tweaked the settings like the top and bottom Z distance, speed etc… to get dumpster and chute to come out clean. Just be sure to keep my settings. You can add to them if you please but it wont be necessary as you can tell by my photos. I have had several people that don't have a printer me to print them one just because they wanted the cute little bin. I have even been changing the sizes per their requests. The dumpster itself is scalable and you can make a smaller or larger one depending on your needs. I am sure it will have many uses. Thank you ahead of time and please enjoy. Have a nice day.

description: This is a filament respooler that uses the structure of the Bambu Lab AMS Lite. It is an improved and updated version of my previously released model. A Bambu Lab AMS Lite is required to use this model. The printed parts cannot be used on their own. By utilizing the AMS Lite’s structure, filament can be transferred to another spool smoothly and reliably with only a small number of printed parts. The complete set requires approximately 90 g of filament to print. It supports manual operation with the included hand crank, as well as electric screwdrivers, electric drills, and ratchet wrenches. A dedicated storage case is also included to keep all the parts neatly organized when not in use. All parts can be printed on an A1 mini. Instructions 1. Assemble the Hand Crank The hand crank is assembled from three printed parts. The small hexagonal adapter is used when respooling with a ratchet wrench and a 10 mm socket. 2. Install the Holder on the AMS Lite Remove one rotary spool holder from the AMS Lite. Insert the printed inner holder onto the exposed AMS Lite shaft. This holder does not rotate, so the fitting is intentionally designed to be tight. 3. Install the Spools Screw the respooling core into the empty spool and tighten it securely. Install the empty receiving spool on the side fitted with the printed inner holder. Install the spool containing the filament on another spool holder of the AMS Lite. Pull out the filament and secure its end to the empty spool. 4. Respool the Filament For manual operation, attach the hand crank. When using an electric screwdriver, insert the hex driver bit fully into the drive socket. When using an electric drill, attach a 10 mm hex bit. When using a ratchet wrench, insert the included adapter and then attach a 10 mm socket. Important Notes An AMS Lite is required to use this model. This respooler does not include a mechanism for automatically distributing the filament evenly across the spool. Guide the filament from side to side by hand while respooling to prevent it from accumulating in one area. When using a power tool, always operate it slowly at a low speed.

model_name: Printer test model when buying used printers 50g
description: Ever buy a used printer and not be confident that it works as advertised? Don't take that gamble! Send the seller this test model to run prior to you arriving, and request that they leave it on the build plate as proof that the printer works as advertised. There is no denying that the printer printed it, if its still stuck to the build plate when you arrive! This model is not a calibration model , it does not test over hangs, extrusion, nothing like that. This test was designed to make sure the printer can print most of the build plate, as well as show that the Z axis is clean and not bend. You can scale it up or down, but going too small will make that first layer pretty thin. I recommend scaling so the bottom is only 1 layer thick. That will show you how even the bed is and if the printer can print big flat models. The vertical part will show the z axis wear and tear, as well as show layer shifts, VFAs, ghosting and overall print quality. Check around the engraved letters for ghosting and VFAs, check around the corners to see proper extrusion and cornering and ringing, check the circle section to see if there are visible layer shifting. Finally check the pyramid top to ensure it can complete a top without knocking the entire model below over. Again, this is not a test of calibration, just a simple test model for you to be confident that the used printer you are buying can perform basic 3D printer tasks. I am uploading profiles for most current BambuLab Printers, as well as including the STL for other printers.

description: I love maCyo42's AMS Riser V3. I put it on my P2S and it does a great job. I've already put up a remix that allows you to mount an AMS-HT on the side using the slots he designed it with. Unfortunately his riser blocks direct access through the top of the P2S for an overhead TPU spool holder. I have never gotten TPU to print properly on my P2S. I don’t print it often enough to buy the Bambu TPU filament feeder. It kind of annoys me that my A1 is able to print it so much easier. I could print a top spool mount for it but that would involve taking down the riser and AMS 2 Pro to use it each time. So I decided to design a front mount system to feed down into the P2S and not have to remove the riser and AMS 2 Pro each time. This heavy-duty, cantilever shelf bracket is designed specifically to solve that problem. It allows you to securely mount a Bambu Lab AMS HT (1.21 kg) and filament spool (up to 1.3 kg) directly above and in front of your printer, keeping your top-front feed path completely clear and accessible. No more moving risers, no more shifting your AMS units around just to print a quick TPU gasket or dampener. Many 3D-printed brackets fail because they are printed in multiple pieces or oriented incorrectly, creating a mechanical "hinge" that sags under a continuous 2.5 kg load. This design completely eliminates that failure point: One-Piece Diagonal Print: Optimized to fit barely but perfectly across a standard 256mm x 256mm build plate . By rotating it 45 degrees and printing it flat on its side, the perimeter walls run continuously from the anchor lip to the front tip. DON’T MOVE THIS ON THE PLATE, IT’S A NIGHTMARE TO GET IT TO FIT PROPERLY! Zero-Joint Cantilever: With no split joints or seams in the middle, the continuous extrusion lines effortlessly handle the forces of the shelf. Advanced Geometry: Features a massive single-diagonal structural gusset to direct the load straight back to the frame anchor and fillets on many internal 90-degree corners to eliminate stress concentration points. Recommended Print Settings Remember, you are relying on this part to securely hold an expensive AMS HT unit. I’ve tested using my settings and found it to be effective and sufficiently strong enough to hold the weight. I STRONGLY ADVISE PRINTING WITH MY EXACT SETTINGS IN PLA-CF. DON’T REARRANGE THE PRINT, IT’S EXTREMELY DIFFICULT TO GET IT ON THE PLATE WITHOUT GETTING AN OVER THE PLATE MESSAGE! To ensure this bracket holds up, use the following settings in Bambu Studio (I've already done that for you): Orientation: Print flat on its side, rotated diagonally to fit the bed. Do not use brims since we’ve hit the maximum length of Wall Loops: 6 to 8 walls (Crucial for structural rigidity). Infill: 40% to 45% (Gyroid recommended for optimal resistance against downward bending forces). Filament Choice: I’ve used PLA-CF and regular PLA, both work well for stiffness, I recommend using PLA-CF to give you the absolute best rigidity and long-term resistance to material creep under a sustained 2.5 kg load. Wall Generator: Arachne (to ensure seamless gap filling at the truss intersections). 👍 Support the Design! description: Hello! I’m excited to introduce my desiccant drying system specifically designed for the Creality Space Pi x4 filament dryer. I dedicated a lot of time and effort to developing this model, going through numerous iterations until I reached this version. After experimenting with a model I found in MakerWorld and encountering several issues, I decided to create my own. My goal was to design a strong, modular system that ensures unobstructed airflow. I also wanted something at incorporated a pour spout without taking up a lot of space or using a lot of filament. This filament drying system is stackable, robust, and easy to use. It’s large enough to accommodate two boxes and a frame on each side of the Space Pi x4. It measures 1500mm by 150mm by 60mm, features 2mm holes and a pour spout in one of the corners. Each box can hold a maximum of 500 grams of desiccant, but I recommend not exceeding 300 grams to expedite drying times and prevent overloading the frame. I successfully dried approximately 400 grams (200 grams per side) of wet desiccant in about 6 hours at 85 degrees Celsius, which is significantly faster compared to other solutions. Please note that to achieve the optimal drying temperature of 85 degrees Celsius, I highly recommend printing this model in ASA filament. I’ve shared my personal settings in the profile I published, which is in ASA. For faster prints, I used a .6mm nozzle, but if you prioritize quality, you can print it with a .4mm nozzle. Make sure to adjust the print settings accordingly. Turn off all cooling, lower the volumetric flow to 12 cubic millimeters per second, heat up the chamber to 65 degrees Celsius, and heat the build plate to 100 degrees Celsius. If you don’t have a heated chamber, heat soak it for at least 30 minutes before printing to minimize the risk of warping. Additionally, ensure that you use a textured PEI plate or an engineering plate. Wash it with soap and warm water, and apply a glue stick. ASA emits toxic fumes so use air filters and a proper mask when printing with ASA. Your health is too important to risk it! If this solution proves beneficial for you, I would greatly appreciate it if you could consider boosting me. Your support means a lot to me. Please also take a moment to comment, bookmark this model, and share it with others. I value all feedback, especially suggestions for model improvements. description: FULL EXPLANATION HERE: https://www.reddit.com/r/FDMminiatures/comments/1v0rerw/introducing_the_curling_tower_a_simple_solution/ This is a “Curling Tower” - A Model designed to combat “Curling”, especially when printing Miniatures. What happened here? When 3D Printing Miniatures with an FDM Printer, we run into some unique issues. One of which is the fact that even though it takes a long time to finish the print, the time spent on each individual layer is fairly short. Ideally, by the time the current layer starts printing, the previous one should have cooled down as much as possible. Now, if you're printing something large this isn't a problem - By the time the nozzle circles back to the starting point of the next layer, the previous one will have solidified. But, as you can probably guess, this isn't always the case for miniatures. It usually doesn't affect the entire model - Most of them are still large enough that the Layers will have enough time to cool down. Where it becomes an issue is with "isolated" parts of the model - Parts that are either only partially connected to the Model, or only become fully connected throughout the print. Examples of partially connected isolated parts are but are not limited to Swords raised towards the sky, Staffs and other weapons. Examples of isolated parts that only become fully connected throughout the print, are usually legs or similar body-parts. But what exactly is Curling, and why is it such an issue? When printing these isolated parts, the time spent on each layer is very short - So short that by the time, say Layer 100 starts, Layer 99 hasn't fully solidified yet. The heat of the Nozzle as well as the new layer of filament being placed on top of the previous Layer will re-soften the material further, causing the layer to be slightly lifted upwards. If this happened only once, it wouldn't be a major issue - The lift per layer is relatively small. But if it happens over multiple layers it becomes a problem. Eventually the filament will be curled enough for the Nozzle to slam into it, at which point it will most likely break of that part and ruin the print. With print times reaching the double digits, this is - as you can imagine - moderately upsetting. So how do we fix it? There are four common solutions to curling: Since Curling is caused by filament not cooling quickly enough, the easiest way is to simply increase the speed of the cooling fans. However, since most HQ Profiles already have these maxed out, this is unlikely to help most people. However: If they are already maxed out, but you still run into the issue - Make sure that they are actually clean. The fans on my A1 were stuffed with dust, which significantly lowered the cooling effect. If it's been a while since you last cleaned the fans, or never cleaned them at all, now might be a good start. If the fans are clean and already running at 100% speed, we might need to give them a little help by lowering our printing temperature. Filament leaving the nozzle at 220° will take longer to cool down than filament leaving the nozzle at 200°. The problem here is that you can only go so low before you start creating new issues, namely Nozzle Clogs. If you are already operating in the 195-200 range, you don't have much room left. If the problem is caused because the surface of the model is too small, we could simply increase the size of the Model. By upscaling it until the "vulnerable" part of the model has enough surface area for it to be printed with regular infill as opposed Solid Infill, the likelyhood of it warping becomes substantially smaller. Of course, this solution substantially increases print time and if you're printing Wargaming Proxies where scale matters, it's not suited for you at all. Printing multiple models. Following the same logic as Solution #3, instead of going for Model Size, we aim to increase the total print volume. By introducing at least a second Model to our print and print by layer, we can give each layer a cooling-buffer. As the printer finishes the Layer on Model A, Model B will have more time to cool down and vice versa. This solution also drasticially increases print-time, and comes with the downside of not only introducing additional risks in case the print fails somewhere, but also the simple fact that not everyone wants or needs multiple models. While all those four solutions work, I wasn't satisfied with any of them. The first two are limited by Hardware which, in some cases, simply isn't enough. The other two force you to print something other than what you actually wanted to print. So, I wanted to use a compromise. The Curling Tower - It's just a simple, hollow, square tower with thin walls. The idea here is simple - You print it alongside your actual model, with some distance between the two. Once the Printer has finished a layer for the Model, it will move to the Tower, giving the Filament on the Model enough time to cool down. Now, you might be thinking - That's just Solution #4 again, printing with more than one model at the same time. And you're right - But there is a catch. Because the Curling Tower is much more basic than any miniature, there isn't a whole lot that can go wrong with it. It's "safer" to print alongside your actual print, because there can't be any failed supports, harsh overhangs or even curling. And, because it's such a simple design - it will add significantly less time to the total print duration than a second, actual miniature would. But the real difference and big advantage, is that the Tower is adjustable. Remember when I said that Curling mostly affects the isolated parts of the model? In this case, it's the leg of the Skeleton - You don't need to print the entire Tower. You can just match the height of the tower to the point where the isolated part re-connects with the model and is out of the "Danger Zone" This means that you will have all the benefits of the "Cooling Buffer" that Solution #4 gives you, at a fraction of the increase in print time and material waste. To give you some numbers: Skelly without Tower or 2nd Model to serve as a Cooling Buffer: 3h45m Skelly with a 2nd Skelly as a Cooling Buffer: 6h56m Skelly with a Curling Tower equal to the Model Height: 4h54m 4h54 Skelly with a Curling Tower adjusted to the "Danger Zone": 4h14m That's an increase of only 13% when compared to the 86% increase you'd get when printing with a 2nd model. Now, is this something that you should use for all of your prints? No, of course not - Although in theory, it should also very slightly improve Overhangs for the same reason it fixes Curling - By giving them more time to cool before the next layer is added on top. But this is primarily meant as a tool for models that have a lot of isolated parts, or if you are struggling with Curling and none of the other solutions work out for you. So next time you're running into Curling even though your fans are already maxed out - Give this one a try.
