description: AMS HT Side Mount für Bambu Lab P2S and X2D Diese Halterung ermöglicht es, das AMS HT seitlich am oberen Rahmen des P2S und X2D zu befestigen. Dadurch kann TPU direkt über die Bypass-Öffnung des AMS HT zum Druckkopf geführt werden. Der große Vorteil dieser Positionierung ist der extrem kurze und nahezu geradlinige Filamentweg. Das reduziert den Wiederstand beim fördern des Filaments auf ein Minimum und verbessert insbesondere den Druck mit sehr weichen TPU-Filamenten, die empfindlich auf lange oder stark gekrümmte Filamentwege reagieren. Zusätzlich kann das AMS HT während des Drucks weiterhin als Filamenttrockner genutzt werden. So bleibt das TPU während des gesamten Druckvorgangs trocken, was die Druckqualität zusätzlich verbessert. Einfache Konstruktion Die Halterung besteht aus drei Steckteilen, die ohne Schrauben oder weiteres Montagematerial zusammengesteckt werden. Diese Bauweise bietet mehrere Vorteile: Sehr einfacher und zuverlässiger Druck. Durch die modulare Bauweise, kann der Halter durch austauschen des Hakens auch für andere Druckermodelle genutzt werden. Die Halterung lässt sich jederzeit wieder zerlegen und dadurch besonders platzsparend verstauen. Hinweis: Je nach verwendeten Material und Kalibrierung des Druckers und Filament, kann es sein, dass die Steckverbindung schwergängig ist. Versuche nicht die Teile mit Gewalt zusammen zu stecken! In diesen Fall ist es hilfreich die Steckverbinder mit etwas Schlafpapier nach zu arbeiten. Etwas Gleitmittel wie Balistol oder WD40 kann ebenfalls helfen. Einfache Montage Für die Montage muss lediglich der Glasdeckel des Druckers entfernt werden. Anschließend wird die Halterung einfach über den oberen Rand des Druckers gesteckt. Das AMS HT wird danach nur auf der Halterung abgestellt - ganz ohne zusätzliche Befestigung. tags: bambu|BAMBU LAB|TPU|tpu spool|tpu spool holder|tpu spool mount|wallmounted tpu|tpu wallmount|tpu holder|tpu bearing|tpu 608|spool|spool holder|spool holder bearings
description: This is the ultimate, fully customizable, wall mounted spool holder which should be suitable for the softest of filaments. It has been tested with: Bambu 95A Bambu 90A Bambu 85A Bambu TPU for AMS Siraya tech flex TPU Of course it should work with all standard filaments too. It features a total of six “tool” holders. The central two (one on each main arm) below the hub are designed to take the flap brake. The flap brake will only work with these two. The other holders are used for the friction brakes. This is the third version of my wall mount and based on the original one which was super smooth but had little control, could run backwards and overrun. I did update it with some brakes which helped but they weren’t very adjustable at all and adding a flap brake just wasn’t practical. I am still in a testing phase but even without adjusting between filaments this version has worked flawlessly so far. I hope it does for you too! Upgrading? For people who already have that old version, this version can re-use at least some parts you already have printed: The original wall brackets will work (although they will be tighter than the new ones). The PTFE tube holder is unchanged. The rear joining bracket is unchanged The wall template is unchanged, no need to redrill anything! Printing Suggestions. The 3MF file contains the settings and support methods I used for this print. Filament: Bambu PLA Metal Iridium Bambu PLA Metal Iron Grey Sparse infill 25% (15% will work just fne) Sparse infill pattern Gyroid Place brim ears on all four parts the two piece arms. In Bambu slicer the brim ears tool set to auto does a great job. You will need to set the brim type to “painted”. Materials you will need: Plugs and screws. Check the screw heads will sit in the countersunk hole and clear the dovetail on the arm. Plugs – if required – I used Fischer 4no. 6x30, 6mm drill bit Screws – 4no. 4x35 – make sure the head will sit within the recess A small amount of PTFE tube. (This is not essential, you can bypass the PTFE holder in use if you choose) Two 608 bearings – these are pretty good: https://www.amazon.co.uk/dp/B08ZN94S5L?ref=ppx_yo2ov_dt_b_fed_asin_title but almost any 608 bearing should be fine. Fleece fabric Tessa tape,19- 20mm ideally 51608-00001-00 Or Cable tie Velcro with the soft side as the brake 10-20mm wide Super glue. Installation and assembly: This video should help you understand how it works when assembled, I’d recommend you have sound turned on whilst I’m fitting the brake. Sorry.. VERY boring video :( https://youtube.com/shorts/ZhJ1bJGjlVE?feature=share Choosing parts: Note that I have named all the parts in the 3MF file. I will refer to them here. There are two types of spool arms. One set is only printable on a large bed printer such as the H2D. The other set should be printable on most printer beds and offers a different aesthetic if you use two colours. Photos/videos are of the two part type. Choose how many tool arms to print and of which type (more on this later!). If in doubt just print one standard tool arm “ARM TYPE1 MEDIUM”, one flap brake arm “ARM TYPE 3 Flap Brake”. Note: Arms can be inserted upside down in the front arm holder. Choose which tool to print, again, if in doubt I would suggest “Brake Tool TYPE 1” which has the ridges around and no chamfer. Choose a cover plate type (you may not want cover plates at all!) Note that the large cover plate has a bambu logo which looks nice if printed in a different colour. Choose your axle cap design round or hex – photos are of the hex type. You can choose not to print the flanges. The hub does not require either of them but you won’t get the non-reverse function of course. There is a filament guide included “Flimanent Guide OPTIONAL”. This helped to stop filament loop drops in version 1. I still have it mounted in this version (in the photos) but I haven’t used it nor needed it so far. I would suggest you don’t print it unless you have problems and think it will help. Wall mounting: I would recommend printing the template and using that to position the drill holes. Accuracy IS important. Check that your screw heads will sit within the counter sunk holes. The wall brackets have a little vertical movement in them. Screw the brackets to the wall. Assembly: The two part version is very easy to put together but make sure you trim any access filament (the brim) off the joint on both sides! You can only push the two parts together from one side. Lay the main arm flat on a table and push the small arm on until the whole thing is flush. It may require some force, it’s designed to be tight. A light tap with a hammer can help. Join the parts of the PTFE tube holder together to match the photos. Attach the PTFE tube holder to one of the arms. Take the rear bracket and insert it, bevel edges forward onto the same arm. Now take the other arm and carefully seat it on both the rear bracket and the PTFE tube carrier. Now slide the whole assembly onto the wall brackets to check alignment. It should slide on easily. Assemble the hubs. Remove any support material, use snipe nose pliers to remove the support in the axel socket. Check the supported edge looks flat with no bits of support left and test fit the flanges (if you are using them) to make sure they are flat and flush when seated. Push an axel in each hub as far as it will go. Put a spacer sleeve on next, then your bearings which should be a fairly snug fit. Finally your choice of axel cap. The cap should take quite a bit of force to get on. If it is loose you might want to add some glue. Fitting the flanges Test fit the flanges again. They should be fairly loose fitting without glue. This is by design. Remove them, run a bead of superglue all the way around the edge of the hub, stick the flanges on and leave to dry. Check they are well stuck! Almost done! The hubs should fit together without any effort. Obviously they need to come apart to insert your spools so don’t glue them! Put them together and try dropping the hub into the wall mount. It should drop in and pull out with almost no effort. If it sticks or doesn’t seat correctly there may be some support materials in the arm sockets. If there isn’t try taking the hib in and our a few times. If it doesn’t and the arms didn’t slide into the the wall brackets with ease then you may have an alignment problem. Check your drilling template against the holes in the wall. How things work and Tuning: Flap Brake (s): The function of the flap brake is primarily to stop the spool from running backwards. You will need the smaller ARM TYPE3 (they aren’t handed) and one flap brake for the side you intend to use it on. Fit the brake to the arm (it should fit fairly tightly). When correctly aligned the outer ARM hex faces should line up with the Flap Brake male end hex faces but the most important part is that the flat end of the flap must line up perfectly with the deep flat edge of the scoops on the flange plate. Once fitted the arm can be adjusted by pulling it in and out. Insert it roughly into position so that the end just sits in a scoop The designed position is when it “ticks” fairly quietly in the forward direction and stops the spool turning in the reverse direction. Tuning the flap brake: “Turn” any other brakes off! Use your hand to manually turn the spool forwards and check that there is little to no resistance and you can hear the flap ticking on the disc. Then try to gently spin with spool in reverse. It should be stopped almost immediately as the flap connects with an edge. Note - If you want you can put flap brakes on both sides of the holder. Note – The flap brakes can actually be used as friction brakes too if you push the tool arm in further – it will just be more noisy! Main friction Brakes: Generally I would recommend installing just one or two but you can use up to four. NOTE: Why four? Partly – just in case and you might only have access to one side of the holder but you may like to have one on each side to keep the spool aligned or all four installed to keep everything aligned with a light pressure on all of them. There are two brake types, one is designed for Tessa tape or Velcro style cable ties to wrap around. The other can also take tape but can be used on it’s own – you can just angle the chamfered part against the spool. Tuning the main friction brakes: You can push and pull the arms and you can also angle the tool head on the arm which should allow to you to really fine tune the amount of friction you are applying perfectly to suit the filament type. My personal preference is to use Tessa tape, it sticks on and the surface is very smooth. Tool arms: The arms are handed for left and right There are three types. Short – This makes the tool easy to remove but doesn’t provide much resistance to stop the tool head from being moved when tilted. Medium – Recommended. Some give but plenty of resistance. However it is quite hard to pull the arm out without breaking it. Long – Loads of resistance, almost impossible to remove the arm. Basically a permanent position once you push the head all the way on. Happy Soft Filament printing! Minor update 14-7-2026: The flap stop could catch on the edge of a flange when a spool is dropped in to the arms. This version adds a chamfer to the flanges to make it smoother and less likely to catch and rotate the flap stops.

This adapter was designed in collaboration with @Kaje , I needed a "downward diagonal" exhaust duct adapter. We further expanded the design to include adapters which "exit" in a multiple choice of directions. These adapters are designed to fit 3-inch duct tubes. The design was developed in OnShape CAD, with design ideas from both of us. I created most of the test prints on my Bambu printer, as well as all of the final prints, and took the photos of the final result. This print requires four socket-head self tapping screws (BT3x12mm) to attach the dovetail base to the printer. The print consists of a dovetail Base , an optional Gasket , and any one of eight different Hood designs (see photos) with the adapter tube exiting in different directions. In use the dovetail base is screwed onto the back of the printer (using existing screw holes for the exhaust duct), and the Hood pieces simply slide down onto the dovetail Base . IMPORTANT : Additional test pieces are included, use these before printing any Base or Hood pieces; see Assembly and Use below for more details. Short version - print the Template first. The eight Hood pieces are as follows : Hood - DL.stl : Tube exits downward and to the left Hood - DR.stl : Tube exits downward and to the right Hood - UL.stl : Tube exits upward and to the left Hood - UR.stl : Tube exits upward and to the right Hood - L.stl : Tube exits to the left Hood - R.stl : Tube exits right Hood - U.stl : Tube exits straight up Hood - D.stl : Tube exits straight down Assembly and Use The existing screw holes in the Bambu printer are arranged in a rectangular pattern, measured as follows : 111mm vertical separation 146mm horizontal separation However, as the print was done in ASA (which shrinks significantly on cooling), the model dimensions were altered to compensate for the shrinkage. To facilitate this adjustment, a Template piece was printed to check for fit. Even if you plan to print this ASA, you should still print the template as not all filaments behave exactly the same. Check for fit to the screw holes using the Template , and if necessary scale the print in with the X or Y (or both) direction to get a good fit, and then scale the final prints in the same way. Getting the top side of the adapter tube on the Hood to print cleanly initially presented some problems, so a TubeSectionTest piece is also included to enable testing of print parameters without having to print an entire Hood piece. To attach the final prints to the printer, fasten the Base piece over the exhaust using the four BT3x12mm screws. The Hood piece of your choice simply slides down onto the dovetails of the Base - no other fasteners are required. A 3 inch duct hose is attached to the tube on the Hood using a 3” key hose clamp (see photos). Print Instructions Printed in ASA using these parameters : 0.16mm layer height 5 "wall loops" (perimeters) 15% infill Supports required for Hood pieces (organic/tree supports recommended) Print the Gasket piece in TPU. description: ## Bumblebee Security Camera Housing – Tapo TC71 Compatible Bring the ultimate Autobot protector to your desk or shelf! This custom-designed, Bumblebee-inspired security camera housing is built specifically to fit the **Tapo TC71** camera. ### The Story Behind the Model This is my **first-ever 3D model**! After seeing an inspiring video online, I decided to take on the challenge. I used AI to generate the initial concept image, converted it into a 3D model, and then heavily modified and engineered the design from scratch to make sure it fits the Tapo TC71 perfectly. I poured a lot of energy, time, and hours of trial and error into this project. As a beginner, I learned so much along the way (and used quite a bit of filament to get it just right!). I would be incredibly happy to hear your feedback, advice, or suggestions—good or bad—to help me improve for my next designs! --- ### Key Features * **Perfect Fit:** Tailored specifically for the Tapo TC71 camera. * **Super Stable Base:** Designed with a heavy, massive torso and legs to ensure your camera stands rock-solid on your desk without tipping over. * **Lightweight Helmet:** The helmet section is optimized to be light and perfectly sized so it doesn't strain the camera rotation. * **Two Versions Included:** Choose between the **Pin-Joint Assembly** version or the **Fixed** version. --- ### Print Settings & Assembly Tips My test models (shown in the photos) were successfully printed with the following setups: * **Yellow Version:** Printed on a **Bambu Lab A1** using the **0.24mm Draft** profile. * **Gold Version:** Printed on a **Bambu X2D** using a **Standard Layout / Settings**. To save you some headaches, here are my highly recommended tips based on my test prints: * **The Golden Rule for the First Layer:** I highly recommend starting your print at **50% speed** until the first layer is perfectly laid down and has solid bed adhesion. Once the ground is good, you can safely bump the speed back up. * **A Warning on Multi-Color Printing (AMS/AMS Lite):** I strongly advise **against** printing this model in multiple colors directly from the slicer. I tested printing just a single leg in 2 colors, and the filament waste (purge) was equivalent to the weight of an entire extra leg! It is much more efficient and cost-effective to print it in a single color and post-process/paint it afterward (which is exactly what I did with my painted version!). * **If you choose the Pin-Joint Version:** * Scale the legs up by **1mm or 1.5mm on the X, Y, and Z axes** in your slicer. * Give the pins a quick, light sanding before assembly. This will make them fit smoothly. If they go in too tight, you risk breaking the pins when trying to disassemble them. * **If you want a hassle-free print (Fixed Version):** * Print the **Fixed version**. It takes a little longer to print, but you won't need to scale anything or worry about joint tolerances. Everything is pre-sized and ready to go! --- ### Feedback is Welcome! Since I am just starting my 3D design journey, please feel free to leave a comment, post your makes, or give me a Boost if you like my work! Your support and advice mean the world to me.

description: Hello everyone! I'm excited to present my first collaboration model. Customizable Navigation Bar Holder / GPS Bar Clamp A customizable two-piece navigation bar holder for motorcycle GPS, phone, tablet and DMD-style mounts. This model is designed as a parametric OpenSCAD / MakerWorld Customizer file. You can adjust the bar diameter, clamp tolerance, block size, bolt spacing, nut pockets and corner radius directly in the MakerWorld customizer. Key Features Fully customizable bar diameter Designed for navigation bars, GPS bars and handlebar-style mounting points Bar runs through the short side of the block Two-piece clamp design: front and back part Both parts are placed print-ready with the groove facing upward M4 bolt holes Optional M4 hex nut pockets in the back part Rounded corners Adjustable clamp undersize for a tighter or looser fit Suitable for common adventure motorcycle navigation bars Common Diameter Examples Recommended starting values: BMW / adventure GPS bar: Bar_Diameter = 12.0 Clamp_Undersize = 0.30 Hardware M4 Bolt 25mm M4 nyloc nuts Some BMW navigation bars: Bar_Diameter = 16.0 Clamp_Undersize = 0.30 Hardware M4 Bolt 30mm M4 nyloc nuts Always measure your own bar with calipers before printing. Small differences matter for clamp fit. Important Assembly Note Both parts are shown in print orientation with the bar groove facing upward. For assembly: Place the back part against the navigation bar. Flip the front part over. Put the front part over the bar. Insert the M4 bolts. Tighten gradually and evenly. The two half-round grooves will clamp around the bar. Parameters Main customizer parameters: Bar_Diameter Nominal diameter of your motorcycle navigation bar. Bar_Offset_X Moves the bar groove left or right from the center of the block. This is useful when the navigation bar needs to sit slightly off-center. Default value: 0.0 mm Range: -10 mm to +10 mm Clamp_Undersize Reduces the actual groove diameter for a tighter clamp. Example: Bar_Diameter = 12.0 and Clamp_Undersize = 0.30 creates an effective 11.7 mm clamp . Block_Length Overall length of the clamp block. Block_Width Overall width of the clamp block. Half_Thickness Thickness of each half. Set to 0 for automatic thickness. Corner_Radius Controls the rounded corners. Bolt Parameters Bolt_Size Selects the bolt size used for the clamp. Options: M3, M4, M5 The model automatically adjusts the bolt hole diameter and nut pocket size based on this setting. Bolt_Clearance Adds extra clearance to the selected bolt diameter. Example : Bolt_Size = M4 Bolt_Clearance = 0.5 This creates a 4.5 mm bolt hole. Increase this value if your printer makes holes too tight. Manual_Hole_Diameter Manual override for the bolt hole diameter. Set this value to 0 to use automatic hole sizing based on Bolt_Size and Bolt_Clearance. Use this only if you want full manual control over the hole diameter. Hole_Spacing_X Horizontal spacing between the left and right bolt holes. Measured center-to-center. Hole_Spacing_Y Vertical spacing between the upper and lower bolt holes. Measured center-to-center. Back Nut Pocket Parameters Nut_Pockets Enables or disables hexagonal nut pockets in the back part. Options : true Adds hex nut pockets to the back part. false Creates normal through-holes only. Nut_Pocket_Clearance Adds extra clearance to the automatic nut pocket size. Increase this value if your nuts are too tight. Decrease this value if your nuts are too loose. Manual_Nut_Flat_To_Flat Manual override for the hex nut pocket size. Measured flat-to-flat. Set this value to 0 to use automatic sizing based on Bolt_Size and Nut_Pocket_Clearance. Manual_Nut_Depth Manual override for the hex nut pocket depth. Set this value to 0 to use automatic depth based on Bolt_Size. Increase this value if your nuts sit proud of the surface. Advanced Parameters Preview_Cutaway Creates a cutaway preview to inspect the internal groove and holes. Options: false Normal printable model. true Cutaway preview mode. Use false before exporting for printing. Facet_Count Controls the smoothness of circular features such as the bar groove, bolt holes and nut pockets. Options : 32, 48, 64, 96, 128 Recommended value : 96 Higher values create smoother curves but may generate larger files. Print Settings Recommended material: PETG ASA ABS PETG-CF Suggested settings: 4–6 walls/perimeters 40–60% infill 0.2 mm layer height Print both parts with the groove facing upward Use supports only if your slicer requires them for the nut pockets For motorcycle use, avoid PLA because heat and sunlight can deform the part. Hardware Recommended hardware: 4x M4 bolts 4x M4 nuts or nyloc nuts Optional washer under bolt heads Optional thin rubber strip or double-sided tape around the bar for extra grip Disclaimer This is a DIY 3D printed motorcycle accessory. Use at your own risk. Check fitment and strength before riding. Re-check bolt tightness after the first ride and inspect the part regularly for cracks or wear. Been having bridging issues with my prints so I put this together to be able to test for an ideal bridge flow ratio and speed combination to get the best results. Not a professional model maker by any stretch of the imagination, but it works for now! This test lays out 21 bridges on one plate — 3 print speeds (10 / 20 / 30 mm/s) across 7 bridge flow ratios (1.0–1.6) — so you can find the combination that gives flat, fully-fused strands with no sag. Uses only ~7 g of filament, so it's cheap to run as often as you calibrate your filaments. How to use: Print it, flip it over, and read the underside of each bridge. The cleanest, flattest strands mark your ideal bridge flow ratio for that speed. Set those values in your slicer and enjoy clean bridges. Printed on a Bambu Lab P1S. No supports, no brim needed. How to read the results: Flip the plate and look at the underside of each bridge: Best: strands are flat, straight, evenly spaced, and fully fused — no sag, no gaps. Too little flow / too fast: strands sag, droop, or break mid-span. Too much flow: strands bulge, blob, or fuse into a rough mass. Settings to modify in slicer Quality > Advanced > Bridge Flow Speed > Other Layers Speed > Bridge Feedback and comments are welcome, I have much to learn still! description: Flow Rate Calibration Cube | Micrometer Dieser einwandige, oben offene Kalibrierungswürfel dient zur präzisen Einstellung der Flussrate beziehungsweise des Flow Ratio eines Filaments. Die tatsächliche Wandstärke wird an mehreren Stellen mit einer Bügelmessschraube oder einem präzisen Mikrometer gemessen. Aus dem Mittelwert aller Messungen lässt sich anschließend der korrigierte Flussratenwert für das verwendete Filamentprofil berechnen. Der Würfel benötigt nur wenig Material, ist schnell gedruckt und eignet sich ideal zur Feinabstimmung neuer oder bereits vorhandener Filamentprofile. Benötigte Hilfsmittel Bügelmessschraube oder präzises Mikrometer Bambu Studio oder ein kompatibler Slicer Das zu kalibrierende Filament Aktueller Flussratenwert des Filamentprofils Eingestellte Linienbreite der Außenwand Durchführung 1. Würfel drucken Drucke den Würfel mit genau dem Filamentprofil, das kalibriert werden soll. Verändere für den anschließenden Kontrolltest möglichst keine anderen Einstellungen wie Temperatur, Geschwindigkeit oder Linienbreite. Lasse das Modell nach dem Druck vollständig abkühlen. 2. Wandstärke messen Miss jede der vier Würfelseiten an mehreren Stellen: mindestens 3 Messungen pro Seite empfohlen sind 5 Messungen pro Seite bei 5 Messungen pro Seite entstehen insgesamt 20 Messwerte Miss möglichst mittig auf den geraden Wandflächen. Vermeide dabei: die Ecken des Würfels die Z-Naht den oberen Rand die ersten Schichten sichtbar unregelmäßige Stellen Verwende bei jeder Messung einen gleichmäßigen und möglichst geringen Messdruck. Mittelwert berechnen Addiere alle gemessenen Wandstärken und teile die Summe durch die Anzahl der Messungen: Mittelwert = Summe aller Messwerte ÷ Anzahl der Messwerte Je mehr saubere Messungen verwendet werden, desto zuverlässiger ist das Ergebnis. Zielwert bestimmen Der Zielwert entspricht der in Bambu Studio eingestellten Linienbreite der Außenwand . Du findest den Wert unter: Qualität → Breite der Linien → Außenwand Beispiel: Außenwand-Linienbreite: 0,42 mm Wichtig: Verwende als Zielwert nicht automatisch den Düsendurchmesser, sondern immer die tatsächlich eingestellte Linienbreite der Außenwand. Aktuellen Flussratenwert ermitteln Öffne das verwendete Filamentprofil und notiere den dort eingestellten aktuellen Wert für die: Flussrate / Flow Ratio Beispiel: Bisheriger Flow Ratio: 0,988 Neuen Flow Ratio berechnen Verwende folgende Formel: Neuer Flow Ratio = Zielwert × bisheriger Flow Ratio ÷ gemessener Mittelwert Beispielrechnung Zielwert: 0,42 mm Bisheriger Flow Ratio: 0,988 Gemessener Mittelwert: 0,421 mm Rechnung: 0,42 × 0,988 ÷ 0,421 = 0,985653 Gerundet ergibt sich ein neuer Flow Ratio von: 0,986 Trage den neuen Wert anschließend in das Filamentprofil ein. Drucke den Würfel danach erneut und kontrolliere die Wandstärke mit einer weiteren Messung. Falls erforderlich, kann die Berechnung wiederholt werden. Excel-Formel Die Berechnung kann auch direkt in Excel oder einer anderen Tabellenkalkulation durchgeführt werden: =Zielwert*Bisheriger_Wert/Mittelwert Beispiel mit Zellbezügen: =I13*I6/D6 Dabei steht: I13 für den bisherigen Flow-Ratio-Wert I6 für den Zielwert D6 für den Mittelwert aller Messungen Ergebnis interpretieren Gemessene Wand ist dicker als der Zielwert: Der Flow Ratio wird reduziert. Gemessene Wand ist dünner als der Zielwert: Der Flow Ratio wird erhöht. Mittelwert entspricht dem Zielwert: Die Flussrate ist bereits passend eingestellt. Hinweise Die Kalibrierung sollte für jedes Filamentprofil separat durchgeführt werden. Hersteller, Material, Farbe, Drucktemperatur und weitere Einstellungen können das Ergebnis beeinflussen. Dieser Würfel dient ausschließlich zur Kalibrierung der Flussrate beziehungsweise des Flow Ratio . Er ist nicht für die Einstellung von Flow Dynamics, Pressure Advance oder K-Wert vorgesehen. Für reproduzierbare Ergebnisse sollten alle Messungen mit derselben Bügelmessschraube und mit möglichst gleichmäßigem Messdruck durchgeführt werden. Druckprofil Einwandiger, oben offener Kalibrierungswürfel Keine Stützstrukturen erforderlich Geringer Materialverbrauch Kurze Druckzeit Ideal für wiederholte Kontrollmessungen Druckzeit und Materialverbrauch können abhängig von Drucker, Filament und verwendeten Einstellungen abweichen.

description: PETG Supportless Perfect Overhang Print Profile This is a print profile setting designed for supportless PETG printing with perfect overhangs, tested on a propeller model. Key features include: 1. Outer/Inner Wall Speed Reduced to 50/60 mm/s Slower printing speeds prevent under-extrusion and stringing. 2. Disable Overhang Speed Slowdown Disable slowdown for overhangs above 45°. This prevents the nozzle from dwelling too long in one spot, which causes heat buildup and sagging. 3. Enable Prime Tower (Wipe Tower) Allows extra layer cooling time and reduces filament blobs/droppings on the model. 4. Lower Layer Height to 0.12 mm A lower layer height provides better support for steep overhang angles. 5. Increase Outer/Inner Wall Line Width to 0.6 mm Enhances the structural support and stability of inner and outer walls. 6. Increase Part Cooling Accelerates model cooling to avoid high-temperature sagging and deformation. 7. Open the Top Lid, Keep the Front Door Closed Keep the top glass lid open for heat dissipation, but close the front door to prevent model warping. If you experience sagging like in the image below, please improve overall printer ventilation, turn on the AC, or print at night. However, do NOT change the heatbed temperature to avoid warping. This isn't just a display piece; it is a complete, wearable cosplay solution engineered for creators who demand screen-accurate detail and structural integrity. The model is comprised of three primary architectural components: The Main Helmet: A masterfully crafted Corinthian-inspired foundation featuring an aggressive, modern aesthetic with sharp geometric planes. The Crest (Perikefalaia): The iconic transverse crest that provides the wearer with an authoritative profile and imposing height The Spinal Bone Braid: A haunting, biomechanical accessory based on the unique "Nolan-esque" imagery from the film's promotional materials. Sizing Note: The default scale is for a full-size adult (approx. 24.5-inch circumference). Because a perfect fit is the difference between a costume and a masterpiece, please use my custom Cosplay Calipers to measure your head and neck width before printing. 🛠️ Functionality & Expert Sizing Guide This model is designed for high-impact cosplay and display. However, if you prefer to use the raw STL files and they are not appearing in the standard list, please watch this: How to find STL files in Makerworld with no print profile 📜 The History: The King of Mycenae meets the Nolanverse The Legend: Agamemnon is the fulcrum of Greek Mythology—the King of Kings and commander of the Greek forces during the Trojan War. His story, famously told in Homer’s Iliad , is one of sacrifice, pride, and tragic homecomings. The Cinema: This design is inspired by Christopher Nolan’s upcoming film, The Odyssey . Known for grounded, "tactile" sci-fi and historical realism, Nolan’s aesthetic for Agamemnon blends the ancient bronze age with a dark, almost skeletal future. The inclusion of the Spinal Bone Braid suggests a ritualistic, darker tone for the character than we have ever seen on screen before. 🔄 Versatility & Remix Potential While designed for The Odyssey , this geometry is a perfect base for numerous other projects. You can remix or "kitbash" this model into: Sci-Fi Spartans: Remove the bone braid and use a metallic silk filament for a Halo -inspired ancient warrior. Roman Centurions: Use the transverse crest orientation to create an officer of the Roman Legion. Grimdark Fantasy: The bone braid can be remixed into pauldrons or spine-armor for Darksouls style builds ( Keyword: Gothic Armor ). Cybernetic Gladiators: Add LED strips into the crest channels for a Cyberpunk-Ancient fusion ( Keyword: Neon Cosplay ). 🖨️ Recommended Print Settings Material: PLA+ or PETG for durability. Infill: 15% Gyroid (provides the best strength-to-weight ratio for wearable helmets). Support: Tree Supports (Manual placement recommended for the eye slits). description: Master Sword in Bloom – Korok Forest Pedestal ⚔️🌸 This is my take on the Master Sword resting in Korok Forest after the Great Calamity. Zelda left the sword there under the protection of the Great Deku Tree, trusting that Link would eventually return to reclaim it. I imagined it sitting untouched for the next hundred years, with vines and flowers inspired by the Silent Princess slowly growing around the blade as the forest began to reclaim its resting place. Recommended settings: ✓ Use a 0.08 mm layer height for quality ✓ Slow down outer wall speeds to improve the surface finish ✓ Supports may be required around the flowers, vines, and cross guard depending on your printer and orientation ✓ Add a brim if you notice any lifting around the base ✓ Matte PLA works especially well for highlighting the sculpted details 🧼 Before Printing Please clean your build plate before starting the print. A dirty or oily plate can cause lifting, warping, or failed adhesion, especially around the large flat base. Assembly Demonstration Maker’s Note I’m a hobby modeler, and I like entering MakerWorld contests with designs that push me a little beyond my limits. This is my biggest project so far, and it took many weekends of modeling, printing, testing, breaking parts, and going back to the drawing board. (I have an ever increasing pile of failed prototypes) My long-term goal is to create a free, easy-to-print and easy-to-assemble parametric generator that lets anyone generate a set of toy fingers fitted to their own hand. I do have a slight tendency toward maximalism, so I’m not ready to publish the fully customizable version until I’ve confirmed that it works reliably across a wide range of finger sizes, but in the meantime, I wanted to see how people react to the idea and whether it is worth putting the extra work into the generator. Please try the current version with an open mind, and feel free to leave constructive feedback. I’ll do my best to incorporate the feedback into the customizable version. Background I first came across this type of finger extension in this Adam Savage video. It immediately looked like something that would be incredibly fun to build and wear… Then I looked at the price tag :D (after spending so much time on this, I fully understand the pricing. Gary's fingers are truly a work of art both aesthetically and mechanically) That sent me down the rabbit hole of researching how I could make my own. While looking through existing projects and mechanisms, I found the work of Dragonator , whose notes were invaluable during the development process. A big shoutout to him. Seeing his amazing model, I’m sure he is one of the few who understand both the pain of designing a mechanism like this and the joy of finally putting it on for the first time and feeling the fingers move with your hand. Design Considerations I’ll demonstrate the main design decisions with pictures below, but these were the areas I focused on most: Cylindrical, adaptive geometry The mechanism is built around mostly cylindrical finger sections. This makes a final design I find aesthetic. I believe most similar finger have an adaptable base section that goes around the fingers, and the rest of the mechanism is interchangeable. I wanted the whole finger to be driven by parameters. Low-profile control shaft movement One thing I struggled a lot with is how to keep the controller shaft as low to the body as possible both at the two end states, and during the movement. With a few tradeoffs, I think I well achieved both. Easy assembly This was the thing I feared the most. In the commercial version, there is obviously no assembly required, it is put together beautifully with additional hardware. I tried different ways of connecting parts, and after multiple failures came up with a snap-in design, which I'm truly proud of. Clean seam lines I wanted the finger to have a clean, cylindrical look when it's straight. However cylinders generally have problems with seam lines. I intentionally placed a straight groove at the bottom of the parts, so you wont need to paint seam lines yourself, you can just hit print and know the lines will look acceptable. The support tradeoff This is the price I decided to pay. Many things in my design are supported, and while many I could have eliminated, I decided the one-time price of removing the supports is well covered by the gains I got in aesthetics and assembly. How the Mechanism Works The finger sections are linked together so that movement from your real finger is transferred through the control shafts to the extended segments. description: Want a realistic life-size V40 Mini Grenade with a flying handle? This model is 100% brand new from the ground-up with stronger parts, easy screw-on assembly, and enhanced realism. What is the v40 Mini Grenade? The V40 Mini Grenade is an unusually compact fragmentation hand grenade developed in the Netherlands that is roughly the size of a golf ball. Weighing just 4.8 ounces, it allowed soldiers to carry the weapon in much greater quantities than standard fragmentation grenades. It gained historical fame for its utilization by U.S. special operations units during the Vietnam War. Spring options (for flying handle) Metal Spring (recommended) – if you have a metal spring, even a pen spring will usually work, then print the metal spring profile. It is designed to work with the Bambu Store's 0.5x7x12mm spring (linked lower on the page). If you use a pen spring, you can usually cut it in half and get two springs. Plastic Spring – if you don't have a metal spring, but still want the handle to fly off, then print the plastic spring profile. If the spring eventually wears out, just print a new one and pop it in. Don't leave the spring under tension when not using it as it will wear out much faster. Avoid Matte and Silk filament for the spring itself, Basic and Metal work better. No Flying Handle - if you don't want the handle to fly off and just want a grenade model, simply print either version and don't put in a spring. Bambu Filaments used Metal Iron Gray black Matte Yellow Polymaker Army Green ( Amazon link ) Bambu Matte Dark Green is the closest Bambu filament Metal Spring Version Assembly 1. Insert the peg into the grenade topper as you see below. 2. Then insert a metal spring int the same way. 3. Lastly, screw the topper onto the body of the grenade – it helps to do this upside down or sideways so the spring doesn't fall out. Plastic Spring Version Assembly 1. Insert the printed plastic spring into the grenade topper as you see below. Make sure the peg at the top of the spring is sticking out the top, rotate it until it pops out if not. 2. Lastly, screw the topper onto the grenade body – its easiest if you do this upside down or sideways.

description: Want a replica of a US WW1 grenade? This is the original "pineapple" grenade from WW1 that was the predecessor to the Mk2 grenade we all know from WW2. This grenade has a spoon handle that flies off when you pull the pin, just like the real thing would. Background: Introduced in 1917, the US Mk1 Grenade was the first fragmentation hand grenade developed by the United States for use in World War I. It was notoriously complicated to operate in the field, often requiring the user to manually ignite the fuse before throwing. Due to soldiers struggling to arm it under pressure, the Mk 1 grenade was quickly recalled and replaced by the improved Mk 2 grenade fuze in 1918 (which this model depicts). Spring options (for flying handle) Metal Spring (recommended) – if you have a metal spring, even a pen spring will usually work, then print the metal spring profile. It is designed to work with the Bambu Store's 0.5x7x12mm spring (linked lower on the page). If you use a pen spring, you can usually cut it in half and get two springs. Plastic Spring – if you don't have a metal spring, but still want the handle to fly off, then print the plastic spring profile. If the spring eventually wears out, just print a new one and pop it in. Don't leave the spring under tension when not using it as it will wear out much faster. Avoid Matte and Silk filament for the spring itself, Basic and Metal work better. No Flying Handle - if you don't want the handle to fly off and just want a grenade model, simply print either version and don't put in a spring. Bambu filaments used Basic Bronze Dark gray filaments are also period appropriate Silk+ Silver Assembly takes seconds Metal Spring Version 1. Insert the peg into the topper while its upside down. 2. description: Want a life-size replica of the Laser Guided APKWS Rocket used by the US, Ukraine, NATO, and many other militaries? This is around ~6ft / ~2m long and can be assembled in seconds just by screwing the printed parts together, no glue is required. It comes with moving fold-out fins for extra realism. You can also print optional wall mounts to place it on the wall. It is designed to use as little filament as possible while still being strong and sturdy. Note: this new model is completely interchangable with my other Hydra rocket models (the screw-together version, not the peg assembly version). So you can print any parts from this model and combine it with other hydra rockets you've printed. Bambu filaments used Warhead at the top Basic Yellow Silk+ Titan Gray Overture Silk Copper ( Amazon link ) Polymaker Army Green ( Amazon link ) Rocket Body Basic Light Gray A white filament would work as well Silk+ Red Silk+ Silver (for the mid-body fins) Polymaker Metallic Silver ( Amazon link ) Basic Silver would work great too Engine Metal Iridium Gold Silk+ Gold would work too Assembly is super easy The parts simply screw together, so if you make a mistake you can just unscrew and re-screw in seconds, no problems. Make sure you don't over tighten – they are quite strong, but all plastic screws can eventually break under enough pressure – you should be able to screw them until they feel snug. 1. Screw the main body together, which includes 4 longer white/gray segments, one shorter red segment, and one short white/gray segment. 2. Then take each of the silver fins and connect all 4 to a base by sliding them together. It may take a little bit of forcer, pushing down on a table can help. 3. Now the assembled fins and clip them into the tall gray section. They should snap in easily if you line it up right. If you can't get the fins to snap in, try a different (probably lower) angle. 4. Next begin screwing on the other parts one by one to the far right end (the end with the red strip). 5. Then, assemble the warhead portion at the tip with the pegs provided like you see below and screw it onto the top of the rocket. 6. Lastly, begin connecting the rocket motor by connecting the top threaded piece to the bottom piece with the two long pegs provided. 7. Then the final step is to attach the fins to the rocket motor – the will snap into place with little force. Note that they must be facing clockwise , not counter clockwise. If you insert them counter clockwise you will find that they don't fold all the way.

The WW2 Bazooka was a shoulder-fired, rocket-propelled anti-tank weapon that gave infantry soldiers the unprecedented ability to destroy armored vehicles . It fired a high-explosive, shaped-charge warhead from a reusable steel tube, relying on venting gases out the back to eliminate dangerous recoil. Named after a novelty musical instrument due to its odd tubular shape, it became one of the most iconic "tools of victory" for the Allied forces. description: Spartan/Trojan War Hound Dog Helmet – Fully Articulated Bring the glory of the ancient world to your furry companion! Whether it’s for a photoshoot, a convention, or just to show the neighborhood who the real "Alpha" is, this helmet is the ultimate accessory for your four-legged warrior. 🏛️ History of the Model The design is inspired by the Corinthian-style helmets used by ancient Greek hoplites and later stylized in Trojan lore. Historically, these helmets were symbols of strength, protection, and status. I wanted to translate that intimidating, majestic silhouette into something comfortable and wearable for pets. The intricate swirls and Celtic-inspired patterns on the cheek guards add a "mythical" flair, bridging the gap between historical accuracy and high-fantasy cosplay. ⚙️ Functional Design & Assembly This model is unique because it features fully functional articulated cheek guards (flaps) . The Hinge System: Unlike static models, this helmet uses custom-designed hinges. You will need to print the included hinge pins separately. Assembly: Once printed, align the cheek guards with the main helmet body and slide the 3D-printed pins through the knuckles. This allows the flaps to swing outward, making it much easier to put on and take off your dog while ensuring a comfortable fit against their jawline. Durability: The crest is reinforced to handle the "zoomies," but it remains lightweight enough for medium to large breeds to wear comfortably. 📏 Sizing and Fitting Your Warrior Because every "Good Boy" is a different size, scaling is critical. Measurement: To get the perfect fit, I highly recommend using my Cosplay Calipers Measuring Tool . Measure the width of your dog's head between the ears and the length from the brow to the back of the skull. Scaling & Orientation: If you need to scale this up for a Great Dane or down for a Terrier, or if you need to slice it to fit a smaller print bed, check out my comprehensive guide: How to Size, Scale, Cut, Pin, and Orient Armor in Bambu Studio . 🛠️ Printing Tips Filament: Looks incredible in Silk Silver PLA or "Antique Gold." description: "Why does that pirate have a ship's wheel attached to his belt?" "Arrr... it's driving me nuts!" Now you can finally tell one of the oldest pirate jokes... while being the punchline. This remix transforms a decorative ship's wheel into a wearable spinning belt buckle accessory . Simply print the included adapter and screw, mount the wheel over your belt buckle, and you're ready for your next Renaissance Faire, pirate festival, cosplay event, or Halloween costume. The wheel actually spins , making it an interactive prop that's guaranteed to get laughs from fellow pirates and confused landlubbers alike. ⚓ Features Wearable pirate belt buckle prop Functional spinning ship's wheel Easy assembly with the included adapter and screw Designed for cosplay and costume use Great conversation starter for Renaissance fairs, pirate festivals, conventions, and themed parties 🎨 Finishing for the Best Look While the model looks great straight off the printer, a few simple finishing touches can make it look surprisingly close to real weathered wood. Recommended Finish Print using a light brown filament . Apply a dark wood stain or dark brown varnish . Immediately wipe away most of the finish with a paper towel or soft cloth. The darker color remains in the layer lines and recessed details, creating a convincing weathered wood appearance. Repeat until you achieve the look you want. Lightly brush again in one direction to give it a ‘wood grain’-style finish Rope Detail For an even more authentic nautical appearance, wrap white nylon cord or string beneath each handle around the outer rim of the wheel. After tying each section: Trim the excess. Position knot on the back side of the wheel. Carefully melt the ends with a lighter to prevent fraying and lock the knot in place. This small detail makes a huge difference and really sells the illusion of a traditional wooden ship's wheel. 🛠 Print Notes I recommend printing the wheel with 35% infill (default profile already has this enabled!) for additional durability while wearing it. Although this version is pretty strong, it is still a 3D-printed prop . Don't sit down while wearing it. Avoid dropping it onto hard surfaces. CYBERPUNK OUTCAST FLINTLOCK MUSKET (DART BLASTER) "In a dark cyberpunk future, everything and everyone belongs to the corporations. Only the outcasts have never been owned. Corporations can lock your implants, freeze your bank account, and disable your smart rifle. But they cannot disable steel, black powder, and flint. Free people are forced to fight with the weapons of the past. A flintlock requires no firmware, no subscription, and answers to no one but its wielder." Inspired by this concept, the CYBERPUNK OUTCAST FLINTLOCK MUSKET is a fully 3D-printable elastic-powered toy dart blaster that combines the appearance of a cyberpunk firearm with the operation of a traditional flintlock musket. Rather than simply resembling a flintlock, it recreates the complete firing sequence with a functional cock, frizzen, powder pan, trigger, sear, and half-cock safety. The blaster is muzzle-loaded. Insert the dart into the barrel, seat it with the ramrod, cock the lock, aim, and fire. The entire loading and firing sequence is designed to resemble the operation of a historical flintlock while using a completely different internal propulsion system. The model features a compact folding design. Both the stock and the front assembly lock securely in their folded and deployed positions, allowing the blaster to be stored or transported in a much smaller package while remaining ready for use within seconds. Designed primarily for PETG printing, the model is almost entirely 3D printed. No metal springs, screws, glue, filament retaining pins, or other additional hardware are required. The only non-printed components are the elastic bands used for propulsion and mechanism operation. In addition to the original HEX 13 mm dart version, the project also includes a separate conversion profile for standard 0.5-inch foam darts. Features Fully functional flintlock-style firing mechanism Functional half-cock safety Muzzle-loaded operation with ramrod Folding stock with adjustable length of pull Folding front assembly for compact storage 99% PETG 3D printed No metal springs, screws, glue, or additional hardware. The only non-printed components are the elastic materials; the carriage guide rails also require lubrication during assembly. Includes a conversion profile for standard 0.5-inch foam darts Compatible with Bambu Lab P1 and A1 build volumes, as well as similar-sized printers (not compatible with the A1 Mini) Ammunition & Performance The primary configuration is designed to fire lightweight HEX 13 mm PETG or TPU printed darts weighing approximately 1–2 g. Typical performance: Muzzle velocity: approximately 40 ft/s (12 m/s) Effective range: approximately 3–10 m Shot dispersion at 3 m may reach approximately 0.25 m A separate conversion profile is included for users who prefer standard 0.5-inch foam darts. This project is intended primarily as an engineering and mechanical showcase that faithfully recreates the operation of a flintlock mechanism using almost entirely 3D-printed components. It prioritizes authenticity of operation and mechanical complexity over maximum performance. Before You Print Please review the listed performance characteristics before starting the project. If you expect significantly higher power, accuracy, or range, this model may not match your expectations.

Want a replica of the frag grenade from game PUBG (Player Unknown Battleground)? This grenade even has a spring-loaded handle that flies off when you pull the pin. The PUBG frag grenade is similar to the real-life M67 grenade, however, there are some distinct differences in its rounded shape and differences with the fuze that this model reflects. Spring options (for flying handle) Metal Spring (recommended) – if you have a metal spring, even a pen spring will usually work, then print the metal spring profile. Bambu Store's 0.5x7x12mm spring is what this model is designed to work with. Pen springs work as well though, many different types have been tested and work fine. You can often cut pen springs in half and get two grenade springs since this model only needs a 12mm long spring and pen springs tend to be about 24mm. Plastic Spring – if you don't have a metal spring, but still want the handle to fly off, then print the plastic spring profile. If the spring eventually wears out, just print a new one and pop it in. Don't leave the spring under tension when not using it as it will wear out much faster. Avoid Matte and Silk filament for the spring itself, Basic and Metal work better. No Flying Handle - if you don't want the handle to fly off and just want a grenade model, simply print either version and don't put in a spring. Bambu filaments used Silk+ Silver Matte Yellow Polymaker Army Green ( Amazon link ) Matte Dark Green works too Metal Spring Version Assembly 1. Use the two pegs to connect the two halves of the grenade together. 2. Flip the silver top upside down and insert the peg. Make sure the peg is sticking out of the top, if not rotate 90 degrees. 3. Insert your spring into the silver top next, just like you did with the peg. 4. Screw the silver top onto the grenade – keeping the silver top upside down makes this easier (so spring doesn't fall out while screwing it on). That's it – now you can attach the spoon handle, put in the pin, and use it – enjoy! Plastic Spring Version Assembly 1. Use the two pegs to connect the two halves of the grenade together. 2. Flip the silver top upside down and insert the spring. Make sure the spring's peg is sticking out of the top, if not rotate 90 degrees. 3. Screw the silver top onto the grenade – keeping the silver top upside down makes this easier (so spring doesn't fall out while screwing it on). That's it – now you can attach the spoon handle, put in the pin, and use it – enjoy!

description: Ever wanted a life-sized Halo energy sword? Me too! I was surprised that I couldn't find a print for this, so I made one myself. Coming in at just over a metre long, this is a faithful replica of the iconic Halo weapon. It looks great printed in either translucent blue or clear PETG, with light channels down the middle of each blade and compartments on both blades for electronics (batteries - sized for 18650 cells, control boards etc). Everything is designed to key together to allow for easy printing and assembly. This print takes up 5 full plates on my P2S and took a few days to print, with around 1.5kg of blade material. Each plate is as packed as it can reasonably be. It can of course be printed on smaller printers like the A1 and can be scaled down appropriately to suit this. Key assembly steps: Print and attach hilt sections together. I printed these in a grey PLA+, then stuck them together with CA glue. The fit is tight and may need a bit of force. There is a channel down the inside of the hilt to route wires for lights or switches. Optional - sand, prime, paint hilt. I painted with a base of black acrylic and then steel / silver acrylic on top, then sanded paint down in places to give a weathered look. Print blade base parts and attach to hilt. The fit between the hilt and blade base is a bit looser than any of the other joins, as this gives a bit more tolerance for any accumulated accuracy errors throughout the print. The intended attachment method is to use an M8 nut / insert / T-nuts heat-set into the handle, and an M8*40mm bolt through the blade into this nut / insert. You could however just use a suitable epoxy to bond the two parts well. Either way, this should be a secure connection once properly glued / torqued down. Attach blade pieces to blade base, finishing up with the optional reinforcing bar (secured using M3 heat inserts and M3*10mm bolts into the blade sections). You could use a suitable glue to attach these together, though the keyed fit is pretty tight. Optional finishing steps. I used a UV-set clear resin to fill the join lines between sections and make things look a bit more continuous. This certainly isn't a magic fix as it is obviously still printed in pieces, but it does help! You can then install electronics if desired. I found LED rope or LED-strips worked well (ideally with high density RGB COBs. If they're too far apart you get a less diffuse effect). Features: Working picatinny rail with attachments. Sights can be quick swapped with each other or a scope if you go with 8x2 magnets. 2 different threaded muzzle options 2 sight options 1 scope option 1 under barrel “flashlight / laser combo” (2 parts held together with magnets) 1 under barrel grip Most parts are separated out for easy color printing. I'll provide an AMS profile for some of the main parts & accessories if you want to go that route. (Grip, main sight, flashlight attachment & buttstock) Assembly: *Assembly is pretty straight forward but there are a lot of pieces. See images for the renders that show where everything goes. Yellow parts in the images are all the connecting / guide pins. You will want to assemble the 3 main sections first. Front, Mid, rear using the larger connecting pins. *Be sure to remember to put in the barrel insert into the mid section prior to any gluing (if you are doing that). Slide rear top (as I call it *on plate 4) into the mid section using connecting pin. Little holes on the top need to be towards the rear of the gun. Buttstock will hold the main rear and top rear sections together with connecting pins. Buttstock covers - There are small alignment holes for pins on the rear top. Add in pins to rear top (may be tight). Place covers onto pins. They only go on one way, see images for reference. Buttstock straps - These should fit snuggle into the openings on the covers. I'd start by inserting the strap on the right side of the gun fist, then push the left side up and in. Straps may need some filing. Mine fit in nice and required no gluing. Magazine connects to the bottom of the rear section using connecting pins. Magazine end cap and loop need to be glued on. Grips & trigger guard - There is an indent in the grip and the upper grip where the trigger guard sits. Due to the design you need to assemble these at the same time. Put 2 pins in the upper grip place it flat side down (in not already attached to mid section). Hold flat side of trigger guard in the grip with one hand while pushing the grip onto the pins guide the angle side of the trigger guard into the indent on the upper grip. Seems difficult when typing it out but its easy. Do test a test fit before gluing anything. I filled my trigger guard down a bit to get perfect fit before gluing. Top picatinny rail is held in my the screw pins. I added the screw pin down into the rails first, then aligned the pins above the holes & pushed them all the way into the main body of the gun. Mine were snug and required no glue. Bottom and side picatinny rails are all the same size & go in as descried above. Cover plates - These are glued on after everything is assembled. Under barrel plates hide some of the seam lines. Top 2 for the bolt area are aesthetic. If you want to use the top 2 be sure to glue them in before you glue in the bolt pin. Slide picatinny mount onto the rails. Add in magnets, make sure you get polarity right on the accessories for easy swapping. There are pins to secure the mount to the rails. Slide the pin in and place on the cap on the other side. You can glue them if you like, I chose not to since the mounts were snug on the rails for me. *Only 2 mounts are in the profile. Print more if you need them. Notes: Most larger flat pieces have 3 walls and 10% infill. I've also slowed the outer / inner wall speeds down to 60-80mm/s to try and negate seeing lines. Smaller items have brims and .16 layer heights to keep the details. Supports are enabled on individual objects where needed. Magazine & magazine end cap have a ton of triangles so you will see that warning. Simplify them at your own risk. Screw pins - I printed them facing up because I didn't want texture to show. Feel free to rotate them 180 if you have smooth plate. Magnets: if you use them for all accessories you will need 16 or 20 8x2 magnets. Be sure to get your polarity correct for easy swapping. description: Clicker Cosplay Mask – The Last of Us Description & Origin Bring the fungal nightmare of the post-apocalypse to life with this highly detailed, screen-accurate Clicker Cosplay Mask . Inspired by the terrifying infected creatures from HBO’s The Last of Us and the iconic Naughty Dog video game franchise, this model captures the grotesque, organic geometry of the Cordyceps brain infection bursting from a human skull. The front of the mask features the signature split, cauliflower-like fungal blooms completely overtaking the upper face, layered over an underlying structure of exposed, decaying teeth and infected skin tissue. Designed with cosplay comfort in mind, the rear of the print is ergonomically contoured to comfortably sit against a human face, making it the ultimate centerpiece for your next convention, Halloween costume, or horror display. Functional Use & Wearability This is a wearable cosplay prop. The internal face cavity is smooth to allow for the addition of foam padding, and the side profiles include clean integration points for a leather or elastic head strap. Because a full Clicker transformation leaves the host blind, this mask is designed for authentic tracking. However, for safe convention wear, the open mouth cavity and deep recesses within the fungal plates can easily be lined with black mesh fabric from the inside—allowing you to see out and breathe comfortably while keeping the actor's face completely hidden from the outside. Sizing, Scaling, and Customization Because everyone's head shape is unique, proper sizing is crucial before you send this multi-hour print to the plate. To ensure a perfect 1:1 fit over your face and brow, I highly recommend using my custom Cosplay Calipers Sizing Tool to grab your exact physical dimensions. If you need to scale the mask up or down, or if you need to slice it to fit a smaller printer bed, check out my step-by-step video guide: How to Size, Scale, Cut, Pin, and Orient Armor in Bambu Studio / OrcaSlicer . Print Settings & Material Recommendations To capture the hyper-organic, textured look of the Cordyceps fungus without glaring layer lines, I highly recommend printing this at a 0.12mm or 0.16mm layer height with organic tree supports. For the absolute best results, post-processing durability, and crisp detail retention, I exclusively recommend using SUNLU Filament . For a Paint-Ready Base: Use SUNLU PLA Plus (PLA+) Filament in Gray or White. It provides incredible impact resistance for convention wear and sands beautifully. For Rugged Outdoor/Con Wear: If you want extra temperature resistance against hot summer conventions, step up to SUNLU PETG Filament . Note: If you plan on modifying this model into a multi-color print using an AMS setup, be sure to watch my tutorial: How to Remesh and Color Prints Effectively in Bambu Studio . Assembly Instructions Depending on your printer build volume, you may choose to print this mask in sections. For a permanent, rock-solid bond that won't snap when under tension from the head strap, I highly recommend using ARKA KRAFTPROTZ UNIVERSAL Superglue . It fuses the printed seams flawlessly, ensuring your mask survives the chaos of a busy con floor. Creative Remix Ideas & Potential Uses Looking to use this geometry for something other than a costume? Here are a few creative ways you can remix or repurpose this file: Halloween Prop Decor: Scale it down, hollow it out, and turn it into a creepy, glowing LED wall sconce or a lampshade. Aquarium/Terrarium Decor: Print it using aquarium-safe materials to create an apocalyptic, overgrown centerpiece for a reptile enclosure or fish tank. Gaming Room Display: Mount the mask onto a plaque or a custom mannequin head stand to create a premium gaming room prop display. description: This one is for Squidward who relentlessly pushed for me to make the model, and then was so grateful when I got started! I hope you enjoy it! I designed this mask a bit different from my others and I am happy with the outcome. Essentially, I incorporated the mesh eyes directly into the mask so they don't need to be added or printed separately. If you would prefer to print it all in one color (to save time and money), you should be able to easily paint the mesh portion black with some black acrylic paint. I also experimented with how the horns are printed and attached to the head to make them more integrated into the design and also to avoid needing supports on them. My first version was a bit to tight to fit on my head, but it fit on everyone else's in my home. In this version I tweaked the hole size for the head and flattened the bottom of the print a bit to improve printability and eliminate some of the supports. I believe this should fit any head pretty easily now. One under appreciated part of my work is figuring out how to get a model absolutely maximize the space of a p1s sized printer. In this case of this print, lots of adjustments were made to get it just right. For this hobby (designing and 3d printing models) I certainly go through phases. After filling up all the wall space in a room with Hollow Knight masks, I prioritized new areas. This was a nice break from my current phase which has been pond fountains, I think I have one more of those left in me before switching again. I am experimenting with designing a toy for kids during long car rides, I am excited about it and hope to share it soon!

I tested some of the prints on my Bambu P2S and they printed fine. I used tree supports on the starting textured plate to test the prints. I will be putting together an assembly video and PDF instructions similar to the one I built for the Dark Saber. Here are the Key Notes if you decide to build this sword prior to me getting that out. NOTE 1: I added integrated supports to some of the taller blade pieces to help with printing. These will require light post processing after printing. None of the supports are on an area that will be visable once assembled but will be required to be cut flush and smooth for proper glue up. See examples below: NOTE 2: This model will require assembly using a strong glue. I recommend THIS GLUE ( This is an amazon affiliate link and I do receive a kick back if purchased from this link) NOTE 3: It is very important to note that when assembling the inner white diffuser pieces, that you leave a 0.100" GAP so the LED light strip can fit into the channel. This gap is what holds the light strip in places and also allows it to be pushed though the blade. I have a plan to improve upon this design for v2.0, but it does work fine if you line everything up properly. NOTE 4: Once the blade is fully assembled with the white diffusers and the outer blade, there are 2 bolt holes that accept m3x28mm screws and m3 nuts. These are here to add a mechanical connection to hold the hilt and blade together without relying only on the 3D printed Threaded Connection NOTE 5: Here is the layout for the electronics in the hilt. Once you are ready to connect the LED strip inside the blade to the Hilt, you must pay careful attention that the wire does not get caught in the threaded connection. Make sure all excess wire is tucked into the hilt and doesnt get crushed between any connection points. NOTE 6: There is also a notch on the Inner Hilt that will line up with the cutout on the “Hilt Wrap” This should keep the piece from spinning. This will also line up the motion board “Reset Port” correctly.

description: Wax seals are fantastic at adding a level of class to letters, in sealing envelopes, or for attatching tags to brithday and christmas presents. Personally I plan on using them for creating immersive TTRPG props for my D&D game, so that I can hand them printed notices ( like these free ones ). Unfortunately, having a wax seal stamp design for every occasion, affiliation, or character can get expensive… so why not design and 3D print them? This is my first attempt at creating a design using one of my illustrations for Fantastical Geographic's debut . This design uses measurements taken from a proper wood and metal wax seal stamp so that the proportions of your seal will be similar, but also so that you can simply swap out the head and handle as you see fit as these are modeled separately. Or if you have a lot of metal stamp heads already you could simply want some fancy handles to accompany them instead of swapping things out. The head design and print profile have been optimized for 0.2mm nozzles as my experiments showed this yielded the best results. The head prints face up and uses ironing to create a smooth stamping surface for easy release, however, it is IMPORTANT to note that your ironing settings may need adjusting as this varies depending on printer, filament type, filament brand, and filament color! I've opted for PLA as it's the most accessible for many printers. If you are interested in reading my experiments I will be uploading a full write-up on my website of how I achieved the cleanest wax seal and release of the stamp (link to come). The TLDR is: 0.2 mm nozzle Head printed face up with ironing on 0.08mm layer height. 50% Infill 100% cooling Release Agent - A thin layer applied with an old brush Pre-cooling - Place the stamp in the freezer for 10-15 minutes (make sure to apply release agent first) Wait - Leave the stamp in the wax for about 1 minute before gently peeling off Additional Notes: I have included a 0.4mm nozzle profile, however, I was not able to get the ironing as smooth as the 0.2mm. It is there primarily for printing the handle, which doesn't require the high detail. These results were achieved with a tuned PLA filament profile for my machine. Your mileage may vary.

model_name: Mandalorian Grav Charge With Lightup Mod (Breach)
description: This is my version of the Grav Charge and holder from the show The Mandalorian. I designed it looking at pictures from the show to be as accurate as I could but also be a light up prop. To that end I designed it around these little magnet operated light up warning lights: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0CMTJQRYX . The lights have a reed sensor in them that when the magnet is on the back they don't do anything but when you remove the magnet they light up. And the pattern is similar to the actual grav charge, close enough without needing expensive electronics or wiring anything. The back of the holder has some indents of 15mm magnets. Glue some magnets to the back and that will be strong enough to keep the light off. When you pull the grav charge off the holder the reed switch turns the unit on and the lights start to flash then after about 10 seconds go to the circular pattern. I added magnets on the bottom of the grav charges themselves also so you can still stick it to something like in the show but without affecting the light. Place it back on the holder and it turns back off. I went with these lights because they also turn themselves off after a couple minutes so they won't kill the battery if you leave them out. Print Details I printed the body and holder in Bambu ABS - Silver. The body has scarf seam turned on in its object settings which leaves less of a seam on the outside but does sometime affect the color slightly in that spot. If you are going to paint them leave scarf seam on, if you are going to leave them as is you may want to turn that off so the color is more consistent but the seam will be more noticeable. The cover is Bambu PETG Translucent Clear that I then used a red Sharpie oil based paint pen on because I couldn't find a good clear red filament. The combination ended up looking really good so that's what I would recommend or even possibly just a red marker. For printing the cover I have the speeds set to 20mm/s and a custom Bambu Transparent PETG setting that turns off cooling. It's the only way to get a mostly clear lens but you can of course use standard settings, the lens just might not be as clear and the LEDs won't be as distinguishable. Or you can buy a after market clear lens sized for about 28mm. I tried to optimize the print so no supports are required and the 2 x 4 magnets on the bottom should be press fit although I'd add a dab of glue behind them. The holder for the light also is press fit but you can also glue that in to be more secure. Since the lights turn themselves off the batteries should last for years so personally I glued them in.

description: A fully 3d printed Single-shot Cap-powered BB pistol! Fully 3d printed springs. Has 10 bodies to print, can fit on an a1 build plate at minimum. Semi-auto hammer and trigger system though it is single shot. hammer action works well. The larger spring is the hammer spring, simply slot into the holes in the hammer and the main body. The smaller spring is the Trigger spring, do the same. The two main halves of the pistol snap together, may need a spot of glue on the joints. To use, get a standard 8-shot ring cap, then cut off an individual cap using a utility knife, being careful with fingers. Break the barrel (shown in images) by pressing the barrel release latch (shown in images as well) on the left hand side of the pistol body, then lift the barrel, tilting it upwards from the end near the hammer. Load the singular cap into the recess at the end of the barrel, making sure it sits snug. To lock the barrel, manually push the barrel release latch now protruding from the right hand side back into its original position. this can be fiddly ads the hole is quite precise. This is a muzzle loader-so from the muzzle, cut out a small square of tissue. Place it on the muzzle and get a standard 6mm BB. place the BB on top of the tissue wad and using a blunt skewer, ram the BB and the wad into the barrel until you feel it stop (do not ram too hard as the cap holder will snap). Then you are ready to fire! To reset the trigger, pull the hammer back manually and hold it, then let go of the trigger and it should spring back into place. You can pull it gently to help with this. *DISCLAIMER* I am not at fault for misuse of this toy causing damage to living beings and surroundings. Be responsible with this toy-never point at any living being , fire with Adult supervision and at a fixed target. Consider wearing Eye pro if necessary. Remember, this is a TOY ONLY and should be used extremely sensibly only in the right conditions.

description: Description A modular cyberpunk / sci-fi gauntlet armor kit designed to turn a simple glove into a futuristic wearable cosplay prop. The model includes separate armor plates for the fingers, thumb, knuckles, back of the hand and wrist area. The pieces are printed separately and then glued onto a real glove. I used a fleece glove, but the parts can be attached to many types of fabric gloves depending on surface, flexibility and glue compatibility. I also included a raw full-glove reference file with all parts placed together, so you can see where each element is intended to go before assembly. This file is mainly for placement reference; for printing, use the separated armor parts / print profile. Sizing / Scaling This gauntlet was designed for my hand size: 20 cm from the wrist crease to the tip of the middle finger . To resize it for your hand, measure the same distance on your own hand and use this formula: Scale (%) = Your hand length / 20 cm × 100 Examples: 18 cm hand → 18 / 20 × 100 = 90% 19 cm hand → 19 / 20 × 100 = 95% 21 cm hand → 21 / 20 × 100 = 105% 22 cm hand → 22 / 20 × 100 = 110% Apply the same scale to all armor parts so the proportions stay consistent. Hand width, finger thickness and glove stretch can vary, so I recommend printing one or two finger plates first and testing the placement before printing the full set. Assembly Print the separate armor plates. Place the parts on the glove and check the full layout before gluing. Start with the larger hand and wrist pieces, then continue with the fingers and thumb. Glue the parts onto the glove one by one. I used hot glue for assembly. Be careful: hot glue can pass through thin fabric and burn your hand. I recommend wearing a second glove underneath the glove you are working on while positioning and pressing the parts. Test each part placement before gluing permanently. Printing Notes The included print profile has support settings tuned for easy removal. The model does use supports, but in my test print they came off cleanly and without much effort. Geralt’s steel sword from The Witcher game series, designed for slaying humans. The silver sword consists of a total of 14 3D-printed parts. Like the other swords from my production, this sword is assembled using an M5 threaded rod that runs through the entire length of the sword. Everything is fully concealed and not visible anywhere. Thanks to the use of the threaded rod, the sword is very sturdy, suitable even for fencing, and will not break. All parts of the sword are connected by an M5 threaded rod with a length of 1000mm , which runs through the center of all components. M5 lock nuts are installed at both ends of the threaded rod. One M5 nut is located in the Blade_4 part, and the other in the Pommel part. Start screwing the threaded rod into the Blade_1 part until the end of the rod is 974 mm from the bottom of the Blade_1 part . Then slide the remaining parts onto the threaded rod according to the assembly drawing. The nut in the Blade_1 and Pommel parts are embedded during printing. To insert the nut, a pause is created in the print profile, allowing the nut to be placed into the 3D print. Blade_1 and Pommel are printed on a separate build plate in order to minimize potential losses in case the nut insertion into the 3D print is unsuccessful. For the first time on this sword, an improved anti-rotation system has been used to prevent the blade sections from twisting relative to each other. The alignment pins are now integrated directly into the printed parts, so there is no need to print and insert them separately. Enjoy the print, and I hope you like Geralt the Witcher’s silver sword.
